cards.statement: A bank should verify identity with whichever documents the client finds easiest to supply, because the most widely available documents give the most reliable evidence.
cards.explanation: The best documents for verifying identity are those that are most difficult to obtain illicitly or to forge, not those that are most convenient or widely available.
cards.originalText: Identity is verified with whichever documents the client finds easiest to supply, because the most widely available documents give the most reliable evidence.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
cards.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.statement: A bank's head office should be able to require every branch and subsidiary to search its files against specified lists of persons suspected of aiding money laundering or terrorist financing, and to report any matches.
cards.explanation: The Basel Committee guidelines expect head office to be able to require all branches and subsidiaries to search their files against specified lists or requests.
cards.originalText: Head oﬀice can require every branch and subsidiary to search its files against specified lists of persons suspected of aiding ML or FT, and to report any matches.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
cards.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.statement: Branches and subsidiaries should send head office information on higher-risk customers only in response to a specific head-office request, to limit cross-border data flows.
cards.explanation: Information on higher-risk customers should be sent to head office proactively, not only on request.
cards.originalText: Branches and subsidiaries send head oﬀice information on higher-risk customers only in response to a specific head-oﬀice request, to limit cross-border data flows.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
cards.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.statement: Significant customer relationships are monitored on a consolidated basis for on-balance-sheet accounts only, while assets under management and fiduciary holdings stay with each local office.
cards.explanation: Consolidated monitoring of significant customer relationships includes off-balance-sheet items, assets under management and fiduciary holdings.
cards.originalText: Significant customer relationships are monitored on a consolidated basis for on-balance-sheet accounts only; assets under management and fiduciary holdings stay with each local oﬀice.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
cards.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.statement: To respect local autonomy, a group AML/CFT officer coordinates strategy but cannot give orders to foreign subsidiaries, relying on their annual self-certification instead of on-site visits.
cards.explanation: The group AML/CFT officer is empowered to give orders group-wide and verifies compliance through regular on-site visits.
cards.originalText: To respect local autonomy, the group oﬀicer coordinates the strategy but cannot give orders to foreign subsidiaries, relying on their annual self-certification instead of on-site visits.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
cards.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.statement: A financial group with banking, securities and insurance businesses should monitor and share customer identity and account activity information across all businesses, watch for customers who use services in more than one sector, and apply sector-appropriate AML/CFT requirements when cross-selling.
cards.explanation: Mixed financial groups should be able to monitor and share information on customer identity, transactions and accounts across the entire group, adjusting requirements to each sector.
cards.originalText: The group monitors and shares customer identity and account activity across all three businesses, watches for customers who use services in more than one sector, and applies sector-appropriate AML/CFT requirements when cross-selling.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
cards.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.statement: In a financial group with banking, securities and insurance businesses, each business monitors only its own customers, and information walls prevent customer data from being shared anywhere within the group.
cards.explanation: The group must monitor and share customer information across banking, securities and insurance businesses.
cards.originalText: Each business monitors only its own customers, and information walls between banking, securities and insurance prevent customer data from being shared anywhere within the group.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
cards.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.statement: When the legal minimum CDD requirements in a host country are lower than those of the home country, the host office applies the host-country minimum, because it must always follow host-country law and practice.
cards.explanation: A lower host-country minimum does not lower the standard. The host office applies the higher standard, which is normally that of the home country.
cards.originalText: Because Country L’s legal minimum is lower, the insurance subsidiary applies Country L’s minimum CDD requirements, since a host oﬀice must always follow host-country law and practice.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
cards.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.statement: Because its businesses belong to one group, a financial group must apply identical AML/CFT requirements in every sector, whatever the differences in activities and customer relationships.
cards.explanation: Differences between sectors may justify variations in the AML/CFT requirements applied.
cards.originalText: Because the three businesses belong to one group, identical AML/CFT requirements must be applied in every sector, whatever the differences in their activities and customer relationships.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
cards.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.statement: A correspondent bank should risk-rate each respondent individually against a set of risk indicators and set the intensity of due diligence and monitoring according to the rating, since relationships differ in risk.
cards.explanation: The Basel Committee guidelines apply a risk-based approach to correspondent banking and recognise that not all correspondent relationships bear the same level of risk.
cards.originalText: Each respondent is risk-rated individually against a set of risk indicators, and the intensity of due diligence and monitoring follows the rating, since relationships differ in risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
cards.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.statement: A correspondent bank should treat respondents that are licensed and supervised in their home country as low risk by default and rely on that licence instead of its own assessment of each respondent.
cards.explanation: A licence says nothing about whether the respondent's AML/CFT standards are as strict as the bank's, and reliance never replaces the bank's own assessment.
cards.originalText: Respondents licensed and supervised in their home country are treated as low risk by default, so the bank relies on that licence instead of its own assessment of each respondent.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
cards.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.statement: All respondent banks should receive identical due diligence, because correspondent banking is classed as uniformly high risk.
cards.explanation: Not all correspondent relationships bear the same risk, so due diligence should be differentiated and risk-based.
cards.originalText: All respondents receive identical due diligence, because correspondent banking is classed as uniformly high risk and differentiated treatment would breach group-wide consistency.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.loText: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context.
cards.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
cards.statement: Payments routed through respondent banks should be monitored only above a fixed value threshold, because the respondents' own CDD already covers their customers' smaller transactions.
cards.explanation: Monitoring should cover all transactions, and small terrorist-financing payments are exactly what a value threshold misses.
cards.originalText: Payments routed through respondents are monitored only above a fixed value threshold, because the respondents’ own CDD already covers their customers’ smaller transactions.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: A one-million rise in direct costs lowers a unit's RAROC by exactly as much as a one-million fall in expected revenues, both effects being reduced by the factor (1 - t) for the tax rate t.
cards.explanation: Every pre-tax item in the RAROC numerator, revenues, costs, funding charge and expected loss, moves RAROC one-for-one before the after-tax factor (1 - t), divided by economic capital.
cards.originalText: A one-million rise in direct costs would lower RAROC by exactly as much as a one-million fall in expected revenues, both effects reduced by the factor $(1 - t)$.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: A higher funding charge transferred from treasury raises a unit's RAROC, because transfer-pricing charges enter the numerator alongside the return on risk capital.
cards.explanation: The funding charge is a cost charged to the business unit and is subtracted in the numerator, so a higher charge lowers RAROC.
cards.originalText: A higher funding charge transferred from treasury would raise RAROC, because transfer-pricing charges enter the numerator alongside the return on risk capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: A rise in a unit's expected loss leaves its RAROC unchanged, because expected loss is priced into the spread and no risk capital is held against it.
cards.explanation: No economic capital is held against expected loss, but expected loss is still subtracted in the numerator, so a higher expected loss lowers RAROC.
cards.originalText: A one-million rise in expected loss would leave RAROC unchanged, because expected loss is priced into the spread and no risk capital is held against it.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Before the 1995 Amendment to Basel I, two offsetting swaps with the same counterparty each attracted an add-on, which discouraged hedging; once master agreements were judged enforceable, bilateral netting could reduce credit equivalent amounts.
cards.explanation: The original Basel I gave almost no credit for netting because master agreements had not yet been shown to be enforceable. The 1995 Amendment allowed bilateral netting to reduce credit equivalent amounts.
cards.originalText: Before 1995, two offsetting swaps with the same counterparty each attracted an add-on, which discouraged hedging; once master agreements were judged enforceable, bilateral netting could reduce credit equivalent amounts.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel I netting rules, a net negative market value with one counterparty may be offset against positive exposures to other counterparties, provided each relationship is covered by its own master agreement.
cards.explanation: Netting is bilateral. A negative value with one counterparty can only be netted against positive exposures to that same counterparty.
cards.originalText: A net negative market value with one counterparty may be offset against positive exposures to other counterparties, provided each relationship is covered by its own master agreement.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The net replacement ratio divides current exposure without netting by current exposure with netting, so it is at least one and scales the add-ons up.
cards.explanation: The NRR is current exposure with netting divided by current exposure without netting, so it is at most one and scales the add-ons down.
cards.correction: The net replacement ratio divides current exposure with netting by current exposure without netting, so it is at most one and scales the add-ons down.

changes.from: divides current exposure without netting by current exposure with netting, so it is at least one and scales the add-ons up
changes.to: divides current exposure with netting by current exposure without netting, so it is at most one and scales the add-ons down

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: When the net replacement ratio is zero, the add-on for potential future exposure falls to zero, because fully offsetting positions cannot create exposure later.
cards.explanation: The netting-adjusted add-on keeps a fixed 40% of its gross amount, so even at a zero net replacement ratio the add-on is not eliminated.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel 2.5 kept the 1996 VaR-based charge and added a stressed VaR term with its own maximum and multiplier.
cards.explanation: Basel 2.5 (end 2011) added stressed VaR on top of the 1996 VaR term, so with equal multipliers the charge at least doubled.
cards.originalText: Basel 2.5 kept the 1996 VaR term and added a stressed VaR term with its own maximum and multiplier, so with equal multipliers the charge at least doubled.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel II replaced the 1996 internal-models VaR with a stressed VaR calibrated to the most stressful year of the previous seven, alongside its three pillars.
cards.explanation: Basel II left the 1996 market risk rules in place. Stressed VaR was introduced in Basel 2.5, at the end of 2011.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The Fundamental Review of the Trading Book keeps both the 10-day 99% VaR and the stressed VaR, scaled from one-day changes with the square-root-of-10 rule, and adds liquidity horizons.
cards.explanation: FRTB replaces VaR and stressed VaR with expected shortfall and uses overlapping 10-day changes rather than square-root-of-10 scaling.
cards.originalText: FRTB keeps both the 10-day 99% VaR and the stressed VaR, scaled from one-day changes with the square-root-of-10 rule, and adds liquidity horizons.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel III added the incremental risk charge, a one-year 99.9% VaR that replaced the stressed VaR for all positions held in the trading book.
cards.explanation: The incremental risk charge came with Basel 2.5, applies to credit-sensitive trading-book positions, and is added to the stressed VaR, not substituted for it.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 input floors, the 5 bp PD floor applies to large corporates under the foundation IRB approach, whereas LGD and EAD floors bind only under the advanced IRB approach.
cards.explanation: PD floors apply under both F-IRB and A-IRB, but the LGD and EAD floors are applicable only in A-IRB approaches, since F-IRB uses supervisory LGD and EAD.
cards.originalText: The 5 bp PD floor applies to the large corporates under the foundation IRB approach, whereas LGD and EAD floors bind only on the advanced IRB portfolios.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 input floors, LGD floors apply under both the foundation and the advanced IRB approach, and a partially secured exposure takes the secured LGD floor on its whole amount.
cards.explanation: LGD floors apply only under A-IRB, and a partially secured exposure takes a weighted average of the unsecured floor on the unsecured part and the secured floor on the secured part.
cards.originalText: The LGD floors apply under both the foundation and the advanced IRB approach, and a partially secured exposure takes the secured LGD floor on its whole amount.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 input floors, QRRE revolvers face the same 5 bp PD floor as QRRE transactors, and unsecured QRRE exposures face a 30% LGD floor.
cards.explanation: QRRE revolvers face a 10 bp PD floor, higher than the 5 bp floor for transactors, and the unsecured QRRE LGD floor is 50%.
cards.originalText: QRRE revolvers face the same 5 bp PD floor as QRRE transactors, and unsecured QRRE exposures face a 30% LGD floor.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 input floors, the EAD floor equals the on-balance-sheet exposure plus 100% of the off-balance-sheet exposure, so no credit conversion factor below one may be applied.
cards.explanation: The EAD floor is the on-balance-sheet exposure plus 50% of the off-balance-sheet exposure, using the standardized approach credit conversion factors.
cards.originalText: The EAD floor equals the on-balance-sheet exposure plus 100% of the off-balance-sheet exposure, so no credit conversion factor below one may be applied.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: After the December 2017 reforms, internal ratings remain available for some exposures, such as retail and specialised lending, but no longer for equities, and all remaining internal models face the output floor.
cards.explanation: A-IRB was removed for banks, other financial institutions and large corporates, and IRB approaches were removed for equities. Retail and specialised lending keep internal estimates.
cards.originalText: Internal ratings remain available for some exposures, such as retail and specialised lending, but no longer for equities; all remaining models face the output floor.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 reforms, a bank may retain the advanced measurement approach for operational risk if it holds more than ten years of high-quality internal loss data.
cards.explanation: The AMA was replaced for all banks by the new standardized approach, whatever the amount of loss data held. Ten years is the window used for the loss component of the new approach.
cards.originalText: The AMA may be retained for operational risk, since the bank holds more than ten years of high-quality internal loss data.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 reforms, a bank may retain an internal CVA model if its non-centrally cleared derivatives notional is EUR 100 billion or less.
cards.explanation: Internal models for CVA were removed. The EUR 100 billion threshold allows a simple multiplier of the counterparty credit risk charge, not an internal model.
cards.originalText: The internal CVA model may be retained, provided the bank’s non-centrally cleared derivatives notional is EUR 100 billion or less.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 reforms, the advanced IRB approach may be retained for exposures to banks and large corporates, provided the new PD, LGD and EAD input floors are applied.
cards.explanation: Input floors constrain the models that remain. They do not restore A-IRB for banks and large corporates, which must use F-IRB or the standardized approach.
cards.originalText: The A-IRB approach may be retained for exposures to banks and large corporates, provided the new PD, LGD and EAD input floors are applied.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: The Basel II output floor was set at 80% of Basel I capital requirements and was applied inconsistently across countries, whereas the new floor is based on the revised Basel III standardized approaches.
cards.explanation: The Basel II floor was calibrated at 80% of the relevant Basel I requirements. The new floor is 72.5% of the RWA computed using only the revised standardized approaches.
cards.originalText: The Basel II floor was set at 80% of Basel I capital requirements and was applied inconsistently across countries; the new floor is based on the revised Basel III standardised approaches.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: The Basel II output floor was set at 72.5% of Basel I capital requirements, and the new floor raises the calibration to 80% of the RWA under the revised standardized approaches.
cards.explanation: The calibrations are swapped. The Basel II floor was 80% of Basel I requirements, and the new floor is 72.5% of standardized-approach RWA.
cards.originalText: The Basel II floor was set at 72.5% of Basel I capital requirements; the new floor raises the calibration to 80% of the RWA under the revised standardised approaches.
cards.correction: The Basel II output floor was set at 80% of Basel I capital requirements, and the new floor lowers the calibration to 72.5% of the RWA under the revised standardized approaches.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: The new output floor limits a bank's RWA to no more than 72.5% of the RWA calculated using only the standardized approaches.
cards.explanation: It is a floor, not a cap. A bank's RWA cannot fall below 72.5% of the RWA calculated using only the standardized approaches.
cards.originalText: The new floor limits a bank’s RWA to no more than 72.5% of the RWA calculated using only the standardised approaches.
cards.correction: The new output floor requires a bank's RWA to be at least 72.5% of the RWA calculated using only the standardized approaches.

changes.from: limits a bank's RWA to no more than
changes.to: requires a bank's RWA to be at least

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: The new output floor applies only to banks using the advanced IRB approach, since banks on the foundation IRB approach already use supervisory LGD and EAD values.
cards.explanation: The floor applies to the total RWA of any bank using internal models. F-IRB banks still estimate PD themselves, and market risk models also count.
cards.originalText: The new floor applies only to banks using the advanced IRB approach, since banks on the foundation IRB approach already use supervisory LGD and EAD values.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: Automated transaction monitoring should be calibrated so that alert volumes are manageable and can be reviewed and assessed in a timely way.
cards.explanation: Alerts that cannot be reviewed provide no control. In the USAA case a system that was too sensitive left roughly 90,000 unreviewed alerts and about 6,900 unreviewed cases.
cards.originalText: Automated monitoring should be calibrated so that alert volumes are manageable and can be reviewed and assessed in a timely way.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: A more sensitive transaction monitoring system is always preferable, because more alerts mean better detection.
cards.explanation: Excess alerts create a backlog that weakens the control. Sensitivity without review capacity does not improve detection.
cards.originalText: A more sensitive monitoring system is always preferable because more alerts mean better detection.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: Regulators impose AML fines only after a specific theft or laundering case has been proven at the institution.
cards.explanation: Regulators can fine an institution for an inadequate AML program, as in the USAA FSB case, even without a proven theft or laundering case.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: Using third-party contractors to review alerts removes the need to train staff in AML matters.
cards.explanation: Contractors reviewing alerts must be trained and qualified. USAA used untrained contractors because of understaffing, which worsened its problems.
cards.originalText: Using third‑party contractors to review alerts removes the need to train staff in AML matters.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: Heavy regulatory fines are typically the result of years of accumulated failings and delay in acting on regulatory findings.
cards.explanation: The USAA FSB fine followed deficiencies that persisted from 2016 to 2021, so timely remediation of regulatory findings is the key lesson.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: Training and staffing are secondary to the technology used in monitoring transactions.
cards.explanation: Inadequate staffing and training were cited deficiencies, and the new technology itself created an unmanageable alert backlog.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: Regulatory fines for AML failures are typically unpredictable and not linked to accumulated failings in the AML program.
cards.explanation: Fines are typically linked to accumulated, unremedied failings, as in the USAA FSB case.
cards.originalText: Regulatory fines are typically unpredictable and not linked to accumulated failings in AML programs.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: Procuring a highly sensitive transaction monitoring system and accepting a backlog of unreviewed alerts is an appropriate way to strengthen an AML control environment.
cards.explanation: A system that generates a backlog of unreviewed alerts replicates the USAA failure rather than fixing it.
cards.originalText: Procure a transaction monitoring system that is highly sensitive, accepting a backlog of unreviewed alerts.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: Conducting Service Organization Control (SOC) audits of third-party providers on an annual basis is an appropriate way to strengthen third-party risk management in an AML control environment.
cards.explanation: Weak third-party risk management was a cited deficiency in the USAA case.
cards.originalText: Conduct SOC (Service Organization Control) audits of third‑party providers on an annual basis.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: Providing AML training to third-party contractors and verifying their qualifications before they review alerts is an appropriate way to strengthen an AML control environment.
cards.explanation: USAA failed to train or qualify the contractors who reviewed its alerts.
cards.originalText: Provide AML training to any third‑party contractors and verify their qualifications before they review alerts.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: In the USAA Bank case, regulators fined the bank for failing, over an extended period, to correct deficiencies they had identified in its management and reporting of suspicious transactions.
cards.explanation: The fine followed years of an ineffective BSA/AML program and a failure to remediate regulator-identified deficiencies, not a specific crime.
cards.originalText: USAA Bank was fined for failing to correct deficiencies identified by regulators in its management and reporting of suspicious transactions after an extended period of time.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: USAA Bank was fined after many retail bankers were found to have opened unwanted accounts for existing customers in order to meet performance incentives.
cards.explanation: That describes the Wells Fargo unauthorized-accounts scandal. USAA was fined for an ineffective AML program.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: USAA Federal Savings Bank was fined in 2022 because it had an ineffective AML program and inadequate AML controls over several years, not because of a specific theft or laundering loss.
cards.explanation: The penalty covered at least five years, 2016 to 2021, of an AML program that failed BSA minimum requirements.
cards.originalText: The bank had an ineffective AML program and inadequate AML controls over several years, even though no specific theft or laundering loss was the basis of the fine.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
cards.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
cards.statement: A backlog of unreviewed alerts led to a significant theft of funds at USAA Federal Savings Bank in 2021, which was the basis of its fine.
cards.explanation: The alert backlog was cited, but no theft of funds was the basis of the fine, which was imposed for an ineffective AML program.
cards.originalText: A backlog of unreviewed alerts led to a significant theft of funds in 2021.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: An outsourced HR agency advertising jobs without regard to existing labor laws is a compliance risk for the bank.
cards.explanation: Compliance risk arises when the service provider does not operate in compliance with relevant laws and regulations.
cards.originalText: Advertising jobs without regard to existing labor laws.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Negative public opinion caused by the poor performance of outsourced activities is a compliance risk.
cards.explanation: Negative public perception from substandard performance by the provider is reputational risk.
cards.originalText: Negative public opinion because of poor performance of outsourced activities.
cards.correction: Negative public opinion caused by the poor performance of outsourced activities is a reputational risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Delays in service delivery by an outsourced provider are a compliance risk.
cards.explanation: Service delays are an execution failure, which is operational risk, not a breach of law or regulation.
cards.originalText: Delays in service delivery.
cards.correction: Delays in service delivery by an outsourced provider are an operational risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Reputational, operational and compliance risks are among the risks a bank should consider before deciding to outsource an activity.
cards.explanation: The guidance names six outsourcing risks: compliance, concentration, reputational, country, operational and legal.
cards.originalText: Reputational, operational, and compliance risks

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Public criticism of an outsourcing provider for legal violations and poor service delivery exposes the bank that chose it to reputational risk.
cards.explanation: Substandard service and public criticism of the provider damage how the public views the bank that chose it, which is reputational risk.
cards.originalText: Reputational risk

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: After an activity is outsourced, senior management remains responsible for the normal functioning of the bank.
cards.explanation: Outsourcing transfers the task, not accountability. The board and senior management remain responsible for ensuring outsourced activities are safe, sound and compliant.
cards.originalText: After the outsourcing of an activity, senior management is still responsible for normal functioning of the bank.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: After an activity is outsourced, all responsibility for it is transferred to the third party.
cards.explanation: Responsibility is never fully transferred. Using service providers does not relieve the board and senior management of responsibility.
cards.originalText: After the outsourcing of an activity, all responsibility with regard to outsourced activities is transferred to the third party.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A bank cannot outsource accounting services.
cards.explanation: Accounting is a commonly outsourced activity named in the guidance.
cards.originalText: It is not possible to outsource accounting services.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: The first step in an outsourcing program is a risk assessment to decide whether an activity is best executed in-house or by a third party.
cards.explanation: The risk assessment comes first because it decides whether outsourcing is appropriate at all. Due diligence, contract terms, oversight and contingency planning follow.
cards.originalText: Perform a risk assessment to decide whether the activity is best executed in‑house or by a third party.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Performing due diligence on a service provider's financial condition and internal controls is the first step a bank should take when considering outsourcing an activity.
cards.explanation: Due diligence is performed when selecting a provider, after the risk assessment has shown that outsourcing is appropriate.
cards.originalText: Perform due diligence on ICAP’s financial condition and internal controls.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A bank following the guidance on managing outsourcing risk should avoid outsourcing risk management activities, especially interest rate risk and model risk, because they are core competencies.
cards.explanation: The guidance permits outsourcing aspects of risk management, such as interest rate risk and model risk, provided evidence and validation are consistent with existing guidance.
cards.originalText: Cityace should avoid outsourcing risk management activities, especially interest rate risk and model risk, because these are core competencies

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: If an outsourcing service provider is foreign-based, a U.S. bank following the guidance should ensure that the provider complies with applicable U.S. laws, regulations and regulatory guidance.
cards.explanation: Foreign-based providers must comply with the applicable U.S. laws and guidance.
cards.originalText: If the service provider is foreign‑based, Cityace should ensure the provider is in compliance with applicable U.S. laws, regulations, and regulatory guidance

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A bank following the guidance on managing outsourcing risk should ensure an effective process is in place to review and approve any incentive compensation embedded in service provider contracts.
cards.explanation: Embedded incentive compensation can encourage imprudent behavior, so the guidance requires an effective review and approval process.
cards.originalText: Cityace should ensure an effective process is in place to review and approve any incentive compensation that may be embedded in service provider contracts

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: The risks a bank should especially consider in outsourcing are compliance, concentration, reputational, country, operational and legal risks.
cards.explanation: These are the six outsourcing risks listed in the guidance.
cards.originalText: Cityace should consider especially the following risks in outsourcing: compliance risks, concentration risks, reputational risks, country risks, operational risks, and legal risks

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A bank should ensure that an effective process exists to review and approve any incentive compensation embedded in a vendor contract, considering whether it could encourage imprudent selling.
cards.explanation: A vendor selling products on the bank's behalf represents the bank, so its incentive structure matters for mis-selling and reputational risk.
cards.originalText: The bank should ensure an effective process exists to review and approve any incentive compensation embedded in the vendor contract, considering whether it could encourage imprudent selling.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A bank should ensure that a vendor's sales representatives are compensated mainly with commissions from the sale of the bank's products.
cards.explanation: Commission-heavy pay is an example of an inappropriate incentive that encourages imprudent selling.
cards.originalText: The bank should ensure that the vendor’s sales representatives are compensated mainly with commissions from the sale of the bank’s products.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A bank should prevent a third-party vendor from having access to any of its critical processes.
cards.explanation: A blanket ban is not required. Risk is managed through due diligence, contract terms and ongoing monitoring.
cards.originalText: The bank should prevent the third‑party vendor from having access to any of its critical processes.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A bank should be responsible for developing its vendor's contingency planning process in order to mitigate its risk exposure to the vendor.
cards.explanation: The provider is responsible for its own contingency plans. The bank reviews and tests them and develops its own contingency plans for critical services.
cards.originalText: The bank should be responsible for developing the vendor’s contingency planning process to mitigate risk exposure to the vendor.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: An accidental public disclosure of confidential customer data by an outsourcing provider exposes the bank to compliance risk.
cards.explanation: Disclosing confidential customer data may breach privacy laws and regulations.
cards.originalText: Compliance risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: An accidental public disclosure of confidential customer data by an outsourcing provider exposes the bank to legal risk.
cards.explanation: Affected customers may sue the bank, creating legal exposure and expense.
cards.originalText: Legal risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: An accidental public disclosure of confidential customer data caused by a computer glitch at an outsourcing provider exposes the bank to operational risk.
cards.explanation: The glitch is a failed system or process at the provider, which is operational risk.
cards.originalText: Operational risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: The depth and complexity of a financial institution's outsourcing risk management program can be relatively low when there are few outsourced activities and the service providers are established and reliable.
cards.explanation: The program is risk-based and proportional. Depth and complexity can be lower when outsourced activities are few and providers are established and reliable, and higher when many providers are involved.
cards.originalText: The depth and complexity of the program can be relatively low when there are few outsourced activities and the service providers are established and reliable.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A financial institution's outsourcing risk management program should focus primarily on business continuity and contingency plans, because service provider failure is the dominant risk.
cards.explanation: The program has six elements: risk assessment, due diligence, contract provisions, incentive compensation review, oversight and monitoring, and business continuity and contingency planning. Risk assessment is the crucial first step, and business continuity is only one element.
cards.originalText: The program should focus primarily on business continuity and contingency plans, because service provider failure is the dominant risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A financial institution's outsourcing risk management program should apply the same level of oversight and controls to every outsourced activity, regardless of its materiality.
cards.explanation: Oversight and controls are proportional: they are concentrated on outsourced activities with a material impact rather than applied uniformly to all.
cards.originalText: The program should apply the same level of oversight and controls to every outsourced activity, regardless of its materiality.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: In an outsourcing risk management program, risk assessments should be updated as a result of updated risk mitigation techniques on a sufficiently regular basis.
cards.explanation: The causality runs the other way: risk mitigation techniques are updated as a result of updated risk assessments.
cards.originalText: Risk assessments should be updated as a result of updated risk mitigation techniques on a sufficiently regular basis.
cards.correction: In an outsourcing risk management program, risk mitigation techniques should be updated as a result of updated risk assessments on a sufficiently regular basis.

changes.to: risk mitigation techniques should be updated

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A bank should analyse a prospective service provider's financial condition as part of due diligence, in order to assess the provider's financial stability and viability.
cards.explanation: Financial performance and condition is one of the three core due diligence areas. It shows whether the provider is viable enough to deliver the service over the contract term.
cards.originalText: Yes, in order to assess the financial stability and viability of the service provider.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: When outsourcing to a foreign service provider, a bank should be concerned only with country risk.
cards.explanation: Country risk is only one of several outsourcing risks. Due diligence is not limited to it, and a review of the provider's financial condition is still required.
cards.originalText: No, because the bank should only be concerned with country risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Outsourcing IT services is illegal for a bank.
cards.explanation: Outsourcing IT services is legal. The outsourcing guidance asks banks to manage the associated risks, not to prohibit the activity.
cards.originalText: No, because it is illegal to outsource IT services in the first place.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: The financial review of a prospective service provider examines the potential impact of the provider's past clients on the bank's financial condition.
cards.explanation: The financial review examines the provider's own financial condition and the effect of the bank's business on the provider. It does not examine the effect of the provider's past clients on the bank.
cards.originalText: The potential impact of the provider’s past clients on the bank’s financial condition.
cards.correction: The financial review of a prospective service provider examines the potential impact of the bank's business on the provider's financial condition.

changes.from: the potential impact of the provider's past clients on the bank's financial condition
changes.to: the potential impact of the bank's business on the provider's financial condition

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: The financial review of a prospective service provider includes the adequacy of the provider's insurance coverage.
cards.explanation: Insurance adequacy is an explicit element of the financial review, alongside financial statements, sustainability and commitment of resources.
cards.originalText: The adequacy of the service provider’s insurance coverage.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: The financial review of a prospective service provider includes the adequacy of the provider's own review of the financial condition of its subcontractors.
cards.explanation: The provider's review of its subcontractors' financial condition is an explicit element of the financial review.
cards.originalText: The adequacy of the service provider’s review of the financial condition of any subcontractors.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: The financial review of a prospective service provider includes the potential financial impact of the bank's business on the provider.
cards.explanation: The impact of the bank's relationship on the provider's financial condition is an explicit element of the financial review.
cards.originalText: The potential financial impact of the bank’s business on the provider.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A review of a service provider's operations and internal controls includes the provider's compliance with environmental sustainability standards.
cards.explanation: The operations and internal controls review covers topics such as internal controls, facilities management, training, systems security, privacy protection, record retention, business resumption planning, service support and delivery, and adherence to laws and regulations. Environmental sustainability is not among them.
cards.originalText: Compliance with environmental sustainability standards of the business.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A review of a service provider's operations and internal controls includes its training, including compliance training for staff.
cards.explanation: Training, including compliance training, is an explicit item in the operations and internal controls review.
cards.originalText: Training, including compliance training for staff.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A review of a service provider's operations and internal controls includes its business resumption and contingency planning.
cards.explanation: Business resumption and contingency planning is an explicit item in the operations and internal controls review.
cards.originalText: Business resumption and contingency planning.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A review of a service provider's operations and internal controls includes its service support and delivery.
cards.explanation: Service support and delivery is an explicit item in the operations and internal controls review.
cards.originalText: Service support and delivery.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Due diligence on a third-party service provider should at a minimum include an evaluation of the provider's performance on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors.
cards.explanation: Due diligence covers three areas: business background, reputation and strategy; financial performance and condition; and operations and internal controls. An ESG evaluation is not one of the minimum review elements.
cards.originalText: An evaluation of the service provider’s performance on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Due diligence on a third-party service provider includes ensuring that the provider has an appropriate background check program for its employees.
cards.explanation: Employee background checks are part of the due diligence review of the provider.
cards.originalText: Ensuring the service provider has an appropriate background check program for its employees.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Due diligence on a third-party service provider includes a financial review of the provider's most recent annual report and financial statements.
cards.explanation: Reviewing the provider's financial statements is part of the financial performance and condition area of due diligence.
cards.originalText: A financial review of the service provider’s most recent annual report and financial statements.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Due diligence on a third-party service provider includes an evaluation of the adequacy of the provider's standards, policies and procedures, including adherence to applicable laws, regulations and supervisory guidance.
cards.explanation: This is part of the operations and internal controls area of due diligence.
cards.originalText: An evaluation of the adequacy of standards, policies and procedures, including adherence to applicable laws, regulations and supervisory guidance.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Ascertaining the sufficiency of a service provider's insurance coverage falls under the financial performance and condition category of due diligence.
cards.explanation: Insurance adequacy is listed explicitly as part of the financial review of the provider.
cards.originalText: Financial performance and condition.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Ascertaining the sufficiency of a service provider's insurance coverage falls under the operations and internal controls category of due diligence.
cards.explanation: The operations and internal controls category covers controls, training, security and compliance. Insurance coverage belongs to the financial performance and condition category.
cards.originalText: Operations and internal controls.
cards.correction: Ascertaining the sufficiency of a service provider's insurance coverage falls under the financial performance and condition category of due diligence.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Oversight and monitoring is one of the three categories of due diligence on a service provider.
cards.explanation: The three due diligence categories are business background, reputation and strategy; financial performance and condition; and operations and internal controls. Oversight and monitoring is a separate element of the overall outsourcing risk management program.
cards.originalText: Oversight and monitoring.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A bank may outsource an activity that requires the use of customers' nonpublic personal information, provided the service provider complies with applicable privacy laws and regulations.
cards.explanation: The guidance does not prohibit outsourcing that involves customer information. The contract must require the provider to comply with privacy laws and protect the confidentiality of customer information.
cards.originalText: Yes, the bank could outsource an activity which requires usage of nonpublic personal information, but the service provider must comply with applicable privacy laws and regulation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: All outsourcing activities that can reasonably be expected to expose customers' nonpublic personal information are forbidden.
cards.explanation: There is no blanket prohibition. Such outsourcing is permitted if the contract requires the provider to comply with privacy laws and safeguard the data.
cards.originalText: No, all outsourcing activities that can reasonably be expected to expose nonpublic personal information are forbidden.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: The cost and compensation provision of a service provider contract should cover the compensation, variable charges and fees for non-recurring items and special requests, and state which party pays legal, audit and examination fees and equipment-related expenses.
cards.explanation: Cost and compensation terms should be comprehensive, covering all forms of compensation and explicitly assigning responsibility for the associated fees and expenses.
cards.originalText: The compensation, variable charges, and any fees for non‑recurring items and special requests, together with which party pays legal, audit and examination fees and equipment‑related expenses.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Under the cost and compensation provision of a service provider contract, incentive terms should be left to the provider because the institution should not review how the provider is paid.
cards.explanation: The institution should be able to review incentives such as variable charges and commissions, to make sure they do not encourage imprudent risk-taking.
cards.originalText: The compensation to be paid, with incentive terms left to the provider because the institution should not review how the provider is paid.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A loss waterfall allocation mechanism, including a credit value adjustment for website downtime, is a likely provision of an outsourcing contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.explanation: Loss waterfalls and credit value adjustments are credit and counterparty risk constructs, not outsourcing contract provisions.
cards.originalText: Loss waterfall allocation mechanism (including sufficient credit value adjustment for website downtime)

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Confidentiality and security of information is a standard provision of a contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.explanation: The contract must address the confidentiality and security of institution and customer information.
cards.originalText: Confidentiality and security of information

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A business resumption and contingency plan is a standard provision of a contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.explanation: The provider's business resumption and contingency plan should be addressed in the contract.
cards.originalText: Business resumption and contingency plan

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Scope of service, including reference to service level agreements and the ability to subcontract, is a standard provision of a contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.explanation: The scope provision covers the rights and responsibilities of the parties, service levels and subcontracting.
cards.originalText: Scope of service (including reference to service level agreement and ability to subcontract)

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
