cards.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: A contract with a service provider should define the events that are considered a default and give the provider an opportunity to cure a default before the contract is terminated.
cards.explanation: The default and termination provision should define events of default, acceptable remedies and opportunities to cure a default before termination.
cards.originalText: The bank should define specific events that are considered a default under the contract and give the provider an opportunity to resolve a default before terminating the contract.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
cards.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
cards.statement: Under the outsourcing guidance, a service provider agreement 'may' provide for the right to audit, whereas other provisions such as performance standards, indemnification and ownership and license are ones it 'should' provide.
cards.explanation: The right to audit and access to audit reports is framed as optional, whereas the other provisions are expected contract terms.
cards.originalText: Right to audit.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: A loss caused by a control failure at an outsourced service provider is, by source of the risk, classified as third-party risk, and the bank remains accountable for it.
cards.explanation: Risks arising from vendors, contractors and service providers to which activities are outsourced are third-party (outsourcing) risks. Operational risk is only the broad parent category, and cyber risk and compliance risk describe the mechanism and the consequence.
cards.originalText: Third‑party risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Continuous monitoring is the step of the third-party risk management life cycle that keeps track of service provision, quality service level agreements and compliance with regulation.
cards.explanation: Tracking ongoing service delivery, SLAs and compliance is what the continuous monitoring step involves. The other steps decide, vet, contract or exit.
cards.originalText: Continuous monitoring

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Evaluation and risk rating is the step of the third-party risk management life cycle that keeps track of service provision, quality service level agreements and compliance with regulation.
cards.explanation: Evaluation and risk rating is the pre-contract assessment of a provider. Tracking ongoing service provision, SLAs and compliance is the continuous monitoring step.
cards.originalText: Evaluation and risk rating
cards.correction: Continuous monitoring is the step of the third-party risk management life cycle that keeps track of service provision, quality service level agreements and compliance with regulation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Shared assessments is one of the steps in the third-party risk management (TPRM) life cycle.
cards.explanation: Shared Assessments is the organisation that proposed the framework, not a stage in it. The five stages are business model decision; evaluation, risk rating and due diligence; contracts, SLAs and contract management; continuous monitoring; and remediation or termination.
cards.originalText: Shared assessments

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Remediation is a step in the third-party risk management (TPRM) life cycle.
cards.explanation: Remediation or termination is the fifth and last stage of the TPRM life cycle.
cards.originalText: Remediation

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Risk rating and evaluation is a step in the third-party risk management (TPRM) life cycle.
cards.explanation: Evaluation, risk rating and due diligence is the second stage of the TPRM life cycle.
cards.originalText: Risk rating & evaluation

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Continuous monitoring is a step in the third-party risk management (TPRM) life cycle.
cards.explanation: Continuous monitoring is the fourth stage of the TPRM life cycle.
cards.originalText: Continuous monitoring

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: The business model decision is the strategic first step of the third-party risk management cycle, tied to the firm's risk appetite and taken before any provider is assessed.
cards.explanation: This step decides whether to outsource or keep an activity in-house, and the quality and price sought from providers. Later steps assess, formalise and monitor the chosen provider.
cards.originalText: Business model decision

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Having an exit strategy is a good risk management practice of the remediation or termination step of the third-party risk management life cycle.
cards.explanation: Good practices in the final step include a grievance procedure, an exit strategy or termination clause, and a planned wind-down.
cards.originalText: Having an exit strategy

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Establishing limits on outsourcing by third parties is a good risk management practice of the remediation or termination step of the third-party risk management life cycle.
cards.explanation: Limits on a third party's own outsourcing are set in the contract terms, which is the contracts, SLAs and contract management step.
cards.originalText: Establishing limits on the outsourcing by third parties
cards.correction: Establishing limits on outsourcing by third parties is a good risk management practice of the contracts, SLAs and contract management step of the third-party risk management life cycle.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: A data breach is an event that can trigger the reassessment of contracts with third parties.
cards.explanation: Data breaches or incidents are listed triggers for reassessment.
cards.originalText: Data breaches

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: A merger or acquisition is an event that can trigger the reassessment of contracts with third parties.
cards.explanation: A merger or acquisition changes business circumstances and is a listed trigger for reassessment.
cards.originalText: A merger or acquisition

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: A regulatory change is an event that can trigger the reassessment of contracts with third parties.
cards.explanation: Legal or regulatory change is a listed trigger for reassessment.
cards.originalText: Regulatory change

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: The evaluation, risk rating and due diligence step of the third-party risk management cycle requires sound due diligence and verification of third-party service providers.
cards.explanation: Due diligence and verification are the defining tasks of this second step. They are applied proportionally, with more depth for a cloud host of sensitive data than for a one-day trainer.
cards.originalText: Evaluation and risk rating

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: A reduction in the firm's own cost of capital is a common risk arising from the use of third parties.
cards.explanation: Common third-party risks include service disruption, failings in service quality, fraud, privacy breaches or leaks, compliance breaches, espionage and IP theft, and reputational damage. A change in the firm's cost of capital is not among them.
cards.originalText: A reduction in the firm’s own cost of capital

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Service disruption is a common risk arising from the use of third parties.
cards.explanation: Service disruption is a listed common third-party risk.
cards.originalText: Service disruption

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Espionage and intellectual property theft are common risks arising from the use of third parties.
cards.explanation: Espionage and IP theft are listed common third-party risks.
cards.originalText: Espionage and intellectual property theft

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Accidental data privacy breaches and intentional information leaks are common risks arising from the use of third parties.
cards.explanation: Privacy breaches and information leaks are listed common third-party risks.
cards.originalText: Accidental data privacy breach or intentional information leak

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Establishing standards on outsourcing by the third party's own vendors is a good practice when addressing fourth-party risk.
cards.explanation: Fourth parties are the third parties of third parties. The contract should set standards or limits on the outsourcing done by the vendor, largely replicating the firm's own vendor rules.
cards.originalText: Establish standards on outsourcing

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Having audit rights on vendors is an action that should be undertaken during the wind-down process of contracts.
cards.explanation: Audit rights are set up in contracts and used in continuous monitoring to verify vendor compliance. Wind-down actions include transferring intellectual property, planning the transition to in-house or another provider, and evidence of data transfer or destruction.
cards.originalText: Having audit rights on their vendors

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: The transmission of intellectual property is an action that should be undertaken during the wind-down process of contracts.
cards.explanation: Transfer of intellectual property when necessary is an explicit wind-down item.
cards.originalText: The transmission of intellectual property

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Planning the transition to in-house services is an action that should be undertaken during the wind-down process of contracts.
cards.explanation: Transition planning is an explicit wind-down item.
cards.originalText: Plan to transition to in‑house services

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Providing evidence of data transfer or destruction is an action that should be undertaken during the wind-down process of contracts.
cards.explanation: Evidence of data transfer or destruction is an explicit wind-down item.
cards.originalText: Provide evidence of data transfer or destruction

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Deciding which activities to keep in-house and which to outsource to third-party vendors, in light of the firm's risk appetite, falls under the business model decision stage of the third-party risk management life cycle.
cards.explanation: This is the first stage of the life cycle. The other stages presuppose that a specific third party has already been identified.
cards.originalText: business model decisions.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Establishing limits on third-party and fourth-party vendor outsourcing falls under the contracts, service level agreements and contract management step of third-party risk management.
cards.explanation: Contract terms are the opportunity to address fourth-party risk, by setting standards or limits on the outsourcing done by the vendor.
cards.originalText: Contracts, service level agreements, and contract management.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Insurance procurement and claims settlement is one of the life cycle stages of third-party risk management.
cards.explanation: The five stages are business model decision; evaluation, risk rating and due diligence; contracts, SLAs and contract management; ongoing monitoring; and remediation or termination.
cards.originalText: Insurance procurement and claims settlement.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: The business model decision is one of the life cycle stages of third-party risk management.
cards.explanation: It is the first of the five stages, at which the firm decides whether and what to outsource.
cards.originalText: Business model decision.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Ongoing monitoring is one of the life cycle stages of third-party risk management.
cards.explanation: It is the fourth of the five stages and covers monitoring of service quality and compliance.
cards.originalText: Ongoing monitoring.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Remediation or termination is one of the life cycle stages of third-party risk management.
cards.explanation: It is the fifth stage and covers the exit strategy, grievance procedure and wind-down.
cards.originalText: Remediation or termination.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: In the Capital One case, a former employee of the bank's cloud services vendor hacked into customer information stored on the vendor's cloud platform and stole much of it.
cards.explanation: The 2019 breach of data on about 100 million people was carried out by a former employee of the cloud provider who exploited a misconfigured web application firewall. It is a third-party data security failure for which the bank remained accountable.
cards.originalText: A former staff member of the vendor hacked into a database of Capital One’s personal customer information that was stored on the vendor’s cloud services platform and stole much of this information.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: The large loss that Capital One incurred from its relationship with a third-party vendor arose because the vendor provided an inaccurate loan pricing model.
cards.explanation: That would be a model risk event, which did not occur. Capital One's loss arose from a data breach at its cloud services vendor.
cards.originalText: The vendor provided an inaccurate loan pricing model to Capital One, which incurred far greater default losses than expected.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: The large loss that Capital One incurred from its relationship with a third-party vendor arose because a bill payment system provided by the vendor failed for an extended period.
cards.explanation: That describes a prolonged service outage. The Capital One case was a theft of customer data held on a cloud platform.
cards.originalText: A bill payment system provided by the vendor failed for an extended period of time, resulting in many Capital One customers canceling their accounts and causing severe reputational damage.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: The regulatory fine in the Capital One case arose because a vendor's sales manager set extremely high incentives that led to inappropriate products being sold to consumers.
cards.explanation: That would be a mis-selling event. The OCC fined Capital One for failing to establish effective risk assessment before migrating significant IT operations to the cloud.
cards.originalText: The vendor’s sales manager established extremely high incentives for its representatives to sell Capital One products, resulting in regulatory fines for selling inappropriate products to consumers.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Accountability for operational risk is not transferable to a third-party vendor.
cards.explanation: In the Capital One and Morgan Stanley cases the regulator penalised the institutions that outsourced. Functions can be outsourced, but ultimate responsibility and accountability cannot be transferred.
cards.originalText: is not transferable.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: Accountability for operational risk arising from an outsourced activity ultimately rests with the third-party vendor.
cards.explanation: The fines in the Capital One and Morgan Stanley cases fell on the banks, not the vendors. Accountability stays with the firm that outsources.
cards.originalText: ultimately rests with the third‑party vendor.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: In the OCC's 2020 enforcement action against Morgan Stanley over decommissioned data servers, the deficiencies cited included inadequate due diligence on vendors and subcontractors, inadequate monitoring of their performance and no appropriate inventory of customer data stored on the devices.
cards.explanation: The bank failed to assess the risks of decommissioning its hardware and of using third-party vendors including subcontractors. Disposed hardware was later found to still contain customer data.
cards.originalText: Perform due diligence on both the vendor and its subcontractor, monitor their performance during the work, and keep an inventory of the client data stored on each device being decommissioned.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: A contract clause that transfers full liability for any exposure of client data to the vendor removes the bank's accountability for the risk.
cards.explanation: Outsourcing can transfer some of the operational risk of an activity, but accountability for that risk cannot be transferred. A liability clause does not remove the bank's responsibility to regulators or customers.
cards.originalText: Include a contract clause that transfers full liability for any exposure of client data to the vendor, so that the bank is no longer accountable for the risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.
cards.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
cards.statement: A misconfigured web application firewall was the main cause of the data exposure in the OCC's 2020 Morgan Stanley enforcement action.
cards.explanation: The misconfigured web application firewall was the weakness exploited in the Capital One breach. The Morgan Stanley deficiencies concerned hardware decommissioning, oversight of vendors and subcontractors, and the inventory of customer data.
cards.originalText: Focus the review on the configuration of the web application firewall protecting the servers, since a misconfigured firewall was the main cause of the data exposure in that case.
cards.correction: A misconfigured web application firewall was the main cause of the data exposure in the Capital One breach.

changes.from: the OCC's 2020 Morgan Stanley enforcement action

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: The Dodd-Frank Act established the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) as an independent regulator overseeing consumer finance markets.
cards.explanation: The CFPB oversees consumer finance markets such as mortgages, student loans and credit cards. It was created by the Dodd-Frank Act, the US response to the 2007-2009 crisis.
cards.originalText: The Dodd‑Frank Act.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: The Markets in Financial Instruments Directive (MiFID) led to the formation of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).
cards.explanation: MiFID is EU investor protection legislation and has no role in creating a US agency. The CFPB was created by the Dodd-Frank Act.
cards.originalText: The Markets in Financial Instruments Directive (MiFID).
cards.correction: The Dodd-Frank Act led to the formation of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).

changes.from: The Markets in Financial Instruments Directive (MiFID)

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: The Volcker Rule created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).
cards.explanation: The Volcker Rule is a provision of the Dodd-Frank Act that restricts bank proprietary trading. The CFPB was created by another part of the Act.
cards.originalText: The Volcker Rule.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: MiFID II and MiFIR address the definition and independence of investment advice.
cards.explanation: Investment advice definition and independence is an explicit topic of the regime.
cards.originalText: Definition and independence of investment advice.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: MiFID II and MiFIR address best execution of trades for clients.
cards.explanation: Best execution of client trades is an explicit topic of the regime.
cards.originalText: Best execution of trades for clients.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: MiFID II and MiFIR address dealings with eligible counterparties.
cards.explanation: Dealings with eligible counterparties is an explicit topic of the regime.
cards.originalText: Dealings with eligible counterparties.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: The Volcker Rule prevents commercial banks from engaging in speculative and proprietary trading.
cards.explanation: The Volcker Rule is part of the Dodd-Frank Act. It prevents commercial banks from speculative proprietary trading for profit and limits their investments in hedge funds and private equity funds.
cards.originalText: Stopping commercial banks from engaging in speculative and proprietary trading.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: The Volcker Rule requires derivatives to be bought and sold through clearinghouses.
cards.explanation: The clearinghouse requirement for OTC derivatives is a separate Dodd-Frank provision. The Volcker Rule restricts proprietary trading and fund investments by commercial banks.
cards.originalText: Requiring derivatives to be bought and sold through clearinghouses.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: The Volcker Rule provides enhanced protection for witnesses and whistleblowers.
cards.explanation: Whistleblower protection comes from the Investor Protection Act component of Dodd-Frank, not from the Volcker Rule.
cards.originalText: Enhanced protection for witnesses and whistleblowers.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: MiFID II, adopted in 2014 together with MiFIR, added requirements on public disclosure of trading data and on disclosure of transaction data to regulators and supervisors.
cards.explanation: MiFID II reinforced investor protection after the 2007-2009 crisis and strengthened public trade disclosure and regulatory transaction reporting.
cards.originalText: Additional requirements on public disclosure of trading data and on disclosure of transaction data to regulators and supervisors.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: A ban on commercial banks' proprietary trading and investments in hedge funds was a key feature of MiFID II.
cards.explanation: That describes the Volcker Rule, part of the US Dodd-Frank Act. MiFID II is EU legislation focused on investor protection and trading data disclosure.
cards.originalText: A ban on commercial banks’ proprietary trading and investments in hedge funds.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: The Investor Protection Act component of the US Dodd-Frank Act gives increased protection to whistleblowers.
cards.explanation: The Investor Protection Act also established a committee to consult with the SEC on new products, fees and trading strategies.
cards.originalText: Increased protection for whistleblowers.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: Best execution of trades for clients is a protection provided by the Investor Protection Act component of the US Dodd-Frank Act.
cards.explanation: Best execution of client trades is a topic of the EU's MiFID II and MiFIR, not of the Dodd-Frank Investor Protection Act.
cards.originalText: Best execution of trades for clients.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: MiFID prescribes conduct of business and organizational requirements for investment firms and defines regulatory reporting and trade transparency obligations to prevent market abuse.
cards.explanation: MiFID (2004, applicable from 2007) already set conduct, organizational, reporting and transparency rules. MiFID II strengthened them.
cards.originalText: MiFID prescribes conduct of business and organizational requirements for investment firms and defines regulatory reporting and trade transparency obligations to prevent market abuse.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: MiFID contains no regulatory reporting requirements, which were introduced for the first time under MiFID II.
cards.explanation: MiFID already defined regulatory reporting and trade transparency obligations. MiFID II strengthened them.
cards.originalText: MiFID contains no regulatory reporting requirements; these were introduced for the first time under MiFID II.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: MiFID II is a US law enacted as part of the Dodd-Frank Act to restrict commercial banks' proprietary trading.
cards.explanation: MiFID II is EU legislation on investor protection. The proprietary trading restriction is the US Volcker Rule.
cards.originalText: MiFID II is a U.S. law enacted as part of the Dodd‑Frank Act to restrict commercial banks’ proprietary trading.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: The Volcker Rule limits commercial banks' investments in hedge funds and private equity funds.
cards.explanation: Alongside its ban on speculative proprietary trading by commercial banks, the Volcker Rule, part of Dodd-Frank, limits their investments in hedge funds and private equity funds.
cards.originalText: The Volcker Rule.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Summarize important regulations designed to protect investors in financial instruments, including Mi- FiD, MiFiD II, and Dodd-Frank.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: Selling a complex product to retail clients without adequate risk disclosure and without assessing suitability is a compliance failure that falls under the Clients, Products and Business Practices event type of the Basel operational risk taxonomy.
cards.explanation: Investor protection violations are breaches of the firm's duties to clients and market conduct. They fall under the Suitability, Disclosure and Fiduciary and Improper Business or Market Practices subcategories, not under process errors or fraud.
cards.originalText: Clients, Products and Business Practices, covering Suitability, Disclosure and Fiduciary, and Improper Business or Market Practices

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: A firm can face regulatory penalties for failing to secure the most favourable execution terms for customers, particularly where it knew of the problems and did not change its order routing.
cards.explanation: In the 2022 FINRA case against Deutsche Bank Securities, best execution failures and inaction on known problems were penalised even though there was no market manipulation.
cards.originalText: A firm can face regulatory penalties for failing to secure the most favorable execution terms for customers, particularly where it knew of the problems, did not change its order routing, and only vaguely disclosed the rebates it received.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: Large regulatory fines arise only from deliberate market manipulation such as spoofing, so routing and execution practices carry little regulatory risk.
cards.explanation: Best execution failures can be fined even without manipulation, as the 2022 FINRA fine on Deutsche Bank Securities showed. Spoofing was the JPMorgan case.
cards.originalText: Large fines arise only from deliberate market manipulation such as spoofing, so routing and execution practices carry little regulatory risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: The 2022 FINRA fine on Deutsche Bank Securities for best execution failures was the largest ever imposed on a single organization.
cards.explanation: The largest penalty in the US data was the 2008 UBS resolution of USD 11.15 billion. The Deutsche Bank Securities fine was USD 2 million.
cards.originalText: The fine was the largest ever imposed on a single organization, showing that best execution breaches are punished more severely than misrepresentation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: Covering the cost of litigation is one of the considerations regulators weigh when imposing fines on financial institutions for investor protection breaches.
cards.explanation: Fines are punitive, deterrent and signalling tools. They are sized to exceed the benefits of the breach, and recovering litigation cost is not a direct objective.
cards.originalText: To cover the cost of litigation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: Regulators impose fines on financial institutions for investor protection breaches in order to deter other firms from manipulative banking practices.
cards.explanation: Deterring further manipulative practices is one of the rationales for fines.
cards.originalText: To deter other firms from manipulative banking practices.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: Regulators set fines for investor protection breaches so that they cover at least the benefits the firm gained from the breaches.
cards.explanation: Fines are set so that the penalty more than offsets the benefits gained from the breach.
cards.originalText: To ensure that fines cover at least the benefits of breaches.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: Regulators impose fines for investor protection breaches in order to signal to other firms that they should change their compliance practices.
cards.explanation: Signalling to peer firms to adjust their compliance and monitoring practices is one of the rationales for fines.
cards.originalText: To signal to other firms to change their compliance practices.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Model risk arises when a model is used outside the context and purpose for which it was intended, even if the model is free of errors.
cards.explanation: Model risk has two sources: a model with fundamental errors that gives faulty outputs, and a model that is used incorrectly, for an unintended purpose or out of context. A sound model applied to a new product without reassessing its limitations still creates model risk.
cards.originalText: Model risk arises because the model is being used outside the context and purpose for which it was intended.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: The quality of a model's output depends on the quality of its inputs and assumptions (garbage in, garbage out).
cards.explanation: Non-representative inputs, such as data from an expansion only, lead to faulty estimates even when the processing is correct.
cards.originalText: The quality of a model’s output depends on the quality of its inputs and assumptions (garbage in, garbage out).

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Models never require assumptions.
cards.explanation: Models necessarily rely on simplifying assumptions, which form part of the input component. Errors in inputs and assumptions are a source of model risk.
cards.originalText: Models never require assumptions, so the loss understatement must come from user error.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: A data understanding component is one of the three essential components of a model.
cards.explanation: The three components are information input (assumptions and data), processing, and reporting. Data understanding is not one of them.
cards.originalText: A data understanding component

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: A data input component is one of the three essential components of a model.
cards.explanation: The information input component delivers assumptions and data to the model.
cards.originalText: A data input component

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: A data processing component is one of the three essential components of a model.
cards.explanation: The processing component transforms inputs into estimates.
cards.originalText: A data processing component

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: A reporting component is one of the three essential components of a model.
cards.explanation: The reporting component translates estimates into useful business information.
cards.originalText: A reporting component

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: The reporting component of a model converts estimates into useful or applied information.
cards.explanation: The input component handles data and assumptions, the processing component converts inputs into estimates, and the reporting component turns estimates into applied business information.
cards.originalText: Reporting.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: The processing component of a model converts estimates into useful or applied information.
cards.explanation: The processing component converts inputs into estimates. Converting estimates into applied information is the job of the reporting component.
cards.originalText: Processing.
cards.correction: The reporting component of a model converts estimates into useful or applied information.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Model risk can lead to adverse outcomes when decisions are based on inaccurate outputs of a model that is flawed or misused, leading to financial and reputational losses.
cards.explanation: Models rely on simplifying assumptions and are never fully accurate. Poor decisions based on faulty or misused outputs create financial and reputational loss.
cards.originalText: Decisions are based on inaccurate outputs of a model that is flawed or is misused, leading to financial and reputational losses.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: A model that is highly accurate on past data eliminates model risk entirely.
cards.explanation: Models are simplified imitations of reality and are never completely accurate. Model risk is always present.
cards.originalText: A model that is highly accurate on past data eliminates model risk entirely.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Model risk arises only when a model contains coding errors and is unrelated to how the model is used.
cards.explanation: Model risk also arises from improper use of a model, such as use for an unintended purpose or out of context.
cards.originalText: Model risk arises only when a model contains coding errors and is unrelated to how the model is used.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: The model owner is primarily responsible for ensuring that a model has undergone appropriate validation and approval processes before it is deployed.
cards.explanation: The model owner has ultimate accountability for model use and performance. This includes ensuring models are properly developed, implemented and used, and that models in use have been validated and approved.
cards.originalText: Model owner

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: An updated inventory of all models in use is a core element of good model risk management documentation.
cards.explanation: A comprehensive, current model inventory records each model's purpose, usage, restrictions, inputs and components, and supports aggregate model risk assessment.
cards.originalText: Presence of an updated inventory of all models used in the process.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: A firm invests in model risk management to ensure that its models are used as required.
cards.explanation: Investment in supporting systems, controls and testing ensures that models are implemented correctly, systems are integrated effectively and models are used appropriately.
cards.originalText: To ensure that the model is used as required

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: The potential impact of a model on the firm's profits and financial position should drive the level and comprehensiveness of model risk management for that model.
cards.explanation: Materiality is the key factor: the greater a model's potential impact, the more detailed and comprehensive its risk management must be.
cards.originalText: The potential impact of the model on the firm’s profits and financial position

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Whether a model was built in-house rather than obtained from a vendor determines the level of model risk management it requires.
cards.explanation: Vendor models still require validation. The level of model risk management depends on the model's potential impact, not on its origin.
cards.originalText: Whether the model was built in‑house rather than obtained from a vendor

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: How long a model has been in use is the key factor that should drive the level of model risk management for that model.
cards.explanation: Length of use is not a measure of materiality, and an old model may even be out of context and riskier. The potential impact on profits and financial position drives the level.
cards.originalText: How long the model has been in use

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Effective challenge is the fundamental guiding principle for managing model risk.
cards.explanation: Effective challenge is critical analysis by objective, informed parties who can identify the limitations and assumptions of a model and drive changes. It depends on incentives, competence and influence.
cards.originalText: Effective challenge

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Managing model risk requires proper segregation of duties.
cards.explanation: Effective challenge requires independence from model development, so those who build a model should not be the ones who review it.
cards.originalText: Managing model risk requires proper segregation of duties.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Shortcuts and simplifications adopted to manage complexity cannot affect the accuracy of model outputs.
cards.explanation: Even innocent simplifications can sacrifice accuracy and introduce error.
cards.originalText: Shortcuts and simplifications adopted to manage complexity cannot affect the accuracy of model outputs.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: With appropriate procedures and tools, model risk can be eliminated.
cards.explanation: Models are simplified imitations of reality, so model risk is always present and cannot be eliminated.
cards.originalText: With appropriate procedures and tools, model risk can be eliminated.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Model risk, like many other risks, has both an upside and a downside component.
cards.explanation: Model risk is defined by negative outcomes such as losses and poor decisions. It has no upside component.
cards.originalText: Like many other risks, model risk has both an upside and a downside component.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Although the nature of testing varies by the context and type of model, testing is an integral part of model development.
cards.explanation: Testing is an integral part of development, and the form of the tests varies with the model and its context.
cards.originalText: Although the nature of testing varies by the context and type of model, testing is an integral part of model development.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Model development should be a straightforward and routine technical process.
cards.explanation: Development depends on developer experience and judgment and requires multidisciplinary skill. Treating it as routine understates model risk.
cards.originalText: Model development should be a straightforward and routine technical process.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Banks should never temper model output with judgmental or qualitative adjustments.
cards.explanation: Quantitative output may be adjusted with judgmental or qualitative adjustments when they have a logical basis and are documented. The word 'never' is too absolute.
cards.originalText: Banks should never model output with judgmental or qualitative adjustments.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: A bank should perform sensitivity analysis on all models it uses to identify market conditions under which they might perform poorly.
cards.explanation: Sensitivity analysis and testing across conditions reveal where models are weak or unreliable, which is a development and validation best practice.
cards.originalText: Perform sensitivity analysis on all models used by the bank to identify market conditions under which they might perform poorly.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: A model that has performed well for one product can be applied to a different, new product on the strength of its track record.
cards.explanation: A model is valid for its intended use. Applying it to a different product is out-of-context use, which is a source of model risk.
cards.originalText: Apply the strongly performing existing model to the new commercial loan product given the model’s successful track record.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: The model development team should be responsible for validating all of the bank's operational models.
cards.explanation: Validation requires effective challenge by independent, unbiased staff. Developers lack independence to validate their own work.
cards.originalText: Make the model development team responsible for validating all of the bank’s models that are currently operational.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Restricting model testing to normal market conditions, because stressed conditions are too rare to be informative, is consistent with sound model testing.
cards.explanation: Sound testing covers a wide variety of conditions, normal and stressed, including scenarios outside ordinary assumptions. Excluding stress hides the situations where a model is most likely to fail.
cards.originalText: Restricting testing to normal market conditions, because stressed conditions are too rare to be informative.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Sound model testing documents the potential weaknesses of the model and the circumstances in which it does not work.
cards.explanation: Identifying weaknesses and failure circumstances is a core aim of testing.
cards.originalText: Documenting potential weaknesses of the model and circumstances in which it does not work.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Sound model testing uses inputs over a wide range of values, including extreme values, to find the boundaries of model effectiveness.
cards.explanation: Extreme input values reveal the acceptable input range and the boundaries of model performance.
cards.originalText: Using inputs over a wide range of values, including extreme values, to find the boundaries of model effectiveness.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Sound model testing includes analysing other models that use the subject model's outputs as their inputs.
cards.explanation: If a model's outputs feed other models, those downstream models must also be analysed.
cards.originalText: Analyzing other models that use the subject model’s outputs as their inputs.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the development and implementation of models.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Any data proxies, unrepresentative data and adjustments made to data, such as those from external sources, should be clearly documented during model development so that users can judge the usefulness of the data themselves.
cards.explanation: Documenting proxies, non-representative data and adjustments gives users transparency about data limitations, which matters because model output is only as good as its inputs.
cards.originalText: Any data proxies, unrepresentative data, and adjustments made to data, such as those from external sources.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Using models without validation, or models with identified weaknesses, is a likely cause of negative supervisory feedback on a bank holding company's model risk management.
cards.explanation: Supervisory guidance expects every model in use to be validated and any weaknesses to be addressed or limited.
cards.originalText: Using models without validation, or models with identified weaknesses

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Using benchmark or challenger models to help assess the reasonableness of a primary model's output is a deficiency in model risk management.
cards.explanation: Benchmark and challenger models are a recommended validation tool, not a deficiency.
cards.originalText: Using benchmark or challenger models to help assess the reasonableness of the primary model output

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Employing independent validation staff to critically evaluate models is a deficiency in model risk management.
cards.explanation: Independent, critical review is the very safeguard supervisors want.
cards.originalText: Employing independent validation staff to critically evaluate the models

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Independent model validation is a function that is typically handled by the developers of the model.
cards.explanation: Validation requires independence from development and use, to avoid bias and conflicts of interest, so developers should generally not validate their own models.
cards.originalText: Independent model validation

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Stating a clear purpose so that development is aligned with the intended use is a function handled by the developers of a model.
cards.explanation: Defining the model's objective is a developer responsibility at the outset.
cards.originalText: Stating a clear purpose so that development is aligned with the intended use

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Rigorous assessment of data quality and relevance is a function handled by the developers of a model.
cards.explanation: Assessing data quality and relevance is part of model development.
cards.originalText: Rigorous assessment of data quality and relevance

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Model testing during development is a function handled by the developers of a model.
cards.explanation: Developmental testing is a key developer task, distinct from independent validation.
cards.originalText: Model testing

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Under supervisory guidance on model validation, work done by model developers can be accepted as validation without critical review by an independent party.
cards.explanation: Guidance allows some validation work to be done by developers or users only if it is subject to critical review by an independent party. Accepting it without that review is inconsistent with the guidance.
cards.originalText: Work done by model developers should be accepted as validation without critical review by an independent party
cards.correction: Under supervisory guidance on model validation, work done by model developers can be accepted as validation only with critical review by an independent party.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Under supervisory guidance, model documentation should indicate where the model does not work effectively.
cards.explanation: Documenting a model's limitations, including where it does not work effectively, is an expected part of sound model documentation and validation.
cards.originalText: Documentation should indicate where the model does not work effectively

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Under supervisory guidance, model validation should be conducted by staff with a degree of independence from model development and use.
cards.explanation: Independence from the people who develop and use a model is a core principle of effective validation and challenge.
cards.originalText: Validation should be conducted by staff with a degree of independence from model development and use

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Under supervisory guidance, the depth of model validation should be commensurate with the complexity and materiality of a bank's models.
cards.explanation: Validation rigor is scaled to the complexity and materiality of each model, so more complex and material models receive deeper validation.
cards.originalText: The depth of validation should be commensurate with the complexity and materiality of the bank’s models

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: The use of vendor models, where the modeling is external and parts of it may be confidential, is a recognized challenge to effective model validation.
cards.explanation: Vendor products limit access to code and implementation details, so validators must rely more on indirect tools such as sensitivity analysis, benchmarking and vendor-provided evidence.
cards.originalText: Use of vendor models, where the modeling is external and parts of it may be confidential

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Having all models developed in-house is a recognized challenge to effective model validation.
cards.explanation: In-house development gives validators full access to the model, so it supports validation rather than hindering it. External vendor models are the recognized challenge.
cards.originalText: Having all models developed in‑house

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Having model validation performed independently of model developers is a recognized challenge to effective model validation.
cards.explanation: Independence from developers is a requirement of good validation, not an obstacle to it.
cards.originalText: Having validation performed independently of model developers

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Ongoing monitoring is one of the three core elements of a strong model validation process.
cards.explanation: The three core elements are evaluation of conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring (including process verification and benchmarking) and outcomes analysis.
cards.originalText: Ongoing monitoring

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Vendor certification is one of the three core elements of a strong model validation process.
cards.explanation: The three core elements are conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis. Vendor models need extra validation work, but a vendor's certification does not replace it.
cards.originalText: Vendor certification

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Regulatory sign-off is one of the three core elements of a strong model validation process.
cards.explanation: Validation is the bank's own responsibility. Supervisors review it but are not part of the validation process, whose core elements are conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis.
cards.originalText: Regulatory sign‑off

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Capital add-on calibration is one of the three core elements of a strong model validation process.
cards.explanation: Capital cushions can address model risk but are not a validation element. The three core elements are conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis.
cards.originalText: Capital add‑on calibration

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
