cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: In 2008 UBS paid a CFTC fine of USD 920 million for spoofing in precious metals markets.
cards.explanation: The USD 920 million CFTC resolution for spoofing was JP Morgan's (2020). UBS's 2008 resolution of USD 11.15 billion concerned auction rate securities sold as cash equivalents.
cards.originalText: UBS (2008): CFTC fine of USD 920 million for spoofing in precious metals markets.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: In 2022 Deutsche Bank Securities reached a USD 11.15 billion resolution for misrepresenting auction rate securities as cash equivalents.
cards.explanation: The USD 11.15 billion resolution of 2008 was UBS's, over auction rate securities. Deutsche Bank Securities was fined USD 2 million by FINRA over best execution.
cards.originalText: Deutsche Bank Securities (2022): USD 11.15 billion resolution for misrepresenting auction rate securities as cash equivalents.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: Any breach of investor protection rules is internal fraud, because any such breach is an unauthorised activity.
cards.explanation: Only intentional breaches are internal fraud. Unintentional compliance breaches typically come from human error or faulty policies.
cards.originalText: Both breaches are internal fraud, because any breach of investor protection rules is an unauthorised activity.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: Deterrent controls such as sanctions are the only way to prevent an intentional trading breach, while monitoring and supervision of trades address only errors.
cards.explanation: Monitoring and supervision of trades are core controls against fraud as well as errors. Deterrent controls are the one group that does not help against unintentional errors.
cards.originalText: The second breach can be prevented only by deterrent controls such as sanctions, while monitoring and supervision of trades address only errors.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: Most controls against internal fraud also help against unintentional compliance breaches, whereas deterrent controls work only against intentional breaches.
cards.explanation: Monitoring, supervision, middle and back office checks, policies and training help against both, but the key difference between an error and a fraud is intention, so deterrence only works on the latter.
cards.originalText: The first is an unintentional breach and the second is internal fraud; most internal fraud controls help against both, but deterrent controls work only against the second.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: Offering customers an opt-out from a routing practice shifts the broker-dealer's best execution duty to the customer.
cards.explanation: The duty stays with the broker: in the Deutsche Bank Securities case customers could also opt out, and FINRA still fined the firm.
cards.originalText: Keep the routing, since customers who prefer direct routing can opt out, and offering an opt-out shifts the best execution duty to the customer.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the case studies involving violations of investor protection or compliance regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-14: Investor Protection and Compliance Risks in Investment Activities
cards.statement: Best execution is judged on price alone, so routing is acceptable as long as orders receive the same price as direct routing.
cards.explanation: Speed of execution and fill rates are part of best execution, alongside price improvement.
cards.originalText: Keep the routing as long as pinged orders receive the same price as direct routing, since best execution is judged on price alone.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Shortcuts, approximations or new data sources introduced at implementation can compromise a model's output even when its theory is sound, and the error can spread to every model that uses that output.
cards.explanation: Errors can occur at any point from design through implementation, and aggregate model risk rises with dependencies among models and reliance on common data.
cards.originalText: The approximation and the new data source can compromise the output even though the theory is sound, and the effect can spread to every model that uses the VaR.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Errors introduced when a validated model is re-coded into the production risk engine are IT risk, not model risk.
cards.explanation: Implementation in information systems is part of the model calculation, so errors there are model risk whatever earlier approval the theory and code received.
cards.originalText: Because the theory and code were approved before the change, errors introduced when the model is re-coded into the production engine are IT risk, not model risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Model risk is assessed one model at a time, so models that take another model's output as an input carry no extra model risk.
cards.explanation: Model risk must be assessed individually and in aggregate. Aggregate model risk arises from dependencies among models and shared inputs.
cards.originalText: Model risk is assessed one model at a time, so the capital and limit models that take the VaR as an input carry no extra model risk from the change.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Model risk falls as a model's output is used more widely across a bank, because broader use exposes errors faster and reduces uncertainty about the model.
cards.explanation: Model risk increases with broader use and larger potential impact.
cards.originalText: Model risk falls as the VaR output is used more widely across the bank, because broader use exposes errors faster and reduces uncertainty about the model.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: The failure of the Gaussian copula in CDO pricing was an execution error, like the hidden rows in the Barclays spreadsheet, because the copula failed to do what it was designed to do.
cards.explanation: The copula did what it was designed to do, on an assumption that stopped holding, which is a conceptual error. The Barclays hidden rows were an implementation failure in a tool that is not even a model.
cards.originalText: The friction is an execution error: like the hidden rows in the Barclays spreadsheet, the copula failed to do what it was designed to do, so replicating its code would have exposed the problem.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Robust validation of a sound model eliminates its model risk.
cards.explanation: Even with skilled modelling and robust validation, model risk cannot be eliminated. Limits on use, monitoring, revision and supplementary analysis are still needed.
cards.originalText: The friction would have been removed by a suﬀiciently rigorous validation of the copula before use, because robust validation of a sound model eliminates its model risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe model risk and explain how it can arise in the implementation of a model.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: The Gaussian copula model produced inaccurate CDO prices in all market conditions.
cards.explanation: The copula assumption was valid and accurate in normal market conditions. Problems arose when correlations rose sharply and users kept pricing with the old assumptions.
cards.originalText: The copula produced inaccurate CDO prices in all market conditions, so the losses came from a fundamental flaw in Li’s formula rather than from how users relied on it.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Under supervisory guidance on model risk management, developers may perform some validation work if an independent party critically reviews it and adds further testing, and independence may be supported by reporting lines but is judged by actions and outcomes.
cards.explanation: This is the guidance's answer to scarce validation resources, since independent critical review keeps the effective challenge intact.
cards.originalText: Developers may perform some validation work if an independent party critically reviews it and adds further testing; independence may be supported by reporting lines but is judged by actions and outcomes.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Model owners in the business units, who carry ultimate accountability for model use and performance, should hold the authority to restrict a model's use once validation finds significant deficiencies.
cards.explanation: The model owner is accountable for use and performance, but the authority to restrict the use of models belongs to risk-control staff.
cards.originalText: Model owners in the business units, who carry ultimate accountability for model use and performance, should hold the authority to restrict a model’s use once validation finds significant deficiencies.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: To preserve independence, no validation work may be performed by developers or users, and any testing they have already done must be discarded and repeated in full by the model risk management team.
cards.explanation: Guidance expressly allows some validation work by developers and users if an independent party critically reviews it, so a blanket ban and full repetition is not required.
cards.originalText: To preserve independence, no validation work may be performed by developers or users, and any testing they have already done must be discarded and repeated in full by the MRM team.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of an effective model risk management process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Incentives for effective challenge in model validation are strongest when validators sit close to the development process, because that proximity gives them the competence to critique a model.
cards.explanation: Incentives to provide effective challenge are stronger when there is greater separation from the model development process. Competence comes from technical skill and business familiarity.
cards.originalText: Incentives for effective challenge are strongest when validators sit close to the development process, because that proximity is what gives them the competence to critique a model.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Effective challenge in model validation requires validators to have explicit authority to elevate findings and sufficient stature to get issues addressed, demonstrated by models actually being changed as a result of validation.
cards.explanation: Influence is one of the three ingredients of effective challenge, alongside incentives and competence. It shows in reporting lines, rank and a pattern of models changed after validation.
cards.originalText: Effective challenge is weakest on influence, so the unit needs explicit authority to elevate findings and the stature to get issues addressed, shown by models actually changed.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Validators' bonuses should be linked to the number of models they approve each year.
cards.explanation: Compensation should be tied to the quality of validations and the degree of critical, unbiased review. Paying for approvals rewards bias.
cards.originalText: Effective challenge is weakest on incentives, so validators’ bonuses should instead be linked to the number of models they approve each year.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.loText: Describe elements of a strong model validation process and challenges to an effective validation process.
cards.reading: ORR-15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
cards.statement: Validators should be embedded in model development teams so that their findings are acted upon faster.
cards.explanation: Incentives for effective challenge are stronger with greater separation from development. Embedding validators removes the independence that makes challenge credible.
cards.originalText: Effective challenge is weakest on independence, so validators should be embedded in the development teams, where their findings would be acted upon faster.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.loText: Define a model and describe different ways that financial institutions can become exposed to model risk.
cards.reading: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.statement: Model risk is a tail risk: most errors are benign or caught early, while large losses arise rarely, under extreme conditions and often from a series of mistakes.
cards.explanation: The rarity of large losses leaves institutions with misplaced confidence and makes the cost of model risk functions seem disproportionate to the risk.
cards.originalText: Disagree: model risk is a tail risk; most errors are benign or caught early, while large losses come rarely, under extreme conditions and often from a series of mistakes.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.loText: Define a model and describe different ways that financial institutions can become exposed to model risk.
cards.reading: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.statement: A five-year record in which every model error found was benign is good evidence that a bank's model risk is low.
cards.explanation: Absence of tail losses over a short window is what a tail risk looks like most of the time, and treating it as evidence of low risk is the misplaced confidence GARP warns about.
cards.originalText: Agree: a five-year record in which every error found was benign is good evidence that the bank’s model risk is low, so the MRM budget can follow the loss record.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.loText: Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.
cards.reading: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.statement: Best practice in model risk management is to tier models by materiality, complexity, client-facing use and regulatory use, with full-scope validation of top-tier models about every 2 to 3 years and an annual review of every model.
cards.explanation: Tiering spends a scarce validation budget where the risk is, while the annual review applies to all models independently of their tier.
cards.originalText: Tier models by materiality, complexity, client-facing use and regulatory use, with full-scope validation of top-tier models about every 2 to 3 years and an annual review of every model.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.loText: Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.
cards.reading: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.statement: A larger second-line validation team means that modeling teams can scale back their own quality assurance.
cards.explanation: The first line must not abdicate its responsibilities. A large validation team can make modeling teams complacent, which is the outcome to avoid.
cards.originalText: Let modeling teams scale back their own quality assurance, because the enlarged second-line team now exists to catch the errors the first line misses.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.loText: Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.
cards.reading: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.statement: Every model should be fully validated each year regardless of its tier, so that model risk management becomes a continuous rather than a point-in-time exercise.
cards.explanation: This ignores tiering and the cost-benefit balance. Every model gets an annual review, but full-scope validation frequency depends on the tier.
cards.originalText: Validate every model in full each year, whatever its tier, so that model risk management becomes a continuous rather than a point-in-time exercise.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.
cards.reading: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.statement: In the securitisation frictions taxonomy, the friction between CDO investors and credit rating agencies is model error, because investors rely on rating models that can be wrong or wrongly used.
cards.explanation: In the Gaussian copula case, ratings relied on correlations inferred from a short, benign CDS history, so assumptions and limitations needed to be challenged and explained.
cards.originalText: Model error: investors relied on rating models built on correlations inferred from a short, benign CDS history, so assumptions and limitations must be challenged and explained.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.
cards.reading: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.statement: In the securitisation frictions taxonomy, the friction between CDO investors and credit rating agencies is a principal-agent problem.
cards.explanation: The principal-agent problem is the friction between the asset manager and the investor. The investor and rating agency friction is model error.
cards.originalText: Principal-agent problem: the investor delegates credit analysis to the agency, so the lesson is to align the agency’s fees with the investor’s returns.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.
cards.reading: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.statement: In the securitisation frictions taxonomy, the friction between CDO investors and credit rating agencies is moral hazard.
cards.explanation: Moral hazard is the friction involving the servicer, with the mortgagor or with third parties. The investor and rating agency friction is model error.
cards.originalText: Moral hazard: the agency stops monitoring the collateral once the deal closes, so the lesson is that investors must audit the agency’s surveillance.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.loText: Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.
cards.reading: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
cards.statement: In the securitisation frictions taxonomy, the friction between CDO investors and credit rating agencies is adverse selection.
cards.explanation: Adverse selection is the friction between the arranger and third parties. The investor and rating agency friction is model error.
cards.originalText: Adverse selection: the agency knows more about the collateral than the investor, so the lesson is that investors should hold only the most senior tranches.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: The December 2017 Basel III reforms replaced the advanced measurement approach and the three standardised approaches for operational risk with a single standardised approach, because operational risk capital proved insufficient and misconduct losses were hard to model.
cards.explanation: Operational risk capital had proved insufficient for some banks' losses, and the nature of misconduct and control-failure losses highlighted the difficulty of using internal models.
cards.originalText: Operational risk capital proved insuﬀicient for some banks’ losses, and misconduct losses were hard to model, so the AMA was replaced by a single standardised approach.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: CVA losses were small relative to default losses in the crisis, so the December 2017 Basel III reforms retained the internal CVA model.
cards.explanation: CVA losses were a major source of crisis losses, and the internal model was removed, leaving the SA-CVA and BA-CVA approaches.
cards.originalText: CVA losses were small relative to default losses in the crisis, so the internal CVA model was retained and the standardised approach removed.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: The December 2017 Basel III output floor is set at 72.5% of Basel I requirements.
cards.explanation: The output floor is 72.5% of the risk-weighted assets calculated under the revised standardised approaches. The Basel II floor was based on Basel I and was inconsistently implemented.
cards.originalText: The Basel II floor was applied too conservatively across countries, so it was replaced by a lower floor of 72.5% of Basel I requirements.
cards.correction: The December 2017 Basel III output floor is set at 72.5% of requirements under the revised standardised approaches.

changes.to: requirements under the revised standardised approaches

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: IRB capital requirements were too uniform across banks, so the December 2017 Basel III reforms gave banks more freedom to estimate LGD and EAD for large corporates.
cards.explanation: The problem was a lack of comparability across banks, and the reforms removed the advanced IRB approach for large corporates, so LGD and EAD are fixed under the foundation approach.
cards.originalText: IRB capital requirements were too uniform across banks, so the reforms gave banks more freedom to estimate LGD and EAD for large corporates.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 Basel III reforms, equity exposures can no longer be treated under any IRB approach, whereas specialised lending may remain on the advanced or foundation IRB approach.
cards.explanation: The advanced IRB option was removed for asset classes that cannot be modelled in a robust and prudent manner, and all IRB approaches are removed for equities.
cards.originalText: Equity exposures can no longer be treated under any IRB approach, whereas specialised lending may remain on the advanced or foundation IRB approach.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 Basel III reforms, exposures to corporates with consolidated revenues above EUR 500 million must move to the standardised approach because the advanced IRB option is removed for them.
cards.explanation: Losing the advanced IRB approach does not mean losing IRB: with supervisory approval, banks use the foundation IRB approach for these corporates, which fixes LGD and EAD.
cards.originalText: Exposures to corporates with consolidated revenues above EUR 500 million must move to the standardised approach, since the advanced IRB option is removed for them.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 Basel III reforms, exposures to banks and other financial institutions may stay on the advanced IRB approach, since only corporate exposures lose the advanced option.
cards.explanation: Banks and other financial institutions are in the same position as large corporates: the advanced IRB option is removed for both.
cards.originalText: Exposures to banks and other financial institutions may stay on the advanced IRB approach, since only corporate exposures lose the advanced option.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for revising the Basel III framework and the goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms to the Basel III framework.
cards.reading: ORR-23: High-level Summary of Basel III Reforms
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 Basel III reforms, PD input floors apply only under the advanced IRB approach, so exposures on the foundation IRB approach face no PD floor.
cards.explanation: PD floors apply under both the foundation and advanced IRB approaches, at 5 basis points for corporates. The LGD and EAD floors apply only under the advanced approach.
cards.originalText: PD input floors apply only under the advanced IRB approach, so exposures moved to the foundation IRB approach face no PD floor.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Near-miss occurrences are included in incident reporting in organizations with strong risk cultures so that the potential consequence that was unintentionally avoided can be analyzed.
cards.explanation: A near miss follows the same causal chain as a loss, but the loss was avoided by chance. Analysing it reveals control weaknesses without suffering an actual loss.
cards.originalText: To analyze the potential consequence that was unintentionally avoided.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Near-miss occurrences are included in incident reporting in organizations with strong risk cultures to assess the cost of close calls.
cards.explanation: A near miss produces no actual loss, so there is no cost to assess. The value of recording it lies in analysing the consequence that was narrowly avoided.
cards.originalText: To assess the cost of close calls.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: The gap between the discovery date and the settlement date of an operational incident should rarely exceed three months and never exceed one year; otherwise the IT reporting system itself probably requires an upgrade.
cards.explanation: Settlement lags of several years are a normal feature of operational events because of late discovery and legal processes, so a hard one-year cap is not a valid data-quality test.
cards.originalText: The gap between the discovery date and the settlement date should rarely exceed three months and never exceed one year; otherwise, the IT reporting system itself probably requires an upgrade.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Each operational incident has at least four important dates: occurrence, discovery, reporting and accounting (settlement).
cards.explanation: These four dates are the ones recorded for each incident in the loss database.
cards.originalText: Each operational incident has (at least) four important dates: occurrence, discovery, reporting, and accounting (settlement).

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: A non-zero minimum threshold for operational loss reporting is acceptable, provided it is supportable and not set to reduce capital requirements.
cards.explanation: Non-zero thresholds are standard, with typical levels of 1,000 to 10,000 and a Basel minimum of EUR 20,000, if they are justified and not used to lower capital.
cards.originalText: A non‑zero minimum threshold for loss reporting (e.g., EUR 5,000) is acceptable, provided it is supportable and not set to reduce capital requirements.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: The general ledger is a good source for benchmarking operational loss data, but it is not a perfect substitute for a dedicated operational event database.
cards.explanation: The ledger shows only accounted effects and lacks causes, dates and near misses, so it benchmarks the event database but cannot replace it.
cards.originalText: Although the general ledger is a good source for benchmarking, it is not a perfect substitute for a dedicated operational event database.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: For concealed frauds such as manipulation of suspense accounts, the interval from the date of occurrence to the date of discovery is the main reason settlement typically occurs years after the event began.
cards.explanation: Concealed manipulation is by nature slow to detect, so the occurrence-to-discovery interval dominates the overall lag before settlement.
cards.originalText: Date of occurrence to date of discovery.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Different events that materialize from a single failure must be grouped as a single loss to reflect the common underlying cause.
cards.explanation: Grouping losses with a common cause is a regulatory requirement, sound modelling practice and needed for correct management information.
cards.originalText: Different events that materialize from a single failure must be grouped as a single loss to reflect the common underlying cause.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Setting the operational loss reporting threshold at zero is now the dominant best practice, especially in large institutions.
cards.explanation: Zero thresholds are becoming rare because of the burden of recording many small incidents. Typical thresholds are 1,000 to 10,000, with a Basel minimum of EUR 20,000.
cards.originalText: Setting the loss reporting threshold at zero is now the dominant best practice, especially in large institutions.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Regulators require firms to record non-financial impacts such as reputational damage and customer detriment as part of internal loss data.
cards.explanation: Regulators require only losses with direct financial effects. Recording indirect effects is good management practice rather than a requirement.
cards.originalText: Regulators require firms to record non‑financial impacts such as reputational damage and customer detriment as part of internal loss data.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Direct operational losses are usually poorly captured, whereas indirect losses are almost always monetized by every firm.
cards.explanation: Direct losses are usually well captured, and only more mature firms monetize indirect losses.
cards.originalText: Direct losses are usually poorly captured, whereas indirect losses are almost always monetized by every firm.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: The threshold for reporting operational losses may differ across firms, but the chosen threshold must be supportable, must not be set to reduce capital requirements, and must still capture all material activities and exposures.
cards.explanation: Firms have discretion over the threshold level, but it must be justified and consistent with comprehensive capture of material exposures.
cards.originalText: Thresholds may differ across firms, but the chosen threshold must be supportable, must not be set to reduce capital requirements, and must still capture all material activities and exposures.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: The operational loss reporting threshold should be set so that only the tail events that drive capital are collected.
cards.explanation: Internal loss data must be comprehensive, capturing all material activities and exposures. Restricting collection to tail events confuses loss collection with capital modelling.
cards.originalText: The threshold should be set so that only tail events that drive capital are collected.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Basel rules prohibit banks from applying any internal loss reporting threshold.
cards.explanation: Basel sets a minimum collection threshold of EUR 20,000 and does not prohibit thresholds. Many firms use lower thresholds of 1,000 to 10,000.
cards.originalText: Basel rules prohibit banks from applying any internal loss reporting threshold.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Material operational incidents should usually be reported within a few working days, while minor incidents can be included in periodic summary reporting.
cards.explanation: A risk-based reporting timeline gets material events escalated quickly without wasting resources on immaterial ones.
cards.originalText: Material incidents should usually be reported within a few working days, while minor incidents can be included in periodic summary reporting.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Raising the operational loss reporting threshold increases the losses recorded and therefore increases operational risk capital.
cards.explanation: A higher threshold excludes small losses, so recorded losses fall rather than rise.
cards.originalText: Raising the loss reporting threshold increases the losses recorded and therefore increases operational risk capital.
cards.correction: Raising the operational loss reporting threshold decreases the losses recorded and therefore decreases operational risk capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Indirect effects of operational events, such as reputational damage, cannot be assessed in monetary terms because their consequences are non-financial.
cards.explanation: Indirect consequences carry real financial implications, such as remediation, attrition and regulatory costs, and mature firms monetize them.
cards.originalText: Indirect effects such as reputational damage cannot be assessed in monetary terms because their consequences are non‑financial.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Events caused by a single IT failure should be recorded as separate unrelated losses so that each stays below the reporting threshold.
cards.explanation: Losses arising from one underlying failure must be grouped as a single loss, and splitting them to stay under the threshold is non-compliant.
cards.originalText: Events caused by a single IT failure should be recorded as separate unrelated losses so that each stays below the reporting threshold.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: A loss database should record the gross loss of an operational event and the insurance recovery separately, so that net loss can be derived from the two.
cards.explanation: Keeping gross loss and recoveries in separate fields shows both the underlying exposure and how effective insurance is, and net loss is simply gross loss minus recovery.
cards.originalText: Record a gross loss of USD 4.0 million and record the USD 2.5 million insurance settlement separately as a recovery, so that net loss (USD 1.5 million) can be derived.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: A loss database should record only the net loss after insurance recoveries, because a gross loss figure adds no information.
cards.explanation: Storing only net loss hides the gross exposure and the effectiveness of insurance, understating the underlying risk. Loss data standards require the gross loss and recoveries to be captured separately.
cards.originalText: Record only the net loss of USD 1.5 million, because the insurance payment has already offset the gross amount and a gross figure adds no information.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: A natural disaster that damages a bank's physical assets is not recorded as an operational loss because its cause is external.
cards.explanation: Damage to physical assets from natural disasters is a standard Basel operational risk event type, so an external cause does not exempt the event from loss recording.
cards.originalText: Do not record the event as an operational loss, because a natural disaster is an external cause outside the bank’s control.
cards.correction: A natural disaster that damages a bank's physical assets is recorded as an operational loss even though its cause is external.

changes.from: is not recorded as an operational loss because
changes.to: is recorded as an operational loss even though

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: The date of occurrence is an important reference date for an operational loss event.
cards.explanation: Date of occurrence, when the event first happened, is one of the standard reference dates collected with each loss event.
cards.originalText: Date of occurrence

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: The date of accounting is an important reference date for an operational loss event.
cards.explanation: Date of accounting is when the financial impact enters the P&L, and it drives the year to which the loss is allocated.
cards.originalText: Date of accounting

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: The date of reporting is an important reference date for an operational loss event.
cards.explanation: Date of reporting, when the event enters the reporting database, is one of the four standard reference dates.
cards.originalText: Date of reporting

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain best practices for the collection of operational loss data and reporting of operational loss incidents, including regulatory expectations.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: The date of assessment is an important reference date for an operational loss event.
cards.explanation: The standard reference dates are occurrence, discovery, reporting and accounting. No assessment date is part of the loss event record.
cards.originalText: Date of assessment
cards.correction: The date of discovery is an important reference date for an operational loss event.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: A key function of the RCSA is to determine whether the control environment of an activity (or unit) is in line with the firm's risk appetite.
cards.explanation: Judging whether controls keep risk within appetite is a central purpose of the risk and control self-assessment.
cards.originalText: A key function of the RCSA is to determine whether the control environment of an activity (or unit) is in line with the firm’s risk appetite.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: At the end of the RCSA exercise, the firm should have a good understanding of its inherent risks, control effectiveness, and residual risks.
cards.explanation: Inherent risk, control effectiveness and residual risk are the standard outputs of an RCSA.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: RCSA impact types commonly include financial, regulatory, customer, and reputation (with service continuity a common addition), and likelihood scales are expressed either as percentages or as frequencies of occurrence.
cards.explanation: These are the usual impact categories, and likelihood is expressed either as a probability or as a frequency such as once in x years.
cards.originalText: Impact types commonly include financial, regulatory, customer, and reputation (with service continuity a common addition), and likelihood scales are expressed either as percentages or as frequencies of occurrence.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Multiplying the ordinal likelihood and impact ratings of an RCSA heatmap into a single score is a valid way to compare loss events on one dimension.
cards.explanation: Qualitative ratings are ordinal labels rather than numbers on a ratio scale, so arithmetic on them is not meaningful: a likely-but-low-impact event and a remote-but-extreme event would both score 4. The heatmap colours, not products, express the risk level.
cards.originalText: To compare loss events on a single dimension, the algorithm should multiply likelihood by impact, giving a score of 4 to both a likely‑but‑low‑impact event (4 x 1) and a remote‑but‑extreme‑impact event (1 x 4).

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: The primary purpose of RCSAs, likelihood scales and heatmaps is to document control activities and compare operational efficiency across departments.
cards.explanation: RCSAs are risk assessment tools, not efficiency benchmarking or control documentation tools. Their purpose is to classify and prioritise risks by likelihood and impact.
cards.originalText: To document control activities and compare operational efficiency across departments.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: RCSAs, likelihood scales and heatmaps are used to classify risks uniformly and to prioritise them according to their impact and likelihood.
cards.explanation: Standardised scales make ratings comparable across risks and units, and the heatmap combines them into colours that rank risks so that mitigation can be prioritised.
cards.originalText: To uniformly classify and prioritize IT department risks based on impact and likelihood.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: An RCSA evaluates only residual risk after controls are implemented and disregards initial risk levels.
cards.explanation: An RCSA covers both inherent risk and residual risk, together with the effectiveness of the controls in between.
cards.originalText: To evaluate only the residual risks post‑control implementation, disregarding initial risk levels.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Staff within a business unit are excluded from providing input into their own unit's RCSA scorecard in order to avoid conflicts of interest.
cards.explanation: An RCSA is a self-assessment: the unit's own staff provide the input, typically through workshops or questionnaires. Excluding them would defeat its purpose.
cards.originalText: Staff within a business unit are excluded from providing input into their own business unit’s RCSA scorecard in order to avoid conflicts of interest.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: In an RCSA, any process whose inherent risk is greater than its residual risk is assigned a red flag because it requires a process fix.
cards.explanation: Residual risk below inherent risk is the normal result of effective controls and is not a red-flag condition. A flag arises when residual risk exceeds the firm's appetite.
cards.originalText: Any process with an inherent risk that is greater than its residual risk will be assigned a ”red flag” because this is a situation that requires a process fix.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: In an RCSA, managers first identify and assess inherent risks by making no inferences about the controls embedded in the process, so controls are assumed to be absent.
cards.explanation: Inherent (gross) risk is the exposure before any controls are considered, so it is assessed with controls assumed absent. Residual risk is assessed afterwards.
cards.originalText: Managers will first identify and assess inherent risks by making no inferences about controls embedded in the process; i.e., controls are assumed to be absent.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: An RCSA identifies risks by assuming the mitigating impact of in-place controls, so that the exposure first assessed is net of controls and mitigation.
cards.explanation: An exposure net of controls is residual risk. An RCSA starts with the inherent assessment, which assumes no controls, and only then evaluates the controls.
cards.originalText: In order to estimate realistic outcomes, risks are identified by assuming the mitigation impact of in‑place controls; that is, the risk exposure sought is net of control and mitigation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Risk and control self-assessments (RCSAs) are a good mixture of qualitative and quantitative aspects.
cards.explanation: RCSAs are qualitative and largely judgment-based, so they are not a balanced mix of qualitative and quantitative methods.
cards.originalText: Risk and control self‑assessments (RCSAs) are a good mixture of qualitative and quantitative aspects.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: The main purpose of risk assessment is to prioritize risk management and risk mitigation responses.
cards.explanation: Comparable assessments allow risks to be ordered, so management can direct mitigation effort to the most important ones.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: When backtesting the results of risk assessment against past incident experience, there is a tendency to overestimate the likelihood of an operational risk event.
cards.explanation: Backtests against past incidents tend to show that the likelihood of operational risk events is underestimated, not overestimated.
cards.correction: When backtesting the results of risk assessment against past incident experience, there is a tendency to underestimate the likelihood of an operational risk event.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: When backtesting the results of risk assessment against past incident experience, there is a tendency to underestimate the impact of an operational risk event.
cards.explanation: Backtests against past incidents tend to show that the impact of operational risk events is overestimated, not underestimated.
cards.correction: When backtesting the results of risk assessment against past incident experience, there is a tendency to overestimate the impact of an operational risk event.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Both KRIs and KCIs measure the potential risks that may impact the achievement of strategic objectives.
cards.explanation: KRIs signal exposure to risk, but KCIs measure how effectively controls are operating rather than the exposure itself.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: KCIs identify potential risks, while KRIs measure the effectiveness of control mechanisms in mitigating those risks.
cards.explanation: The definitions are reversed: KRIs signal risk exposure and KCIs measure control effectiveness.
cards.correction: KRIs identify potential risks, while KCIs measure the effectiveness of control mechanisms in mitigating those risks.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Both KRIs and KCIs monitor the effectiveness of risk control mechanisms.
cards.explanation: Only KCIs measure control effectiveness. KRIs measure exposure to risk through its likelihood or impact.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: KRIs identify potential risks that may hinder the achievement of an objective, while KCIs measure the effectiveness of mitigation mechanisms.
cards.explanation: A KRI points at the risk, signalling a change in its likelihood or impact, whereas a KCI points at the control and tests whether it works.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Some metrics can be both KPIs and KRIs, or even share elements of all three (KPI, KRI, and KCI).
cards.explanation: The three metric types overlap significantly; a control failure, for example, can be a KPI, a KRI and a KCI at once.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: KRI thresholds and governance vary according to the organization's risk appetite and risk tolerance levels.
cards.explanation: KRI thresholds show how strict management wants to be in controlling a risk, so they reflect appetite and tolerance.
cards.originalText: KRI thresholds and governance vary according to the organization’s risk appetite and risk tolerance levels.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Natural language processing (NLP) machine learning methods are a cost-effective substitute for risk and control self-assessment (RCSA) because they eliminate the need to select and design KRIs.
cards.explanation: Machine learning, including NLP, can support the selection and design of KRIs, but it neither replaces the RCSA nor removes the need for KRIs.
cards.originalText: Natural language processing (NLP) machine learning methods are a cost‑effective substitute for risk and control self‑assessment (RCSA) because they eliminate the need to select and design KRIs.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: A KPI is more likely to be a lagging metric, while a KRI is more likely to be a leading metric.
cards.explanation: Preventive KRIs are forward-looking, while KPIs typically report performance that has already been achieved.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: An increase in the number of transactions processed per employee is a key risk indicator (KRI) of the likelihood of error.
cards.explanation: A rising workload per employee is a cause of errors, so it is a preventive KRI that measures likelihood.
cards.originalText: An increase in transactions processed per employee is a KRI of likelihood (risk of error).

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Business continuity plans not reviewed before their due dates are a key performance indicator (KPI).
cards.explanation: An overdue plan review shows that a review control is not operating effectively, so it is a key control indicator (KCI).
cards.originalText: Business continuity plans not reviewed before due dates are a KPI.
cards.correction: Business continuity plans not reviewed before their due dates are a key control indicator (KCI).

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: An increase in the sensitivity of data held on a server is a key control indicator (KCI).
cards.explanation: Higher data sensitivity raises the impact if a leak occurs, so it is a KRI of impact. It says nothing about how well controls are working.
cards.originalText: An increase in the sensitivity of data held on a server is a KCI.
cards.correction: An increase in the sensitivity of data held on a server is a key risk indicator (KRI).

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: A business continuity plan that has not been reviewed by its due date is best described as a key control indicator (KCI).
cards.explanation: KCIs measure how effectively controls are operating, and an overdue review shows that the review control is not working.
cards.originalText: key control indicator.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: KRI intervention thresholds should be set identically across all processes so that results are comparable, regardless of risk appetite.
cards.explanation: Tolerance differs by risk, so thresholds should reflect the organisation's risk appetite and tolerance rather than being uniform.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: KRI thresholds express how strict management wishes to be in controlling and mitigating each risk, and so reflect risk appetite and tolerance.
cards.explanation: The thresholds of intervention show management's priorities and tolerance, so they differ by risk and are tied to risk appetite.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: A KRI should only be used if it is also a KCI, since a KRI that does not measure control effectiveness gives no useful signal.
cards.explanation: KRIs measure exposure and may overlap with KCIs, but they need not be control measures to be useful.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: KRIs should be lagging measures of realized losses, since leading measures cannot signal a change in exposure.
cards.explanation: Preventive KRIs are leading indicators of rising cause intensity, which is their purpose. Realised losses are lagging.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: The ability to generate VaR reports is sufficient evidence that a bank's risk management practices are satisfactory.
cards.explanation: VaR is a market risk measurement capability and is not evidence of sound internal controls. It would not detect concealed unauthorised trades.
cards.originalText: Since the bank has the capability to generate VaR reports, its risk management practices are satisfactory.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Having an advanced credit risk management system is sufficient evidence that a bank's risk management practices are satisfactory.
cards.explanation: A good credit risk system addresses credit risk only. It says nothing about operational control gaps such as missing segregation of duties.
cards.originalText: Since the bank has an advanced credit risk management system in place, its risk management practices are satisfactory.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Combining front-office and back-office responsibilities in the same few employees makes a bank more vulnerable to trading fraud.
cards.explanation: It removes segregation of duties, the best-known preventive control for fraud, so one person can initiate, settle and conceal unauthorised trades.
cards.originalText: The joint responsibility for front‑ and back‑office functions makes the bank more vulnerable to trading frauds.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Reconciling internal investment records with the brokerage statement each month is a corrective control.
cards.explanation: Corrective controls lessen the impact of an event, as back-ups and continuity plans do. A reconciliation finds errors that already exist, so it is a detective control.
cards.originalText: corrective control.
cards.correction: Reconciling internal investment records with the brokerage statement each month is a detective control.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Reconciling internal investment records with the brokerage statement each month is a detective control.
cards.explanation: The reconciliation is done after transactions are recorded, so it uncovers errors that have already occurred rather than stopping them.
cards.originalText: detective control.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Reconciling internal investment records with the brokerage statement each month is a preventive control.
cards.explanation: Preventive controls act before the event. A monthly after-the-fact reconciliation only detects errors that already exist.
cards.originalText: preventative control.
cards.correction: Reconciling internal investment records with the brokerage statement each month is a detective control.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Detective controls are implemented to reduce the likelihood of risks materializing by addressing their possible causes.
cards.explanation: Detective controls alert the firm after an incident occurs. It is preventive controls that address causes in advance.
cards.originalText: Detective controls
cards.correction: Preventive controls are implemented to reduce the likelihood of risks materializing by addressing their possible causes.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Corrective controls are implemented to reduce the likelihood of risks materializing by addressing their possible causes.
cards.explanation: Corrective controls lessen the impact of an event once it has occurred and do not influence its likelihood.
cards.originalText: Corrective controls
cards.correction: Preventive controls are implemented to reduce the likelihood of risks materializing by addressing their possible causes.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Preventive controls are implemented to reduce the likelihood of risks materializing by addressing their possible causes.
cards.explanation: Preventive controls take place before a potential risk event and address its causes. Segregation of duties, access controls and levels of authorization are examples.
cards.originalText: Preventative controls

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: According to the Institute of Internal Auditors, controls can be of four types: preventive, detective, corrective, and directive controls.
cards.explanation: The IIA classification used in the reading consists of exactly these four types.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Directive controls aim to alert the firm if an incident occurs, in order to accelerate its resolution and limit the impact of the incident on the firm or its stakeholders.
cards.explanation: Alerting the firm and limiting the impact of an incident defines a detective control. Directive controls are rules and guidance such as policies and training.
cards.originalText: Directive controls aim to alert the firm if an incident occurs to accelerate its resolution and limit the impact of the incident on the firm or its stakeholders.
cards.correction: Detective controls aim to alert the firm if an incident occurs, in order to accelerate its resolution and limit the impact of the incident on the firm or its stakeholders.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Examples of preventive controls include smoke alarms and credit card notifications of potentially fraudulent transactions.
cards.explanation: Smoke alarms and fraud notifications alert the firm after something has happened, so they are detective controls.
cards.correction: Examples of detective controls include smoke alarms and credit card notifications of potentially fraudulent transactions.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Preventive controls are one of the control types in the classification of the Institute of Internal Auditors.
cards.explanation: Preventive, detective, corrective and directive are the four IIA control types.
cards.originalText: Preventive controls

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
