cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Key controls are one of the control types in the classification of the Institute of Internal Auditors.
cards.explanation: Key controls are classified by whether they can sufficiently mitigate a risk on their own, and they can be of any of the four IIA types.
cards.originalText: Key controls

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Manual controls are one of the control types in the classification of the Institute of Internal Auditors.
cards.explanation: Manual versus automated is a classification by execution method. The IIA types are preventive, detective, corrective and directive.
cards.originalText: Manual controls

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Segregation of duties is a preventive control.
cards.explanation: Segregation of duties stops one person from initiating, approving and concealing a transaction, so it acts before the event.
cards.originalText: In regard to (I.), the segregation of duties is a preventative control.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: An intrusion detection system is an example of a detective control.
cards.explanation: Intrusion detection and network monitoring alert the firm to an incident after it starts.
cards.originalText: In regard to (II.), the intrusion detection system is an example of a detective control.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Policies and procedures are directive controls.
cards.explanation: Policies, procedures and training prescribe how a process is to be executed, which defines directive controls.
cards.originalText: In regard to (IV.), the policies and procedures are directive controls.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Control automation transforms model risk into human error risk.
cards.explanation: Automation removes the risk of human error in executing a control but replaces it with technology and model risk.
cards.originalText: In regard to (V.), control automation transforms model risk into human error risk.
cards.correction: Control automation transforms human error risk into technology and model risk.

changes.from: model risk into human error risk
changes.to: human error risk into technology and model risk

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: An employee training program that explains the policies and procedures for reviewing new account applications is a directive control.
cards.explanation: Training that explains policies and procedures gives guidance on how to execute a process, which is the defining feature of a directive control.
cards.originalText: An employee training program that explains the policies and procedures for reviewing new account applications

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: A notification to a credit card customer about a potentially fraudulent transaction on the customer's account is a directive control.
cards.explanation: Such a notification alerts after suspicious activity has occurred, so it is a detective control.
cards.originalText: A notification to a credit card customer about a potentially fraudulent transaction on that customer’s account
cards.correction: A notification to a credit card customer about a potentially fraudulent transaction on the customer's account is a detective control.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: A dual-factor authentication protocol used to control access to critical business systems is a directive control.
cards.explanation: It is an access control that stops unauthorised entry, so it is a preventive control.
cards.originalText: A dual‑factor authentication protocol that is used to control access to critical business systems
cards.correction: A dual-factor authentication protocol used to control access to critical business systems is a preventive control.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Business continuity planning is a corrective control.
cards.explanation: Continuity plans, back-ups and redundancies reduce the impact of an adverse event once it occurs, without changing its likelihood.
cards.originalText: corrective control.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Business continuity planning is a preventive control.
cards.explanation: Preventive controls reduce likelihood, but a continuity plan cannot stop a disruption from happening. It limits the impact afterwards, which makes it a corrective control.
cards.originalText: preventive control.
cards.correction: Business continuity planning is a corrective control.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: An exception report that flags payments exceeding authorized limits after they are made is a preventive control.
cards.explanation: A preventive control acts before the event, such as a requirement for two managers to approve a contract. An exception report that works after payment is a detective control.
cards.originalText: Preventive control
cards.correction: An exception report that flags payments exceeding authorized limits after they are made is a detective control.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Compare different types of internal controls and provide examples of each type of internal control.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: An exception report that flags payments exceeding authorized limits after they are made is a detective control.
cards.explanation: It alerts the firm to a breach after the fact so that it can be resolved quickly, which defines a detective control.
cards.originalText: Detective control

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: A key control is a control that can sufficiently mitigate risk on its own.
cards.explanation: A key (primary) control is sufficient, by itself, to mitigate the risk it addresses.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Controls can either be manual or automated in nature.
cards.explanation: Manual versus automated is a classification of controls by execution method.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Control automation can transform human error risk into technology and model risk.
cards.explanation: Automating a control removes the risk of a person failing to execute it but adds the risk that the system fails or its underlying model is wrong.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Automated data back-up is an essential component of control testing.
cards.explanation: An automated data back-up is itself a control, and an example of control automation and of a corrective control. It is not part of testing a control.
cards.originalText: Automated data back‑up is an essential component of control testing.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: An 'optimistic control', such as a tick-box sign-off that needs exceptional ability or motivation from the controller, is a type of weakly designed control.
cards.explanation: Optimistic controls rely on exceptional ability or motivation of the person performing them and are one of the named weak designs.
cards.originalText: ”Optimistic control.”

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: The 'more of the same' approach, which adds further controls of a design that has already failed, is a type of weakly designed control.
cards.explanation: 'More of the same' is one of the three named weak control designs, alongside optimistic and collective controls.
cards.originalText: ”More of the same.”

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: A 'collective control', such as a four-eyes check that dilutes individual accountability, is a type of weakly designed control.
cards.explanation: Collective controls spread responsibility across several people so that nobody is clearly accountable, which makes them a named weak design.
cards.originalText: ”Collective controls.”

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: System-based data validation is a type of weakly designed control.
cards.explanation: System-based data validation is an example of control automation. The named weak designs are optimistic controls, collective controls and 'more of the same'.
cards.originalText: ”System‑based data validation.”

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Examination, the review of supporting documentation and evidence, is a type of control testing.
cards.explanation: Examination is one of the four main control testing types, alongside self-certification, observation and reperformance.
cards.originalText: Examination

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Observation, the real-time oversight of control execution, is a type of control testing.
cards.explanation: Observation is one of the four main control testing types.
cards.originalText: Observation

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Self-certification (inquiry) is a type of control testing.
cards.explanation: Self-certification is the weakest of the four control testing types, but it is still a testing type.
cards.originalText: Self‑certification

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Independence is one of the four main types of control testing.
cards.explanation: Independence of the testing party is a factor that influences how effective testing is. The four types are self-certification, examination, observation and reperformance.
cards.originalText: Independence

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: The independence of the testing party influences the effectiveness of control testing.
cards.explanation: Independence avoids conflicts of interest and bias, so it is one of the factors that determine how effective testing is.
cards.originalText: The independence of the testing party

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: The frequency of testing influences the effectiveness of control testing.
cards.explanation: Testing frequency should be proportionate to the severity of the risk, so it is a factor in testing effectiveness.
cards.originalText: The frequency of testing

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: The scope and sample of testing influence the effectiveness of control testing.
cards.explanation: The scope and sample size directly affect the results, so they are factors in testing effectiveness.
cards.originalText: Scope and sample

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.statement: Total capital aggregated across credit, market and operational risk equals the sum of the stand-alone capital amounts because each risk class must be fully covered independently.
cards.explanation: Simple summation assumes perfect correlation between the risk classes and ignores diversification.
cards.originalText: Total aggregated capital equals the sum of the stand‑alone capital amounts because each risk class must be fully covered independently.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.statement: Total capital aggregated across credit, market and operational risk is lower than the sum of the stand-alone amounts because not all risks materialize at the same time, which produces inter-risk diversification benefits.
cards.explanation: Aggregation uses correlations below 1 across risk classes with different drivers, so total capital is below the simple sum and the difference is the diversification benefit.
cards.originalText: Total aggregated capital is lower than the sum of the stand‑alone amounts because not all risks materialize at the same time, which produces inter‑risk diversification benefits.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.statement: Total capital aggregated across credit, market and operational risk is higher than the sum of the stand-alone amounts because interactions between risk classes compound losses.
cards.explanation: With imperfect correlation, aggregated capital is lower than the sum of stand-alone capital, not higher.
cards.originalText: Total aggregated capital is higher than the sum of the stand‑alone amounts because interactions between risk classes compound losses.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.statement: Operational risk provides no diversification benefit because it is perfectly correlated with credit and market risk.
cards.explanation: Operational risk typically has low correlation with other risk types, so it adds substantial diversification benefit.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.statement: An enterprise risk management framework consists only of regulatory capital and economic capital.
cards.explanation: An ERM framework also covers governance, risk appetite, risk culture and risk-taking processes, not just capital measures.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.statement: Regulatory capital is the internal capital that firms estimate to reflect their own risk profile and potential unexpected losses.
cards.explanation: That describes economic capital. Regulatory capital is the externally mandated minimum set by regulators.
cards.correction: Economic capital is the internal capital that firms estimate to reflect their own risk profile and potential unexpected losses.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.statement: Pillar 2 of the Basel framework concerns market discipline through mandatory risk disclosures.
cards.explanation: Market discipline through disclosure is Pillar 3. Pillar 2 is supervisory review.
cards.correction: Pillar 3 of the Basel framework concerns market discipline through mandatory risk disclosures.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain and differentiate between regulatory capital and economic capital requirements as prescribed in Basel regulations.
cards.reading: ORR-7: Integrated Risk Management
cards.statement: Basel standards are not laws and are not legally binding in themselves; they take legal force only where national authorities enact them.
cards.explanation: The Basel Committee issues guidance without legal force, and its standards bind only when national legislation or regulators adopt them.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.loText: Describe practices for the governance of risks of interconnected third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.statement: Strategic risk is included in the risk analysis conducted as part of an outsourcing risk management framework.
cards.explanation: Strategic risk is explicitly covered in the analysis of risks arising from an outsourcing relationship.
cards.originalText: Strategic risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.loText: Describe practices for the governance of risks of interconnected third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.statement: Compliance risk is included in the risk analysis conducted as part of an outsourcing risk management framework.
cards.explanation: Compliance risk, covering the regulatory and contractual obligations of the outsourced activity, is explicitly part of the analysis.
cards.originalText: Compliance risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.loText: Describe practices for the governance of risks of interconnected third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.statement: Vendor lock-in risk is included in the risk analysis conducted as part of an outsourcing risk management framework.
cards.explanation: Vendor lock-in risk, the ability to withdraw from the provider and absorb or transfer the activity, is explicitly part of the analysis.
cards.originalText: Vendor lock‑in risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.loText: Describe practices for the governance of risks of interconnected third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.statement: Scenario analyses of provider disruptions need only be run once every three years, after the contract is renewed.
cards.explanation: Advanced regulators expect tests of critical activities based on realistic and probable disruptive scenarios to be conducted at least yearly, not only at contract renewal.
cards.originalText: Run scenario analyses of provider disruptions only once every three years, after the contract is renewed.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.loText: Describe practices for the governance of risks of interconnected third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.statement: A cloud computing arrangement falls outside the outsourcing framework because the provider, not the bank, operates the infrastructure.
cards.explanation: Cloud computing is expressly within the broad definition of third parties and outsourcing, so it falls under the outsourcing framework.
cards.originalText: Treat the cloud arrangement as outside the outsourcing framework because the provider, not the bank, operates the infrastructure.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.loText: Describe practices for the governance of risks of interconnected third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.statement: A bank can rely on a critical provider's own incident response and recovery policies without aligning them to the bank's own policies.
cards.explanation: Regulators stress that firms should align the policies of critical suppliers with their own and plan for incident management, response and recovery.
cards.originalText: Rely on the provider’s own policies for incident response and recovery without aligning them to the bank’s policies.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.loText: Describe practices for the governance of risks of interconnected third-party service providers.
cards.reading: ORR-8: Cyber-resilience: Range of Practices
cards.statement: Supervisory expectations on third-party relationships include maintaining an inventory of outsourced functions and gaining visibility into the provider's sub-outsourcing arrangements.
cards.explanation: Because the firm has no direct control over a provider's subcontractors, supervisors expect disclosure of outsourcing arrangements, an inventory of outsourced functions and visibility into sub-outsourcing.
cards.originalText: Maintain an inventory of outsourced functions and obtain visibility into the provider’s sub‑outsourcing arrangements.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: GDP growth was one of the macro variables in the 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) scenario.
cards.explanation: The SCAP scenario had only three dimensions: GDP growth, unemployment and the house price index.
cards.originalText: GDP growth.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: Unemployment was one of the macro variables in the 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) scenario.
cards.explanation: The SCAP scenario had only three dimensions: GDP growth, unemployment and the house price index.
cards.originalText: Unemployment.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The house price index was one of the macro variables in the 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) scenario.
cards.explanation: The SCAP scenario had only three dimensions: GDP growth, unemployment and the house price index.
cards.originalText: House price index.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: Inflation was one of the macro variables in the 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) scenario.
cards.explanation: SCAP used a simple tri-variate scenario of GDP growth, unemployment and the house price index. Inflation appeared later, as one of eight macro factors in the 2011 EBA test.
cards.originalText: Inflation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) was a macro-prudential stress test run by US supervisors.
cards.explanation: SCAP was the first macro-prudential stress test conducted after the 2007-2009 crisis.
cards.originalText: SCAP 2009 ‑ Supervisory Capital Assessment Program

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The 2010 CEBS exercise run by the Committee of European Banking Supervisors was a stress test of European banks.
cards.explanation: The 2010 CEBS test covered 91 European banks.
cards.originalText: CEBS 2010 ‑ Committee of European Bank Supervisors

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The 2009 Treasury's Capital Assistance Program (TCAP) was a stress test conducted by an authoritative body.
cards.explanation: The Capital Assistance Program was a mechanism to supply equity capital to banks that failed SCAP and could not raise capital privately. It was not a stress test.
cards.originalText: TCAP 2009 ‑ Treasury’s Capital Assistance Program

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR) is a stress test exercise run annually by the US Federal Reserve since 2011.
cards.explanation: CCAR is the Federal Reserve's annual capital review and stress test of large bank holding companies.
cards.originalText: CCAR 2011/2012 ‑ Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The US Federal Reserve conducts an annual assessment of bank holding companies (BHCs) which includes the Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR) and Dodd-Frank supervisory stress tests.
cards.explanation: The Fed's annual BHC assessment combines CCAR with the Dodd-Frank supervisory stress tests.
cards.originalText: The U.S. Federal Reserve conducts an annual assessment of bank holding companies (BHC) which includes a Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR) and Dodd‑Frank supervisory stress tests

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The Committee of European Banking Supervisors (CEBS) oversees the most forward-looking and comprehensive regulatory stress tests, in particular with respect to liquidity risks and emerging cyber-risks.
cards.explanation: The 2010 CEBS test covered only market and credit risk with limited disclosure, and CEBS was succeeded by the EBA.
cards.originalText: The Committee of European Banking Supervisors (CEBS) oversees the most forward‑looking and comprehensive regulatory stress tests, in particular with respect to liquidity risks, emerging cyber‑risks, and the linkage between macro and intermediate risk factors

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) was the first macro-prudential stress test of the global financial crisis; its state space had only three dimensions (GDP growth, unemployment and house price index) and its market risk scenario was based on historical experience.
cards.explanation: SCAP used a tri-variate macro scenario, and its market risk scenario was drawn from observed market moves.
cards.originalText: The Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) was the first of the macro‑prudential stress tests of the global financial crisis (GFC); its state space had only three dimensions (GDP growth, unemployment, and house price index), and the market risk scenario was based in historical experience

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: For the 2011 European Banking Authority (EBA) test, supervisors specified over 70 risk factors for the trading book and eight macro-factors for each of 21 countries.
cards.explanation: The 2011 EBA scenario was far richer than SCAP's three variables, with many trading-book risk factors, eight macro-factors per country and sovereign haircuts across seven maturity buckets.
cards.originalText: For the 2011 European Banking Authority (EBA) test, the supervisors specified over 70 risk factors for the trading book, eight macro‑factors for each of 21 countries (GDP growth, inflation, unemployment, residential and commercial real estate price indices, short and long‑term government rates, and stock prices), plus sovereign haircuts across seven maturity buckets

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: Post-SCAP stress tests take a comprehensive, firm-wide look at the effect of the stress scenarios on the institution.
cards.explanation: After SCAP, stress testing moved from product or business-unit level to the whole firm.
cards.originalText: Post‑SCAP stress tests take a comprehensive, firm‑wide look at the effect of the stress scenarios on the institution.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: Pre-SCAP stress tests were explicitly tied to capital adequacy.
cards.explanation: Pre-SCAP tests were not usually linked to capital adequacy. Tying results to an explicit post-stress capital threshold is a post-SCAP feature.
cards.originalText: Pre‑SCAP stress tests were explicitly tied to capital adequacy.
cards.correction: Post-SCAP stress tests were explicitly tied to capital adequacy.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: Pre-SCAP stress tests focused on losses only, rather than on losses, revenues and costs.
cards.explanation: Before SCAP, tests looked at potential losses only. Post-SCAP tests cover losses, revenues and costs.
cards.originalText: Pre‑SCAP stress tests focused on losses only, rather than losses, revenues and costs.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: Post-SCAP stress tests use broad macro scenarios with market-wide, multi-factor stresses.
cards.explanation: Pre-SCAP tests were mostly single shocks, whereas post-SCAP tests use broad macro scenarios.
cards.originalText: Post‑SCAP stress tests use broad macro scenarios with market‑wide, multi‑factor stresses.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) did not result in any capital raising by participating banks.
cards.explanation: Ten of the 19 SCAP banks had to raise about USD 75 billion of capital, and they raised about USD 77 billion.
cards.originalText: The SCAP scenario was less severe than later U.S. tests and did not result in any capital raising by participating banks.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The 2011 CCAR disclosed bank-level loss rates, whereas the 2012 CCAR published only the macro scenario.
cards.explanation: The years are reversed. The 2011 CCAR published only macro results, while the 2012 CCAR disclosed bank-level detail similar to SCAP.
cards.originalText: The 2011 CCAR disclosed bank‑level loss rates, whereas the 2012 CCAR published only the macro scenario.
cards.correction: The 2012 CCAR disclosed bank-level loss rates, whereas the 2011 CCAR published only the macro scenario.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The 2011 EBA stress test made bank-level results available in downloadable form, including exposures by asset class and geography, which was more detailed than the 2010 CEBS test.
cards.explanation: The 2011 EBA test gave bank-by-bank, asset-class and geography data, a step beyond the limited disclosure of the 2010 CEBS test.
cards.originalText: The 2011 EBA test made bank‑level results available in downloadable form, including exposures by asset class and geography, which was more detailed than the 2010 CEBS test.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: SCAP disclosed only overall retail and corporate loss rates, while the EBA test expanded disclosure to asset classes and regions.
cards.explanation: SCAP released loss rates by major asset class. It was the 2010 CEBS test that gave loss rates only for overall retail and corporate.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) introduced the requirement that banks provide the results of their own scenario stress tests.
cards.explanation: SCAP imposed a common supervisory scenario. Submission of banks' own scenario results came later with the 2011 and 2012 CCAR.
cards.originalText: Banks are now required to provide the results of their own scenario stress tests.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: One result of the 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) was that stress scenarios became broader in nature.
cards.explanation: SCAP moved stress testing to a broad macro scenario.
cards.originalText: Stress scenarios are now broader in nature.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: One result of the 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) was that stress testing came to focus on the whole firm.
cards.explanation: SCAP introduced a comprehensive, firm-wide view in place of product or business-unit tests.
cards.originalText: Stress testing now focuses on the whole firm.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: One result of the 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) was that stress testing came to focus on revenues, costs and projected losses.
cards.explanation: After SCAP, stress tests cover losses, revenues and costs rather than losses only.
cards.originalText: Stress testing now focuses on revenues, costs, and projected losses.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The 2011 CCAR did not require banks to provide results from their own stress scenarios.
cards.explanation: In 2011 and 2012 CCAR did require banks to submit their own baseline and stress results.
cards.originalText: CCAR did not require banks to provide results from their own stress scenarios.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: The 2011 CCAR required disclosure of macro-level, not bank-level, scenario results.
cards.explanation: Only macro-scenario results were published in 2011, whereas the Irish and EBA tests disclosed extensive bank-level detail.
cards.originalText: CCAR required disclosure of macro‑level, not bank‑level, scenario results.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: Stress testing simulates how an institution's results hold up under deteriorating conditions, using adverse scenarios (such as a severe recession) or sensitivities (such as a sharp rise in interest rates).
cards.explanation: After 2007-2009 supervisors used stress tests to judge whether banks held enough capital and liquidity to support their risk taking.
cards.originalText: A simulation of how an institution’s results hold up under deteriorating conditions, using adverse scenarios (e.g., a severe recession) or sensitivities (e.g., a sharp rise in interest rates)

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: Stress testing is a comparison of predicted losses with actual observed losses to judge the reliability of a bank's prediction models.
cards.explanation: That describes backtesting. Stress testing is a forward-looking simulation of results under adverse conditions.
cards.originalText: A comparison of predicted losses with actual observed losses to judge the reliability of a bank’s prediction models

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: Stress testing is a statistical estimate of the maximum loss over a given horizon at a given confidence level under normal market conditions.
cards.explanation: That describes value at risk. Stress tests examine adverse conditions rather than normal markets.
cards.originalText: A statistical estimate of the maximum loss over a given horizon at a given confidence level under normal market conditions

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: A multi-factor stress scenario can be made coherent by specifying an extreme move in the single most volatile risk factor and holding all other risk factors constant.
cards.explanation: Risk factors move together, so holding the others constant ignores their interdependence. This is the one-factor-at-a-time error.
cards.originalText: Specify an extreme move in the single most volatile risk factor and hold all other risk factors constant.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: Setting every risk factor to its own worst-case value independently produces a coherent stress scenario.
cards.explanation: Independent worst cases ignore dependencies and can be mutually impossible, for example all currencies depreciating with no safe haven. Severity is not the same as coherence.
cards.originalText: Set every risk factor to its own worst‑case value independently, so that the scenario is as severe as possible.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: In a trading book with tens of thousands of risk factors, using historical realizations of risk-factor changes is a practical way to achieve a coherent stress scenario.
cards.explanation: Historical moves embed the joint behaviour that actually occurred, so they are coherent without specifying thousands of interdependent moves. The 2009 SCAP market scenario used the moves from June 30 to December 31, 2008.
cards.originalText: Use historical realizations of risk‑factor changes, such as the market moves from June 30 to December 31, 2008 used in the 2009 SCAP.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: Using historical scenarios supports the coherence of the risk-factor moves in a stress test.
cards.explanation: Historical risk-factor moves were observed together, so they are coherent by construction, although they test nothing new.
cards.originalText: Use historical scenarios

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: Excluding safe havens (flight to quality) from a stress scenario supports the coherence of the risk-factor moves.
cards.explanation: A flight to quality requires safe-haven assets, so excluding them makes the scenario incoherent.
cards.originalText: Exclude safe havens (i.e., flight to quality)

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: Depreciating all foreign exchange rates simultaneously is a coherent assumption for a stress scenario.
cards.explanation: Exchange rates are relative prices, so not all currencies can depreciate at once.
cards.originalText: Depreciate all foreign exchange rates simultaneously

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: A stress scenario in which the USD, EUR and JPY all depreciate at the same time against a basket of world currencies is incoherent.
cards.explanation: Exchange rates are relative prices, and these currencies are major components of a world basket, so they cannot all depreciate against it at once.
cards.originalText: The USD, EUR, and JPY all depreciate at the same time against a basket of world currencies.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: A stress scenario in which the correlations between industrial commodity returns and industrial sector equity returns rise at the same time is incoherent.
cards.explanation: Correlations typically rise in stress, so this is a plausible assumption. A severe assumption is not the same as an incoherent one.
cards.originalText: Correlations between returns of commodities used for industrial production and returns of industrial sector equities increase at the same time.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: A stress scenario in which yields on BBB-rated corporate debt rise while yields on AAA-rated short-term sovereign debt fall is incoherent.
cards.explanation: Widening credit spreads alongside falling safe-haven yields is the classic flight to quality, so the combination is coherent.
cards.originalText: Yields on BBB‑rated corporate debt increase as yields on AAA‑rated short‑term sovereign debt decrease.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.loText: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors.
cards.reading: ORR-17: Stress Testing Banks
cards.statement: A key design challenge in stress testing is coherence: the extreme values specified for many risk factors at once must be possible together.
cards.explanation: Stress scenarios are inherently multi-factor, so the joint outcomes must be extreme but still coherent.
cards.originalText: coherence.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: The main purpose of calculating risk capital is to show the level of expected losses that a bank could absorb.
cards.explanation: Expected losses are a cost of doing business covered by pricing and loss reserves. Risk capital covers unexpected losses.
cards.originalText: To show the level of expected losses that the bank could absorb.
cards.correction: The main purpose of calculating risk capital is to show the level of unexpected losses that a bank could absorb.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: The main purpose of calculating risk capital is to find the differences between regulatory capital and risk capital.
cards.explanation: Comparison with regulatory capital can be useful, but it is a by-product and not the purpose. Risk capital is a buffer against unexpected losses.
cards.originalText: To find differences between regulatory and risk capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: The main purpose of calculating risk capital is to show the level of unexpected losses that a bank could absorb.
cards.explanation: Risk capital is a buffer that keeps the firm solvent and a going concern against unexpected losses at the target confidence level.
cards.originalText: To show the level of unexpected losses the bank could absorb.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: In the alternative definition used when linking risk capital to RAROC, economic capital is risk capital plus strategic risk capital (burned-out capital and goodwill).
cards.explanation: Economic capital is usually identical to risk capital, but the broader definition adds an allocation for strategic risk.
cards.originalText: Risk capital plus strategic risk capital (burned‑out capital and goodwill).

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Economic capital is risk capital minus expected losses.
cards.explanation: Risk capital already excludes expected losses, which are covered by pricing and reserves, so subtracting them again is wrong.
cards.originalText: Risk capital minus expected losses.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Economic capital is the greater of regulatory capital and risk capital.
cards.explanation: The greater of regulatory and risk capital is the rule for allocating capital to a division, not a definition of economic capital.
cards.originalText: The greater of regulatory capital and risk capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Economic capital is risk capital plus regulatory capital.
cards.explanation: Adding the two would double count. Regulatory capital is a separate, rule-based minimum and not a component of economic capital.
cards.originalText: Risk capital plus regulatory capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Economic capital is less than risk capital because risk capital must guarantee shareholders with 100% confidence that the firm can ride out any eventuality.
cards.explanation: Risk capital and economic capital are normally identical, and no firm can offer a 100% confidence level.
cards.originalText: ”Economic capital is less than risk capital because risk capital is the capital required to guarantee shareholders with 100.0% confidence that it holds enough risk capital to ride out any eventuality”

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Whenever regulatory capital exceeds economic capital for a business, there is no need to know that business's economic capital.
cards.explanation: Economic capital is still needed to assess the economic viability of an activity, even where regulatory capital is the larger figure.
cards.originalText: ”Regulatory capital is almost certainly higher than economic capital in our securitization business; therefore, we do not need to know its economic capital; in other words, whenever regulatory capital exceeds economic capital, there is no reason or need to know economic capital”

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Risk capital must absorb unexpected losses and keep the firm solvent over a time horizon at a selected confidence level, and unlike regulatory capital, the horizon and confidence level are policy parameters chosen by the firm.
cards.explanation: Regulatory capital follows industry-wide rules, whereas the horizon and confidence level of risk capital are set by senior management and the board.
cards.originalText: ”We need enough risk capital to absorb unexpected losses and remain solvent over a time horizon with a selected confidence level, but with respect to risk capital, (unlike regulatory capital) the horizon and confidence belong to us as policy parameters.”

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: In RAROC, economic capital is the numerator and regulatory capital replaces it as the denominator for performance evaluation.
cards.explanation: Economic capital is the denominator of RAROC, the capital against which risk-adjusted return is measured, and it is not replaced by regulatory capital.
cards.originalText: ”For capital budgeting purposes, we should use ex‑ante RAROC with economic capital in the numerator; for performance evaluation, we should use ex‑post RAROC with regulatory capital in the numerator”

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Economic capital must equal or exceed regulatory capital.
cards.explanation: Regulatory capital is an industry-wide, formula-based minimum that can be above or below a firm's economic capital, so economic capital need not equal or exceed it.
cards.originalText: I only

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Economic capital absorbs unexpected losses up to a certain confidence level and over a specified time horizon.
cards.explanation: Economic capital is a VaR-type buffer against unexpected losses at a stated confidence level and horizon. Expected losses are handled by pricing and reserves.
cards.originalText: V only

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Economic capital absorbs expected losses and should equal the firm's reserves.
cards.explanation: Expected losses are covered by pricing and reserves or provisions. Economic capital absorbs unexpected losses.
cards.originalText: All are true

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Economic capital, if properly calibrated, guarantees that a bank will never default.
cards.explanation: Economic capital covers losses only up to a chosen confidence level, such as 99.9%, so a small residual probability of default always remains.
cards.originalText: Economic capital, if properly calibrated, guarantees the bank will never default

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Economic capital is designed to keep a bank solvent, so it is a solvency measure.
cards.explanation: Economic capital is the amount of capital needed to keep the firm solvent.
cards.originalText: Economic capital is designed to keep a bank solvent; i.e., it is a solvency measure

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Economic capital provides a means for capital allocation within a bank.
cards.explanation: Economic capital is used to allocate capital, and the cost of capital, to business lines.
cards.originalText: Economic capital provides a means for capital allocation within the bank

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: Economic capital is a metric, a risk currency, that can be aggregated across and up and down the organization.
cards.explanation: It serves as a common risk currency that can be aggregated across and within business units.
cards.originalText: Economic capital is a metric (a risk currency) that can be aggregated across and up and down the organization

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: A bank that wants to maintain a AA credit rating should compute economic capital at a 95% confidence level, the level typically used for trading desk VaR limits.
cards.explanation: A 95% level implies a far higher default probability than a AA rating allows. The confidence level must match the target rating.
cards.originalText: At 95%, the level typically used for trading desk VaR limits, because the AA rating is based on day‑to‑day losses

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: The confidence level for economic capital must be the same as the one used for regulatory capital.
cards.explanation: Regulatory capital uses general industry benchmarks and is usually far below risk capital. The confidence level for economic capital is driven by the firm's target rating.
cards.originalText: At 99%, the level used for regulatory capital, because regulatory and economic capital must share the same confidence level

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.loText: Define, compare, and contrast risk capital, economic capital, and regulatory capital and explain methods and motivations for using economic capital approaches to allocate risk capital.
cards.reading: ORR-18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
cards.statement: The confidence level for economic capital should correspond to the default probability implied by the target credit rating, so a AA target requires a confidence level above 99.95%.
cards.explanation: A rating is tied to a probability of default, and a very high rating such as AA or AAA implies a very low default probability, hence a very high confidence level.
cards.originalText: Above 99.95%, because the confidence level should correspond to the default probability implied by the target credit rating

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Effective loss-estimation methodologies is one of the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process under the Federal Reserve's Capital Plan Rule.
cards.explanation: It is principle 2 of the seven principles.
cards.originalText: Effective loss‑estimation methodologies

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Sufficient capital adequacy impact assessment is one of the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process under the Federal Reserve's Capital Plan Rule.
cards.explanation: It is principle 4, which combines loss and resource estimates to assess capital adequacy.
cards.originalText: Sufficient capital adequacy impact assessment

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Adequate IT resources is one of the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process under the Federal Reserve's Capital Plan Rule.
cards.explanation: The seven principles are sound foundational risk management, effective loss-estimation methodologies, solid resource-estimation methodologies, sufficient capital adequacy impact assessment, comprehensive capital policy and planning, robust internal controls, and effective governance. IT resourcing is not a stand-alone principle.
cards.originalText: Adequate IT resources

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Robust internal controls is one of the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process under the Federal Reserve's Capital Plan Rule.
cards.explanation: It is principle 6, covering model validation, documentation and internal audit.
cards.originalText: Robust internal controls

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Under the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process, validation and independent review of models used in capital planning fall under the principle of robust internal controls.
cards.explanation: The internal controls principle covers policies and procedures, change control, model validation and independent review, documentation and internal audit.
cards.originalText: Robust internal controls

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Under the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process, validation of the models used in capital planning falls under the principle of effective governance.
cards.explanation: Governance concerns board and senior management oversight and approval of capital decisions. Model validation sits with the robust internal controls principle.
cards.originalText: Effective governance

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: The principle of effective loss-estimation methodologies requires effective processes for translating risk measures into loss estimates over a range of stressful scenarios and environments.
cards.explanation: A bank holding company that does not cover a satisfactory range of stress scenarios when estimating losses breaches this principle, the second of the seven.
cards.originalText: Effective loss‑estimation methodologies

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: The Federal Reserve's Capital Plan Rule requires bank holding companies to project revenues, expenses, losses and capital over a nine-quarter planning horizon.
cards.explanation: The rule specifies a nine-quarter planning horizon.
cards.originalText: Nine quarters

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: The Federal Reserve's Capital Plan Rule requires bank holding companies to project revenues, expenses, losses and capital over an eight-quarter planning horizon.
cards.explanation: The planning horizon is nine quarters, not the round-number eight quarters of two years.
cards.originalText: Eight quarters
cards.correction: The Federal Reserve's Capital Plan Rule requires bank holding companies to project revenues, expenses, losses and capital over a nine-quarter planning horizon.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
