cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: The Federal Reserve's Capital Plan Rule does not define an explicit length of time for the planning horizon of capital projections.
cards.explanation: The Capital Plan Rule explicitly defines the planning horizon as nine quarters.
cards.originalText: There is no explicit length of time defined by the Federal Reserve

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Periodic review by the board and senior management of a bank holding company's risk infrastructure and loss-estimation methodologies falls under the principle of robust internal controls.
cards.explanation: Internal controls cover validation, documentation, change control and internal audit. Periodic senior-level review of infrastructure and methodologies belongs to effective governance.
cards.originalText: Robust internal controls

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: The principle of effective governance requires periodic review by the board and senior management of the bank holding company's risk infrastructure and loss-estimation methodologies.
cards.explanation: Governance is the seventh principle and assigns oversight, including periodic review of risk infrastructure and estimation methodologies, to the board and senior management.
cards.originalText: Effective governance

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: The Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR) is the Federal Reserve's supervisory program for assessing the capital plans of large bank holding companies.
cards.explanation: CCAR is the Fed's program for evaluating the capital plans of large BHCs.
cards.originalText: The Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR) is the Federal Reserve’s supervisory program for assessing the capital plans of large BHCs.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: The Dodd-Frank Act supervisory stress tests play an important role in CCAR, using supervisory adverse and severely adverse scenarios.
cards.explanation: The supervisory stress tests feed into CCAR and use adverse and severely adverse scenarios.
cards.originalText: The Dodd‑Frank Act supervisory stress tests play an important role in CCAR, using supervisory adverse and severely adverse scenarios.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Once a bank holding company meets the minimum regulatory capital requirements in normal, non-stressed times, the Federal Reserve cannot restrict its freedom to pay dividends or repurchase shares.
cards.explanation: The Federal Reserve assesses planned capital actions under stress and can object to a capital plan, so meeting minimum ratios in good times does not remove supervisory limits on payouts.
cards.originalText: Once a BHC meets the minimum regulatory capital requirements in normal, non‑stressed times, the Federal Reserve cannot restrict its freedom to pay dividends or repurchase shares.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: The seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process are: sound foundational risk management; effective loss-estimation methodologies; solid resource-estimation methodologies; sufficient capital adequacy impact assessment; comprehensive capital policy and capital planning; robust internal controls; and effective governance.
cards.explanation: This is the complete list of the seven principles of the Federal Reserve's capital adequacy process.
cards.originalText: The seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process are: sound foundational risk management; effective loss‑estimation methodologies; solid resource‑estimation methodologies; sufficient capital adequacy impact assessment; comprehensive capital policy and capital planning; robust internal controls; and effective governance.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Under the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process, internal controls should be documented and subjected to internal audit.
cards.explanation: Principle 6 requires comprehensive documentation and internal audit review of controls.
cards.originalText: Internal controls should be documented and subjected to internal audit.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Under the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process, a bank holding company should have a process to estimate potential losses and aggregate them on a firm-wide basis.
cards.explanation: This is principle 2, effective loss-estimation methodologies.
cards.originalText: A process should be in place to estimate potential losses and aggregate them on a firm‑wide basis.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Under the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process, oversight should be managed by a third-party risk assessor appointed by the board of directors of the bank holding company.
cards.explanation: The governance principle assigns oversight to the board and senior management of the bank holding company itself.
cards.originalText: Oversight should be managed by a third‑party risk assessor appointed by the BHC’s board of directors.

cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Under the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process, loss estimates and capital resources should be considered together in determining the impact on capital adequacy.
cards.explanation: This is principle 4, sufficient capital adequacy impact assessment.
cards.originalText: Loss estimates and capital resources should be considered in determining the impact on capital adequacy.

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Oversight from peer bank holding companies is one of the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process.
cards.explanation: Oversight is assigned to the bank holding company's own board and senior management, not to peers.
cards.originalText: I only.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe the Federal Reserve’s Capital Plan Rule and explain the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process for bank holding companies (BHCs) subject to the Capital Plan Rule.
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Annual reporting to the stock exchange on which a bank holding company's stock is listed is one of the seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process.
cards.explanation: The seven principles concern internal risk management, estimation, impact assessment, policy, controls and governance. Exchange reporting is not among them.
cards.originalText: II only.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas: - Risk identification - Internal controls, including model review and validation - Corporate governance - Capital policy, including setting of goals and targets and contingency planning - Stress testing and stress scenario design - Estimating losses, revenues, and expenses, including quantitative and qualitative methodologies - Assessing the impact of capital adequacy, including risk-weighted asset (RWA) and balance sheet projections
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Credit risk is a well-defined, quantifiable risk category, not one of the hard-to-quantify 'other risks' that a stress test must still account for.
cards.explanation: Reputational, strategic and compliance risk are the standard examples of 'other risks' that are hard to quantify or not attributable to a specific firm-wide risk category. Credit risk is a core, quantifiable category modelled directly.
cards.originalText: Credit risk

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Reputational risk is an example of an 'other risk' that is difficult to quantify and not directly attributable to a specific integrated firm-wide risk category.
cards.explanation: Reputational, strategic and compliance risk are the standard examples of 'other risks' that BHCs must still account for in capital planning.
cards.originalText: Reputational risk

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Best practice for stress testing complex derivative exposures is a full-revaluation approach, because payoffs are nonlinear and stress scenarios involve very large risk-factor moves.
cards.explanation: Approximations such as delta-gamma can mismeasure losses under large moves in nonlinear positions, so full revaluation is the leading practice.
cards.originalText: Use a full‑revaluation approach to model the bank’s complex derivative exposures.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Best practice uses the minimum required regulatory capital ratios as the initial trigger for contingency capital actions.
cards.explanation: Triggers set at the regulatory minima leave no time to act. Contingency triggers should be set above the minima and consider stakeholder expectations.
cards.originalText: Use minimum required regulatory capital ratios as the initial trigger for potential contingency capital actions to be taken.
cards.correction: Best practice sets the initial trigger for contingency capital actions above the minimum required regulatory capital ratios.

changes.from: uses the minimum required regulatory capital ratios as

changes.to: trigger for contingency capital actions above the minimum required regulatory capital ratios.

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Best practice models the loss given default of a bank's loan portfolio using a single weighted-average approach at the aggregate portfolio level.
cards.explanation: An aggregate weighted-average LGD hides variation across segments and ignores LGD rising under stress. Leading practice segments LGD and ties it to scenario severity.
cards.originalText: Model the loss given default of the bank’s loan portfolio using a weighted‑average approach at the aggregate portfolio level.

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Best practice in stress testing is to test a wide range of adverse effects that reach outside established internal data patterns.
cards.explanation: Stress tests should challenge historical patterns with severe adverse outcomes rather than assume past performance persists, especially for a business with a short and benign history.
cards.originalText: Test a wide range of adverse effects reaching outside the established data patterns.

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Best practice in stress testing is to ensure minimal variation from established internal data patterns.
cards.explanation: Staying close to internal data patterns assumes that past, possibly benign, behaviour continues. The Federal Reserve expects conservative assumptions and testing of outcomes outside historical patterns.
cards.originalText: Ensure minimal variation from established internal data patterns.

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: When documenting its estimates, a BHC should explain its key methodologies and assumptions concisely and present them in a well-organized manner.
cards.explanation: Leading practice documentation concisely explains key methodologies, drivers and assumptions and how they relate to the estimates.
cards.originalText: Concisely explained key methodologies and assumptions presented in a well‑organized manner.

cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: When documenting its estimates, a BHC should give extremely detailed explanations of its methodologies and present every bit of available data.
cards.explanation: Documentation should be concise and focus on key methodologies and assumptions. Presenting every piece of data is not concise.
cards.originalText: Extremely detailed explanations of key methodologies with every bit of data available being presented.

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: A feeder model produces projections or estimates that are used as inputs to another model, which generates the final figures for expected losses, expenses and revenues.
cards.explanation: BHCs should keep an inventory of all models used in capital planning, including feeder (input) models whose outputs flow into the downstream models that produce final projections.
cards.originalText: Models used to produce projections or estimates that can then be used in another model to generate final figures for expected losses, expenses and revenue.

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Feeder models are the models used to generate the final projected figures for losses, expenses and revenues.
cards.explanation: Feeder models supply intermediate estimates. The downstream models they feed into produce the final projected losses, expenses and revenues.
cards.originalText: Models used to generate the final projected figures for losses, expenses, and revenues.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Internal controls over capital planning should ensure that management information systems are robust enough to support capital analysis and decision making, with enough flexibility to run ad hoc analysis when necessary.
cards.explanation: Robust and flexible MIS is one of the specific control measures expected over the capital planning process.
cards.originalText: Making sure that there is sufficient robustness in MIS for capital analysis and decision making to be supported, with sufficient flexibility to run ad‑hoc analysis whenever necessary.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Internal controls over capital planning should provide for reconciliation and data integrity processes for all key reports.
cards.explanation: Reconciliation and data integrity processes for key reports are among the specific control measures expected at all levels of the capital planning process.
cards.originalText: Provide for reconciliation and data integrity process for all key reports.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.loText: Describe practices that can result in a strong and effective capital adequacy process for a BHC in the following areas: - Risk identification - Internal controls, including model review and validation - Corporate governance - Capital policy, including setting of goals and targets and contingency planning - Stress testing and stress scenario design - Estimating losses, revenues, and expenses, including quantitative and qualitative methodologies - Assessing the impact of capital adequacy, including risk-weighted asset (RWA) and balance sheet projections
cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: For market and counterparty credit risk, the Federal Reserve much prefers probabilistic approaches to deterministic approaches because deterministic approaches do not link stress scenarios to risk factor shocks.
cards.explanation: The Federal Reserve does not state a strong preference. Probabilistic and deterministic approaches each have strengths and weaknesses, and most BHCs used deterministic approaches that do tie scenarios to risk factor shocks.
cards.originalText: With respect to Market and Counterparty Credit Risk, the Federal Reserve much prefers probabilistic approaches to deterministic approaches because deterministic approaches do not link stress scenarios to risk factor shocks

cards.topic: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Most BHCs use some form of expert judgment for some purposes, often as a management adjustment overlay to modelled outputs.
cards.explanation: Expert judgment is widely used in capital planning, commonly as an overlay applied to model results.
cards.originalText: Most BHCs use some forms of expert judgment for some purposes, often as a management adjustment overlay to modeled outputs

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: With expected loss approaches, BHCs with leading practices break losses down into PD, LGD and EAD components and separately identify the key risk drivers of each component.
cards.explanation: Decomposing expected loss into probability of default, loss given default and exposure at default lets the key drivers of each component be identified separately.
cards.originalText: With respect to Expected Loss Approaches, BHCs with leading practices were able to break down losses into PD, LGD, and EAD components, separately identifying key risk drivers for each of those components

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Operational-risk loss estimation for stress scenarios commonly uses regression models, modified loss-distribution-approach (LDA) models and scenario analysis, although best practice is still evolving.
cards.explanation: Regression models, modified LDA and scenario analysis are the common approaches to stressed operational loss estimation.
cards.originalText: Although best practices in operational‑risk models are still evolving, common approaches to operational loss estimation for stress scenarios include regression models, modified loss‑distribution‑approach (LDA), and scenario analysis

cards.statement: Under the Capital Plan Rule, a BHC must project its revenue and expenses over a planning horizon of at least five years.

cards.statement: Credit-sensitive securities should be tested for other-than-temporary impairment using ratings that are projected to migrate under the stress scenario, rather than holding ratings static.
cards.explanation: Stronger practice projects rating migration under the scenario and applies the impairment test to the migrated ratings.
cards.originalText: Test credit‑sensitive securities for other‑than‑temporary impairment using ratings that are projected to migrate under the stress scenario, rather than holding ratings static.

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Applying scalar adjustments to baseline loss estimates is an appropriate way to project stressed losses for large loan portfolios.
cards.explanation: Scalars lack transparency and sensitivity to portfolio composition and scenario variables. Their use should be limited, at most, to immaterial portfolios.
cards.originalText: Rely on scalar adjustments to baseline loss estimates for large loan portfolios to project losses during adverse market conditions.

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: A stress test should model better-than-average revenue performance during stress to reflect the bank's competitive advantage.
cards.explanation: Assuming outperformance because of competitive strength benefits the BHC and defeats the purpose of a stress test.
cards.originalText: Model better‑than‑average revenue performance during times of stress to reflect the bank’s competitive advantage.

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Seasonality can be removed from loss and revenue projections by dividing annual estimates for products evenly across the quarters of the year.
cards.explanation: Spreading annual figures evenly ignores seasonality and the true quarterly path of losses. It is a weak practice.
cards.originalText: Remove the impact of seasonality by dividing annual revenue and loss estimates for different types of products evenly across the year.

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Stressed operational loss estimates should incorporate forward-looking factors and idiosyncratic risk exposures rather than relying only on historical experience.
cards.explanation: Stronger BHC practice blends historical operational loss experience with forward-looking elements and the bank's idiosyncratic risks.
cards.originalText: Incorporating forward‑looking factors and idiosyncratic risk exposures into stressed operational loss estimates.

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Operational losses should be modelled by projecting an annual loss estimate and then distributing it evenly across the four quarters of the year.
cards.explanation: Even quarterly allocation is a weak practice because it ignores the likely timing of operational losses.
cards.originalText: Modeling operational losses by projecting an annual loss estimate and then evenly distributing the losses across the four quarters of the year.

cards.reading: ORR-20: Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies
cards.statement: Designing and testing a scenario in which a major counterparty defaults is an example of a BHC's stress testing and stress scenario design policy.
cards.explanation: Counterparty-default scenarios are a standard element of stress testing and scenario design.
cards.originalText: Designing and testing a scenario‑related default of a major counterparty is an example of BHC stress testing and a stress scenario design policy.

cards.statement: Net interest income projections should incorporate prepayment rates.
cards.explanation: NII projections should reflect changing conditions in balance sheet positions, embedded options, prepayment rates, loan performance and repricing rates.

cards.statement: Net interest income projections should incorporate embedded options.
cards.explanation: Embedded options affect cash flows and repricing, so they belong in scenario-consistent NII projections.
cards.originalText: Embedded options.

cards.explanation: NII projections are driven by scenario-consistent balance sheet and rate-behaviour drivers such as positions, embedded options, prepayments, loan performance and repricing, not by management earnings guidance.

cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The original Basel accord was motivated by the growth of cross-border finance, which gave the G10 nations a common interest in banks holding enough equity to absorb large losses, and by the perception that banks in countries with low minimum capital had a competitive advantage.
cards.explanation: Basel I aimed at bank solvency in an era of cross-border finance and at a level playing field given widely differing national capital minimums.
cards.originalText: The growth of cross‑border finance, which gave the G10 nations a common interest in banks having enough equity to absorb large losses, and the perception that banks in countries with low minimum capital had a competitive advantage.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The original Basel I accord was motivated by the need to capture operational and market risk in capital requirements and to let banks use internal models to set capital.
cards.explanation: Operational risk capital and internal models arrived with Basel II, and market risk with the 1996 amendment. Basel I covered credit risk only, using standardized risk weights.
cards.originalText: The need to capture operational and market risk in capital requirements, and the need to let banks use internal models to set capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The main goal of the original Basel I accord was to ensure that internationally active banks hold enough capital, tied to risk-weighted assets, to remain solvent in times of distress, while creating a more level competitive playing field.
cards.explanation: Basel I set risk-based capital ratios to keep banks adequately capitalized relative to risk and to reduce competitive inequality arising from differing national minimums.
cards.originalText: To ensure internationally active banks hold enough capital, tied to risk‑weighted assets, to remain solvent in times of distress while creating a more level competitive playing field.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The main goal of the original Basel I accord was to make Basel standards legally binding on all banks worldwide so that national regulators lose discretion.
cards.explanation: Basel I has no legal authority of its own. Countries adopt it through their domestic law and regulation.
cards.originalText: To make Basel standards legally binding on all banks worldwide so that national regulators lose discretion.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The main goal of the original Basel I accord was to eliminate settlement (Herstatt) risk in foreign exchange transactions by synchronizing delivery times across time zones.
cards.explanation: Settlement risk from the Herstatt failure led to the creation of the Basel Committee in 1974. Basel I set risk-based capital ratios.
cards.originalText: To eliminate settlement (Herstatt) risk in foreign exchange transactions by synchronizing delivery times across time zones.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The growth of cross-border finance required both the solvency of banks during stressful periods and fair competition between banks competing in each other's home countries, so the motivations for the original Basel accord were bank safety and competitive concerns.
cards.explanation: Basel I addressed bank solvency in an era of cross-border finance and the competitive distortion from differing national capital minimums.
cards.originalText: The growth of cross‑border finance required both the solvency of banks during stressful periods and fair competition (a level playing field) between banks competing in each other’s home countries; i.e., the motivations were bank safety and competitive concerns.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The motivation for the original Basel accord was the need for specific measures of short- and long-term liquidity, because liquidity crunches had been the common denominator of recent financial disasters.
cards.explanation: Liquidity measures such as the LCR and NSFR came with Basel III. Basel I was a solvency (capital) standard.
cards.originalText: Regulators realized that specific measures of short‑ and long‑term liquidity were necessary given that liquidity crunches had been the common denominator of recent financial disasters; i.e., the motivation was liquidity.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel I was motivated by national capital rules that differed widely, were based on total assets and ignored the riskiness of individual banks and off-balance-sheet exposures, and by the perceived competitive advantage of internationally active banks in low-requirement countries.
cards.explanation: Before 1988 capital rules were inconsistent across countries and ratios to total assets ignored asset risk and growing off-balance-sheet derivatives, which Basel I addressed with risk weighting.
cards.originalText: Capital rules differed widely across countries and were based on total assets, ignoring the riskiness of individual banks and off‑balance‑sheet exposures; internationally active banks in low‑requirement countries were seen to have a competitive advantage.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the motivations for introducing the Basel regulations, including key risk exposures addressed, and explain the reasons for revisions to Basel regulations over time.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel I was motivated by a need to impose capital charges for market risk and operational risk, which banks had previously left unmeasured.
cards.explanation: Market risk capital came with the 1996 amendment and operational risk capital with Basel II. Basel I covered credit risk only.
cards.originalText: A need to impose capital charges for market risk and operational risk, which banks had previously left unmeasured.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, banks must hold at least USD 8 of capital for every USD 100 of risk-weighted assets.
cards.explanation: The Basel I minimum total capital ratio is 8% of risk-weighted assets, with Tier 1 capital at least 4%.
cards.originalText: All banks must hold at least \$8 of capital for every \$100 of risk‑weighted assets.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, banks must hold at most USD 8 of capital for every USD 100 of risk-weighted assets.
cards.explanation: The 8% capital ratio is a regulatory floor, not a ceiling.
cards.originalText: All banks must hold at most \$8 of capital for every \$100 of risk‑weighted assets.
cards.correction: Under Basel I, banks must hold at least USD 8 of capital for every USD 100 of risk-weighted assets.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The original Basel I accord judged the capital sufficiency of banks by capital divided by risk-weighted assets, including off-balance-sheet and derivative exposures.
cards.explanation: Basel I chose a risk-sensitive ratio over a plain leverage ratio so that capital requirements reflect the riskiness of assets, including off-balance-sheet items.
cards.originalText: Capital divided by risk‑weighted assets, including off‑balance‑sheet and derivative exposures

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The original Basel I accord judged the capital sufficiency of banks by capital divided by the book value of total on-balance-sheet assets.
cards.explanation: A ratio to total assets ignores asset risk and off-balance-sheet exposures. Basel I used risk-weighted assets as the denominator.
cards.originalText: Capital divided by the book value of total on‑balance‑sheet assets

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, claims on OECD central governments, such as government bonds, carry a risk weight of 0%.
cards.explanation: Basel I assumed that OECD governments would not default on their obligations, so these claims receive a 0% weight.
cards.originalText: Claims on OECD central governments (e.g., government bonds)

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, uninsured residential mortgages carry a risk weight of 0%.
cards.explanation: Uninsured residential mortgages carry a 50% risk weight under Basel I.
cards.originalText: Uninsured residential mortgages
cards.correction: Under Basel I, uninsured residential mortgages carry a risk weight of 50%.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, claims on OECD banks and OECD public sector entities carry a risk weight of 0%.
cards.explanation: Claims on OECD banks and OECD public sector entities carry a 20% risk weight under Basel I.
cards.originalText: Claims on OECD banks and OECD public sector entities
cards.correction: Under Basel I, claims on OECD banks and OECD public sector entities carry a risk weight of 20%.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The capital adequacy ratio under the Basel framework is the sum of Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital divided by risk-weighted assets.
cards.explanation: The ratio compares total regulatory capital with risk-weighted assets, so assets are scaled by their riskiness.
cards.originalText: Sum of Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital divided by risk‑weighted assets (RWA)

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The capital adequacy ratio under the Basel framework is the sum of Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital divided by total unweighted assets.
cards.explanation: Dividing by unweighted total assets gives a leverage-type ratio, which Basel rejected because it ignores asset risk. The denominator is risk-weighted assets.
cards.originalText: Sum of Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital divided by total (unweighted) assets

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, the credit equivalent for derivatives was their current market value, so out-of-the-money positions reduced the bank's risk-weighted assets.
cards.explanation: The derivative credit equivalent was the greater of zero and market value, plus an add-on. Out-of-the-money positions therefore contributed zero and never reduced RWA.
cards.originalText: The credit equivalent for derivatives was their current market value, so out‑of‑the‑money positions reduced the bank’s RWA

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I there were only four risk weights: 0%, 20%, 50% and 100%.
cards.explanation: Basel I used four risk-weight buckets: 0%, 20%, 50% and 100%.
cards.originalText: There were only four risk weights: 0%, 20%, 50%, and 100%

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, total regulatory capital had to exceed 8.0% of risk-weighted assets and Tier 1 capital had to exceed 4.0% of risk-weighted assets.
cards.explanation: These are the Basel I (Cooke ratio) minimums: 8% total capital and 4% Tier 1 capital, both relative to RWA.
cards.originalText: Total regulatory capital had to exceed 8.0% of risk‑weighted assets (RWA), and Tier 1 capital had to exceed 4.0% of RWA

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, traditional off-balance-sheet exposures were converted to a credit equivalent that was then assigned a risk weight based on the counterparty.
cards.explanation: Off-balance-sheet items were multiplied by a credit conversion factor and the resulting credit equivalent was weighted by counterparty type.
cards.originalText: Traditional off‑balance‑sheet exposures were converted to a credit equivalent that was then assigned a risk weight based on the counterparty

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, equity and noncumulative perpetual preferred stock are Tier 1 capital, while subordinated debt with an original maturity of over five years is Tier 2 capital.
cards.explanation: Tier 1 is permanent, loss-absorbing capital that preserves solvency. Subordinated debt protects depositors rather than the going concern, so it is Tier 2.
cards.originalText: Tier 1 capital includes equity and noncumulative perpetual preferred stock, and Tier 2 includes subordinated debt.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, subordinated debt with an original maturity of over five years is Tier 1 capital.
cards.explanation: Subordinated debt only protects depositors in a failure, so it is Tier 2 capital.
cards.originalText: Tier 1 capital includes equity, noncumulative perpetual preferred stock, and subordinated debt.
cards.correction: Under Basel I, subordinated debt with an original maturity of over five years is Tier 2 capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, noncumulative perpetual preferred stock is Tier 2 capital.
cards.explanation: Because its dividends need not accumulate, noncumulative perpetual preferred stock counts as Tier 1 capital under Basel I.
cards.originalText: Tier 1 capital includes equity, and Tier 2 capital includes noncumulative perpetual preferred stock and subordinated debt.
cards.correction: Under Basel I, noncumulative perpetual preferred stock is Tier 1 capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, total capital equals Tier 1 capital plus Tier 2 capital.
cards.explanation: Total regulatory capital is the sum of Tier 1 (core) and Tier 2 (supplementary) capital.
cards.originalText: Tier 1 capital + Tier 2 capital = Total capital

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, common equity is a constituent of Tier 2 capital.
cards.explanation: Common equity is core, loss-absorbing Tier 1 capital, not Tier 2.
cards.originalText: Common equity
cards.correction: Under Basel I, common equity is a constituent of Tier 1 capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, undisclosed reserves are a constituent of Tier 2 capital.
cards.explanation: Undisclosed reserves are supplementary (Tier 2) capital.
cards.originalText: Undisclosed reserves

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, hybrid instruments are a constituent of Tier 2 capital.
cards.explanation: Hybrid instruments, such as subordinated instruments with deferrable payments, are supplementary (Tier 2) capital.
cards.originalText: Hybrid instruments

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel I, general loan loss reserves that are not allocated to non-performing assets are a constituent of Tier 2 capital.
cards.explanation: General loan loss reserves not tied to particular impaired assets are Tier 2 capital, subject to a cap.
cards.originalText: Loan loss reserves not allocated to non‑performing assets

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Pillar 2 of Basel II, supervisors should discourage banks from operating above the minimum regulatory capital limits because this tends to be associated with regulatory arbitrage.
cards.explanation: Pillar 2 expects banks to operate above the minimum capital ratios, and supervisors should be able to require them to do so.
cards.originalText: Supervisors should discourage banks from operating above the minimum regulatory capital limits because this tends to be associated with regulatory arbitrage.
cards.correction: Under Pillar 2 of Basel II, supervisors should expect banks to operate above the minimum regulatory capital limits.

changes.from: discourage banks from operating above the minimum regulatory capital limits because this tends to be associated with regulatory arbitrage
changes.to: expect banks to operate above the minimum regulatory capital limits

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Pillar 2 of Basel II, banks should have a process for assessing their overall capital adequacy in relation to their risk profile and a strategy for maintaining their capital levels.
cards.explanation: This is the internal capital adequacy assessment (ICAAP) principle, a duty of the bank rather than of the supervisor.
cards.originalText: Banks should have a process for assessing their overall capital adequacy in relation to their risk profile and a strategy for maintaining their capital levels.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Pillar 2 of Basel II, supervisors should seek to intervene at an early stage to prevent capital from falling below the minimum levels required to support a bank's risk characteristics, and should require rapid remedial action if capital is not maintained or restored.
cards.explanation: Early intervention is one of the four key principles of supervisory review.
cards.originalText: Supervisors should seek to intervene at an early stage to prevent capital from falling below the minimum levels required to support the risk characteristics of a particular bank and should require rapid remedial action if capital is not maintained or restored.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Pillar 3 of Basel II, if a bank publishes an annual report with GAAP-compliant financial reports, additional Pillar 3 disclosure is waived because of redundancy.
cards.explanation: Pillar 3 is a separate regulatory disclosure requirement, and accounting statements do not substitute for it.
cards.originalText: If a bank publishes an annual report with GAAP‑compliant financial reports, then additional Third Pillar disclosure is waived due to redundancies.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Pillar 3 of Basel II, banks should disclose the structure of the risk management function and how it operates.
cards.explanation: Disclosure of the risk management function's structure and operation is among the Pillar 3 requirements.
cards.originalText: Banks should disclose the structure of the risk management function and how it operates.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Pillar 3 of Basel II, banks should disclose the terms and conditions of the main features of all capital instruments.
cards.explanation: Disclosure of the terms and conditions of capital instruments is a Pillar 3 requirement.
cards.originalText: Banks should disclose the terms and conditions of the main features of all capital instruments.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Pillar 3 of Basel II, banks should disclose the entities in the banking group to which Basel II is applied and the adjustments made for entities to which it is not applied.
cards.explanation: The scope of application of Basel II within the banking group must be disclosed under Pillar 3.
cards.originalText: Banks should disclose the entities in the banking group to which Basel II is applied and adjustments made for entities to which it is not applied.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The internal models-based approach for market risk allows a bank to explicitly recognise diversification benefits.
cards.explanation: The bank's own VaR model uses estimated correlations across positions, so diversification is reflected in the capital charge.
cards.originalText: The internal models‑based approach for market risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The standardized approach for operational risk allows a bank to explicitly recognise diversification benefits.
cards.explanation: The standardized approach simply adds the capital charges of the business lines, which implicitly assumes perfect correlation and gives no diversification credit.
cards.originalText: The Standardized approach for operational risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The Foundation Internal Ratings Based approach for credit risk allows a bank to explicitly recognise diversification benefits.
cards.explanation: IRB approaches use a supervisory formula with prescribed correlations, so no bank-specific diversification is recognised.
cards.originalText: The Foundation Internal Ratings Based approach for credit risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The Advanced Internal Ratings Based approach for credit risk allows a bank to explicitly recognise diversification benefits.
cards.explanation: Under advanced IRB the bank estimates LGD and EAD, but the correlation in the capital formula remains prescribed, so no bank-specific diversification is recognised.
cards.originalText: The Advanced IRB approach for credit risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Operational risk was the new risk that Basel II added to the Pillar 1 minimum capital requirement.
cards.explanation: Credit risk was covered by Basel I (1988) and market risk by the 1996 amendment. Basel II added operational risk.
cards.originalText: Operational risk

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel II introduced the capital requirement for market risk in the trading book.
cards.explanation: Market risk capital was introduced by the 1996 amendment to Basel I and was unchanged in Basel II.
cards.originalText: Market risk in the trading book

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel II, interest rate risk in the banking book is subject to a Pillar 1 minimum capital charge.
cards.explanation: Interest rate risk in the banking book is addressed under Pillar 2 (supervisory review), not through a Pillar 1 charge.
cards.originalText: Interest rate risk in the banking book

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Sound corporate governance is one of the three pillars of Basel II.
cards.explanation: The three pillars are minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline. Corporate governance is not a pillar.
cards.originalText: Sound corporate governance

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Minimum capital requirements are a pillar of the Basel II framework.
cards.explanation: Pillar 1 of Basel II is minimum capital requirements.
cards.originalText: Minimum capital requirements

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Supervisory review is a pillar of the Basel II framework.
cards.explanation: Pillar 2 of Basel II is supervisory review.
cards.originalText: Supervisory review

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe changes to the Basel regulations made as part of Basel II, including the three pillars.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Market discipline is a pillar of the Basel II framework.
cards.explanation: Pillar 3 of Basel II is market discipline, achieved through disclosure.
cards.originalText: Market discipline

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The incremental risk charge (IRC) captures jump-to-default risk, together with rating-migration risk, on credit-sensitive trading book positions.
cards.explanation: The IRC was added in Basel 2.5 to capture credit-related losses in the trading book that the 10-day VaR and specific risk charge missed.
cards.originalText: Jump‑to‑default risk

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The incremental risk charge (IRC) is designed to capture general interest rate risk in the trading book.
cards.explanation: Interest rate risk is captured by the regular and stressed VaR. The IRC is credit-focused.
cards.originalText: Interest rate risk

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The incremental risk charge (IRC) is designed to capture foreign exchange risk in the trading book.
cards.explanation: Foreign exchange risk is a market risk captured by VaR and stressed VaR. The IRC is focused on credit risk.
cards.originalText: Foreign exchange risk

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The incremental risk charge (IRC) is designed to account for correlation risks in the correlation book, which includes securitizations and re-securitizations.
cards.explanation: Correlation-sensitive positions such as securitizations and re-securitizations fall under the comprehensive risk charge, not the IRC.
cards.originalText: The IRC is designed to account for correlation risks in the correlation book, which includes securitizations and re‑securitizations

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The incremental risk charge (IRC) is calculated as the one-year 99.9% value at risk (VaR) for losses on credit instruments in the trading book.
cards.explanation: The IRC is a one-year, 99.9% VaR on credit-sensitive trading book positions.
cards.originalText: The IRC is calculated as the one‑year 99.9% value at risk (VaR) for losses on credit instruments in the trading book

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The incremental risk charge (IRC) excludes ratings changes or migrations because a rating change does not itself lead to default within the one-year horizon.
cards.explanation: The IRC covers rating migrations (downgrades) as well as defaults, because many crisis losses came from downgrades and spread widening rather than from defaults.
cards.originalText: The IRC excludes ratings changes or migrations because a rating change does not itself lead to default within the one‑year horizon
cards.correction: The incremental risk charge (IRC) includes ratings changes or migrations in addition to default.

changes.from: excludes ratings changes or migrations because a rating change does not itself lead to default within the one-year horizon
changes.to: includes ratings changes or migrations in addition to default

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The incremental risk charge (IRC) was introduced because instruments in the trading book often required less regulatory capital than equivalent instruments in the banking book.
cards.explanation: Lower trading book capital created regulatory arbitrage, which the IRC (originally the IDRC) was designed to remove.
cards.originalText: The IRC was introduced because instruments in the trading book often required less regulatory capital than equivalent instruments in the banking book

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The 2005 incremental default risk charge (IDRC) proposal used an internal default model calibrated to the 99.9th percentile at a one-year horizon, as in the IRB approach, or, absent such a model, a standardized or current exposure approach similar to Basel I specific risk charges.
cards.explanation: The IDRC aimed to remove the incentive to hold default-risky, illiquid assets in the trading book, where capital was lower.
cards.originalText: An internal default model calibrated to the 99.9th percentile at a one‑year horizon, as in the IRB approach, or, absent such a model, a standardized or current exposure approach similar to Basel I specific risk charges

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The 2005 incremental default risk charge (IDRC) proposal used an internal default model calibrated to a 99% confidence level over a 10-day horizon, multiplied by a factor of at least three.
cards.explanation: That describes the old trading book VaR, the measure that produced low capital. The IDRC used a 99.9th percentile, one-year horizon.
cards.originalText: An internal default model calibrated to a 99% confidence level over a 10‑day horizon, multiplied by a factor of at least three

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The requirement to specify a liquidity horizon for each instrument and to rebalance at the end of that horizon is part of the incremental risk charge calculation.
cards.explanation: Under the IRC, defaulted or downgraded positions are replaced at the end of the liquidity horizon by positions of the original rating, a constant level of risk.
cards.originalText: incremental risk charge calculation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Explain the process of calculating the incremental risk capital charge for positions held in a bank’s trading book.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The requirement to specify a liquidity horizon for each instrument and to rebalance at the end of that horizon is part of the comprehensive risk charge calculation.
cards.explanation: The comprehensive risk charge covers the correlation book, such as securitizations. Liquidity-horizon rebalancing of credit positions belongs to the incremental risk charge.
cards.originalText: comprehensive risk charge calculation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the standardized approach to the comprehensive risk measure, the maximum capital charge is 28.0%, which applies to the securitization with the lowest credit rating.
cards.explanation: A 28% charge applies to BB-rated securitizations. The maximum charge is 100% for unrated securitizations or those rated below BB-.
cards.originalText: The maximum capital charge under the standardized approach is 28.0% which applies securitization with the lowest credit rating

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The comprehensive risk measure is a single capital charge that replaces the incremental risk charge and the specific risk charge for instruments dependent on credit correlation.
cards.explanation: The comprehensive risk charge takes the place of both the IRC and the specific risk charge for correlation-dependent positions.
cards.originalText: The CRM is a single capital charge replacing the incremental risk charge and the specific risk charge for instruments dependent on credit correlation

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The comprehensive risk measure can be calculated using a standardized approach that determines the charge from the credit rating of the securitization or re-securitization.
cards.explanation: The standardized approach is purely rating-based, with re-securitizations charged more than securitizations of the same rating.
cards.originalText: The CRM can be calculated using a standardized approach which determines a charge based on the credit rating (e.g., BBB+ to BBB‑) of the securitization or re‑securitization

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The comprehensive risk charge applies to the correlation book and replaces both the incremental risk charge and the specific risk charge for those positions.
cards.explanation: It is a single charge for positions sensitive to default correlation, such as ABS, CDOs and re-securitizations.
cards.originalText: The CR charge applies to the correlation book and replaces both the incremental risk charge and the specific risk charge for those positions.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the standardized approach to the comprehensive risk charge, a re-securitization carries the same capital charge as a securitization with the same rating.
cards.explanation: Re-securitizations are more vulnerable to changes in correlation and carry higher charges, for example 18% versus 8% for BBB.
cards.originalText: Under the standardized approach, a re‑securitization carries the same capital charge as a securitization with the same rating because the charge depends only on the rating.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Highly rated securitization tranches are excluded from the comprehensive risk charge because they are not exposed to losses even when default correlations rise.
cards.explanation: When correlations rise in stress, even highly rated tranches can lose value, which is why they are included.
cards.originalText: Highly rated securitization tranches are excluded from the CR charge because they are not exposed to losses even when default correlations rise.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the comprehensive risk (CR) capital charge for portfolios of positions that are sensitive to correlations between default risks.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A bank approved to use an internal model may set the comprehensive risk charge at whatever level the model produces, since approval removes any link to the standardized approach.
cards.explanation: The model-based charge may not fall below a specified fraction of the standardized charge, and the model needs supervisory approval.
cards.originalText: A bank approved to use an internal model may set the CR charge at whatever level the model produces, since approval removes any link to the standardized approach.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, total Tier 1 capital must be at least 6% of risk-weighted assets.
cards.explanation: Basel III minimums are CET1 4.5%, total Tier 1 6% and total capital 8% of RWA.
cards.originalText: No, total Tier 1 capital should be at least 6% of RWA.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, total Tier 1 capital must be at least 4% of risk-weighted assets.
cards.explanation: 4% was the Tier 1 minimum under Basel I and II. Basel III raised it to 6% of RWA.
cards.originalText: Yes, total Tier 1 capital should be at least 4% of RWA.
cards.correction: Under Basel III, total Tier 1 capital must be at least 6% of risk-weighted assets.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Share capital is a component of Tier 1 capital under Basel III.
cards.explanation: Common equity (share capital) is the highest-quality, permanent loss-absorbing capital and forms the core of Tier 1.
cards.originalText: Share capital

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Subordinated debt is a component of Tier 1 capital under Basel III.
cards.explanation: Qualifying subordinated debt with an original maturity of five years or more is Tier 2 capital.
cards.originalText: Subordinated debt

cards.subject: Operational Risk
