cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Goodwill is a component of Tier 1 capital under Basel III.
cards.explanation: Goodwill and other intangibles are deducted from Tier 1 capital, not added to it.
cards.originalText: Goodwill

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: General loan loss reserves are a component of Tier 1 capital under Basel III.
cards.explanation: General loan loss reserves are Tier 2 capital, capped at 1.25% of standardized RWA or 0.6% of IRB RWA.
cards.originalText: General loan loss reserves

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, the minimum Tier 1 capital requirement rose from 4% to 6% of risk-weighted assets.
cards.explanation: The Basel III Tier 1 minimum is CET1 of 4.5% plus Additional Tier 1 of 1.5%, or 6% of RWA, up from 4% under Basel I and II.
cards.originalText: Rose from 4% to 6% of risk‑weighted assets.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, the minimum Tier 1 capital requirement rose from 4% to 7% of risk-weighted assets.
cards.explanation: The new minimum is 6%. The 7% figure is CET1 including the 2.5% capital conservation buffer, not the Tier 1 minimum.
cards.originalText: Rose from 4% to 7% of risk‑weighted assets.
cards.correction: Under Basel III, the minimum Tier 1 capital requirement rose from 4% to 6% of risk-weighted assets.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Common equity and retained earnings are components of Tier 1 capital under Basel III.
cards.explanation: Tier 1 equity capital consists of common equity and retained earnings, with limited minority interest and unrealized gains and losses.
cards.originalText: Common equity and retained earnings

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: General loan loss reserves are a component of Tier 2 capital under Basel III.
cards.explanation: Tier 2 capital is made up of long-dated subordinated debt and general (unallocated) loan loss reserves, the latter subject to a cap relative to RWA.
cards.originalText: General loan loss reserves

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Common equity is a component of Tier 2 capital under Basel III.
cards.explanation: Common equity is the core of Tier 1 equity (going-concern) capital, not Tier 2.
cards.originalText: Common equity

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Retained earnings are a component of Tier 2 capital under Basel III.
cards.explanation: Retained earnings are part of Tier 1 equity capital, not Tier 2.
cards.originalText: Retained earnings

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, Tier 2 capital is going-concern capital that must be equity, cannot be debt, ranks above depositors in a liquidation and includes noncumulative preferred stock.
cards.explanation: Tier 2 is gone-concern capital that absorbs losses after failure. It consists largely of subordinated debt, ranks below depositors, and noncumulative preferred stock is Additional Tier 1.
cards.originalText: Tier 2 capital is ”going‑concern capital” that must be equity, cannot be debt, ranks above depositors in a liquidation, and includes noncumulative preferred stock

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, Tier 1 equity capital includes share capital and retained earnings.
cards.explanation: Share capital and retained earnings form the core of Tier 1 equity capital.
cards.originalText: Tier 1 equity capital (core Tier 1) includes share capital and retained earnings

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, Additional Tier 1 capital consists of items such as noncumulative perpetual preferred stock that are not common equity.
cards.explanation: Additional Tier 1 is non-core going-concern capital, which includes noncumulative perpetual preferred stock.
cards.originalText: Additional Tier 1 capital (non‑core) consists of items such as noncumulative preferred stock that are not common equity

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, Tier 2 capital must be at least 5.5% of risk-weighted assets, and the capital conservation buffer can be counted toward Tier 2 capital.
cards.explanation: Basel III sets no stand-alone Tier 2 minimum, since 8% total capital less 6% Tier 1 leaves only 2%. The capital conservation buffer must be met with common equity.
cards.originalText: Tier 2 capital must be at least 5.5% of risk‑weighted assets; the capital conservation buffer can be counted toward Tier 2 capital

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, core Tier 1 equity capital must be at least 4.5% of risk-weighted assets, and including the capital conservation buffer the requirement is 7.0%.
cards.explanation: The 7.0% figure is the 4.5% minimum plus the 2.5% capital conservation buffer.
cards.originalText: Core Tier 1 equity capital must be at least 4.5% of risk‑weighted assets; including the capital conservation buffer, the core Tier 1 requirement is 7.0%

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, total Tier 1 capital (Tier 1 equity capital plus Additional Tier 1 capital) must be at least 6.0% of risk-weighted assets at all times.
cards.explanation: The minimum total Tier 1 ratio under Basel III is 6.0% of RWA.
cards.originalText: Total Tier 1 capital (Tier 1 equity capital plus Additional Tier 1 capital) must be at least 6.0% of risk‑weighted assets at all times

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, total capital must be at least 8.0% of risk-weighted assets, and including the capital conservation buffer the minimum total capital requirement is 10.5%.
cards.explanation: The 10.5% figure is the 8.0% minimum plus the 2.5% capital conservation buffer.
cards.originalText: Total capital (total Tier 1 plus Tier 2) must be at least 8.0% of risk‑weighted assets at all times; including the capital conservation buffer, the minimum total capital requirement is 10.5%

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, capital must be adjusted downward to reflect deficits in defined benefit pension plans.
cards.explanation: Basel III deducts defined-benefit pension deficits, along with items such as cross-holdings and excess mortgage servicing rights, from capital.
cards.originalText: Deficits in defined benefit pension plans.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel III, there is no requirement to adjust capital downward for any items.
cards.explanation: Basel III specifies several deductions from capital, including goodwill, deferred tax assets and defined-benefit pension deficits.
cards.originalText: There is no requirement under Basel III to adjust capital downward for anything.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Systemically important financial institutions (SIFIs) are entities whose failure or distress would cause substantial problems for the whole financial system or economy.
cards.explanation: Systemic importance is defined by spillover: the failure or distress of the institution damages the wider financial system or the real economy.
cards.originalText: They are entities whose failure or distress would cause substantial problems for the whole financial system or economy.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Systemically important financial institutions (SIFIs) are entities that are subject to less supervision and regulation.
cards.explanation: SIFIs, and G-SIBs in particular, face more regulation, such as additional capital buffers and TLAC requirements.
cards.originalText: They are entities subject to less supervision and regulation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The capital conservation buffer raises the Tier 1 equity capital requirement to 7% of risk-weighted assets in normal economic periods.
cards.explanation: The 2.5% buffer is added to the 4.5% CET1 minimum, giving 7% in normal periods.
cards.originalText: causes the Tier 1 equity capital ratio requirement to increase to 7% of risk‑weighted assets in normal economic periods.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The capital conservation buffer can be set between 0.0% and 2.5% of risk-weighted assets at the discretion of regulators in individual countries.
cards.explanation: That describes the countercyclical buffer. The capital conservation buffer is a fixed 2.5% of risk-weighted assets.
cards.originalText: can be set between 0.0% and 2.5% of risk‑weighted assets, and is at the discretion of the regulators in individual countries.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A global systemically important bank (G-SIB), whose distress would cause substantial problems for the global financial system or economy, must hold an additional capital buffer of 1% to 3.5% of RWA, depending on its systemic importance score.
cards.explanation: G-SIB status reflects systemic importance. The extra buffer of 1% to 3.5% of RWA is held on top of the other Basel III requirements.
cards.originalText: Its distress would cause substantial problems for the global financial system or economy, so it must hold an additional capital buffer of 1% to 3.5% of RWA, depending on its systemic importance score.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The G-SIB capital buffer replaces the 2.5% capital conservation buffer.
cards.explanation: The G-SIB buffer is additional to the 2.5% capital conservation buffer, not a substitute for it.
cards.originalText: Its distress would cause substantial problems for the global financial system, so its G‑SIB buffer replaces the 2.5% capital conservation buffer.
cards.correction: The G-SIB capital buffer is held in addition to the 2.5% capital conservation buffer.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A bank is designated a G-SIB because its total assets exceed a fixed size threshold.
cards.explanation: Designation rests on a multi-factor score covering size, interconnectedness, complexity, international activity and other factors, not on a single size threshold. The score places the bank in a buffer bucket.
cards.originalText: It is designated because its total assets exceed a fixed threshold, and national supervisors set an additional buffer of 0% to 2.5% at their discretion.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: G-SIBs are exempt from the capital conservation buffer and dividend restrictions because governments are expected to rescue them.
cards.explanation: Post-crisis reforms aim to end 'too big to fail' bailouts, so G-SIBs face more capital requirements, not fewer.
cards.originalText: Because governments are expected to rescue it, it is exempt from the capital conservation buffer and dividend restrictions.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) are debt in normal periods, so they do not dilute equity or drag down return on equity, but they become equity in stress and so absorb losses using private-sector rather than government funds.
cards.explanation: A CoCo is debt-like in good times and automatically creates equity in distress. The loss cushion is therefore funded privately rather than by a bailout.
cards.originalText: They are debt in normal periods, so they do not dilute equity or drag down return on equity, but they become equity in stress and so absorb losses using private‑sector rather than government funds.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A CoCo bondholder can choose when to convert the bond into shares.
cards.explanation: CoCo conversion is automatic once an indenture trigger is hit, not at the holder's option. A holder-option conversion describes a traditional convertible bond.
cards.originalText: They give the bank a higher return on equity in stress periods because bondholders can choose when to convert into shares.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos are cheaper for a bank than common equity because CoCo holders accept losses only after all equity holders have been wiped out.
cards.explanation: CoCo holders bear losses much like equity holders but get little upside, so CoCos are expensive to issue rather than cheap. They are also not junior to equity.
cards.originalText: They are cheaper than common equity because CoCo holders accept losses only after all equity holders have been wiped out.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos are treated as equity from the date of issue, which lets the bank defer all loss recognition.
cards.explanation: A CoCo is debt until it converts, so it is not in the equity account before conversion. That debt treatment is what spares return on equity in normal times.
cards.originalText: They let the bank defer all loss recognition because the bonds are treated as equity from the date of issue.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos guarantee repayment of principal even if the issuing bank fails.
cards.explanation: CoCos carry no principal protection: on a trigger they are converted into equity or written down, so holders absorb losses.
cards.originalText: They guarantee repayment of principal even if the issuing bank fails.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos pay a risk-free return that does not depend on the issuing bank's condition.
cards.explanation: CoCo returns depend on the bank staying above its trigger, and holders can be converted or written down in distress, so the return is not risk free.
cards.originalText: They pay a risk‑free return that does not depend on the bank’s condition.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos offer higher yields than ordinary bonds as compensation for bearing equity-like losses if they are converted or written down.
cards.explanation: CoCo holders can lose heavily on conversion or write-down while receiving little of equity's upside. Investors demand a higher coupon for that contingent loss risk.
cards.originalText: They offer higher yields than ordinary bonds as compensation for bearing equity‑like losses if converted or written down.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos rank ahead of senior debt in bankruptcy.
cards.explanation: CoCos are subordinated, loss-absorbing debt and are not senior to other debt.
cards.originalText: They rank ahead of senior debt in bankruptcy.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCo bondholders raise the bank's equity by exercising a conversion option when the share price rises above a threshold set in the indenture.
cards.explanation: Holder-option conversion at a high share price is the traditional convertible bond mechanism, the mirror image of a CoCo. A CoCo raises equity in distress through indenture triggers.
cards.originalText: Bondholders exercise a conversion option when the share price rises above a threshold set in the indenture.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Triggers written into the indenture cause a CoCo either to convert into equity or to be written down, regardless of the holder's wishes, which raises the bank's equity in distress.
cards.explanation: Equity rises automatically when a trigger is hit, either through conversion into shares or through a write-down of the debt. The holder has no option.
cards.originalText: Triggers written into the indenture lead the bond either to convert into equity or to be written down, regardless of the holder’s wishes.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A CoCo increases the bank's equity in distress by forcing the bank to repurchase the bonds at par, funded with new government equity.
cards.explanation: CoCos raise equity through conversion or write-down on a trigger. A repurchase would drain capital and rely on government money, which CoCos are designed to avoid.
cards.originalText: The bank must repurchase the bonds at par, funding the repurchase with new government equity.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: When a CoCo is triggered, interest on it is suspended permanently and its principal becomes a deposit.
cards.explanation: On a trigger a CoCo either converts into equity or is written down. Nothing in its mechanics turns principal into a deposit.
cards.originalText: Interest on the bonds is suspended permanently and the principal becomes a deposit.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A CoCo whose trigger is a Core Tier 1 capital to risk-weighted assets ratio of 5.125% or higher may be included in common equity Tier 1 capital.
cards.explanation: A CoCo is debt until it converts, so it is not common equity Tier 1. With a trigger of 5.125% or higher it may be included in Additional Tier 1 capital.
cards.originalText: Common equity Tier 1 capital.
cards.correction: A CoCo whose trigger is a Core Tier 1 capital to risk-weighted assets ratio of 5.125% or higher may be included in Additional Tier 1 capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A CoCo whose trigger is a Core Tier 1 capital to risk-weighted assets ratio of 5.125% or higher may be included in Additional Tier 1 capital.
cards.explanation: A trigger at or above 5.125% qualifies the CoCo as Additional Tier 1 capital. If the trigger threshold is lower, the CoCo is included in Tier 2 capital instead.
cards.originalText: Additional Tier 1 capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A CoCo whose trigger is a Core Tier 1 capital to risk-weighted assets ratio of 5.125% or higher may be included in Tier 2 capital only.
cards.explanation: Tier 2 treatment applies only when the trigger threshold is below 5.125%. At 5.125% or higher the CoCo may be included in Additional Tier 1 capital.
cards.originalText: Tier 2 capital only.
cards.correction: A CoCo whose trigger is a Core Tier 1 capital to risk-weighted assets ratio of 5.125% or higher may be included in Additional Tier 1 capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A CoCo whose trigger is a Core Tier 1 capital to risk-weighted assets ratio of 5.125% or higher cannot be included in any category of regulatory capital.
cards.explanation: CoCos can qualify as regulatory capital: Additional Tier 1 when the trigger is 5.125% or higher, and Tier 2 when it is lower.
cards.originalText: No regulatory capital category.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A CoCo converts to equity when the bank's stock price exceeds a threshold specified in the indenture.
cards.explanation: A high share price is the holder-option condition of a traditional convertible bond. CoCo triggers are tied to distress, not to share-price strength.
cards.originalText: Conversion occurs if the bank’s stock price exceeds a threshold specified in the indenture.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A supervisory-judgment trigger converts a CoCo automatically when supervisors determine that the bank needs public-sector aid (equity capital) to avoid insolvency.
cards.explanation: One of the CoCo trigger types rests on supervisors' judgement that the bank is nonviable without public support. The other typical triggers are a Tier 1 equity to RWA ratio below a threshold and a minimum market capitalization to assets ratio.
cards.originalText: Conversion occurs automatically if supervisors determine the bank needs public‑sector aid (equity capital) to avoid insolvency.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A CoCo converts to equity only if bondholders vote to convert at their option.
cards.explanation: CoCo conversion is automatic once a contractual trigger is hit, not at the holders' option.
cards.originalText: Conversion occurs only if bondholders vote to convert at their option.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A market-value trigger converts a CoCo when the ratio of the bank's market capitalization to its assets rises above a set level.
cards.explanation: The market-value trigger activates when the ratio of market capitalization to assets falls below a minimum, which signals distress.
cards.originalText: Conversion occurs when the ratio of market capitalization to assets rises above a set level.
cards.correction: A market-value trigger converts a CoCo when the ratio of the bank's market capitalization to its assets falls below a set level.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: On a trigger, a CoCo either converts into equity or is written down, so the bank's equity increases; the trigger is set in the indenture and is not at the holder's option.
cards.explanation: CoCos absorb losses automatically on indenture triggers, through conversion or write-down. This raises the bank's equity cushion without a government bailout.
cards.originalText: On a trigger, the bond either converts into equity or is written down, so the bank’s equity increases; the trigger is set in the indenture and is not at the holder’s option.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A CoCo holder may choose, at any time before maturity, to convert the bond into equity once the bank's share price exceeds a threshold.
cards.explanation: This describes a traditional convertible, which converts at the holder's option when the share price is high. CoCos are triggered by distress and the holder has no option.
cards.originalText: The holder may choose, at any time before maturity, to convert the bond into equity once the bank’s share price exceeds a threshold.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: When a CoCo is triggered, the bond is converted into short-term debt, which improves the bank's liquidity but leaves its equity unchanged.
cards.explanation: Converting into short-term debt would add no loss-absorbing equity. A triggered CoCo is converted into equity or written down, which increases equity.
cards.originalText: On a trigger, the bond is converted into short‑term debt, which improves the bank’s liquidity but leaves its equity unchanged.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A triggered CoCo is always converted into equity at a fixed rate, and a write-down is never possible because it would breach the creditor hierarchy.
cards.explanation: Conversion is not the only route: a CoCo's trigger can lead either to conversion into equity or to a write-down of the bond's value. Both raise the bank's equity.
cards.originalText: The bond is always converted into equity at a fixed rate; a write‑down is never possible because it would breach the creditor hierarchy.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCo bonds contain an embedded put option that gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to purchase equity at a predetermined conversion price.
cards.explanation: CoCo conversion is mandatory and trigger-based, not a holder option. The holder cannot choose to buy equity at a set price.
cards.originalText: CoCo bonds contain an embedded put option that gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to purchase equity at a predetermined conversion price

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCo bonds are attractive to banks because they do not decrease return on equity (ROE) prior to conversion, and attractive to regulators because they absorb losses when triggered if distress occurs.
cards.explanation: CoCos are debt in good times, so there is no ROE drag, and they automatically add equity in distress. That suits both banks and regulators.
cards.originalText: CoCo bonds are attractive to banks because they do not decrease return on equity (ROE) prior to conversion, and they are also attractive to regulators because they absorb losses when triggered if distress occurs

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The FSB's TLAC minimums will be gradually phased out and replaced by the leverage and liquidity ratios in Basel IV as they are phased in.
cards.explanation: TLAC is an additional loss-absorbency requirement that complements the capital, leverage and liquidity requirements. It is not being replaced by them.
cards.originalText: The TLAC minimums developed by the FSB will be gradually phased out and replaced by the leverage and liquidity ratios in Basel IV as they are phased in

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A drawback of CoCo bonds is that, prior to conversion, they hurt the bank's return on equity (ROE).
cards.explanation: Before conversion a CoCo is debt and sits outside the equity account, so it does not reduce ROE.
cards.originalText: A drawback of CoCo bonds is that, prior to conversion, they hurt the bank’s return on equity (ROE)

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A popular trigger for CoCo bonds is the ratio of Tier 1 equity capital to risk-weighted assets.
cards.explanation: A capital ratio such as Tier 1 equity to risk-weighted assets falling below a threshold is a standard CoCo conversion trigger. Supervisory judgement of nonviability and a market-capitalization-to-assets floor are the other typical triggers.
cards.originalText: A popular trigger for CoCo bonds is the ratio of Tier 1 equity capital to risk‑weighted assets

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Regulators do not like CoCo bonds because they encourage regulatory arbitrage.
cards.explanation: Regulators favor CoCos because they add loss-absorbing capital in stress.
cards.originalText: Regulators do not like CoCo bonds because they encourage regulatory arbitrage

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCo bonds are not attractive to banks because they increase the odds of a public-sector bailout if the bank experiences financial difficulty.
cards.explanation: CoCos recapitalize the bank with private bondholders' funds in distress and so reduce the odds of a public-sector bailout.
cards.originalText: CoCo bonds are NOT attractive to banks because they increase the odds of a public sector bailout if the bank experiences financial difficulty

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos give their holders the option to convert them into the equity of the issuing bank either before maturity or at maturity, depending on the type of CoCo.
cards.explanation: A holder conversion option belongs to the traditional convertible. CoCo conversion is driven by triggers in the indenture, not by the holder.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos give their holders the option to convert their medium- or long-term debt to short-term debt if certain interest rate conditions specified in the indenture are met.
cards.explanation: CoCos have no such debt-maturity conversion feature. On a trigger they convert to equity or are written down.
cards.originalText: CoCos give their holders the option to convert their medium‑ or long‑term debt to short‑term debt if certain interest rate conditions specified in the indenture are met.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos may be included in Tier 2 capital but not in Tier 1 or Additional Tier 1 capital.
cards.explanation: CoCos with a trigger of at least 5.125% can count as Additional Tier 1 capital. Only those with a lower trigger are included in Tier 2.
cards.originalText: CoCos may be included in Tier 2 capital but not in Tier 1 or Additional Tier 1 capital due to the risks they pose to the issuing bank and the difficulties in pricing them.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos can be more expensive for banks to issue than equity, but they allow the issuing bank to report a higher return on equity until they are converted.
cards.explanation: CoCo holders bear equity-like losses with little upside, so CoCos are costly to issue. Until conversion they sit outside the equity account, which flatters reported ROE.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos are debt in normal times and so do not dilute return on equity, but they convert automatically to equity in stress, providing a loss-absorbing cushion funded by private investors rather than the government.
cards.explanation: CoCos give debt-like treatment in good times and automatic equity-like loss absorption in bad times. The capital comes from private bondholders, so a taxpayer bailout can be avoided.
cards.originalText: CoCos are debt in normal times and so do not dilute return on equity, but convert automatically to equity in stress, providing a loss‑absorbing cushion funded by private investors rather than the government.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos convert to equity at the option of the bondholder once the share price exceeds a threshold.
cards.explanation: This describes a traditional convertible bond. CoCos convert automatically when a stress trigger is hit.
cards.originalText: CoCos convert to equity at the option of the bondholder once the share price exceeds a threshold, allowing the bank to avoid issuing equity until its performance improves.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos rank senior to deposits in liquidation.
cards.explanation: CoCos are subordinated, not senior to deposits.
cards.originalText: CoCos are senior to deposits in liquidation, which lowers the bank’s funding cost and reduces its required Tier 1 capital in normal times.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: CoCos convert to equity only when the bank applies for public-sector support, so the government supplies the capital needed to avoid insolvency.
cards.explanation: Conversion is triggered automatically by contractual triggers, although a supervisory nonviability determination is one of them. The point of CoCos is that private holders, not the government, supply the capital.
cards.originalText: CoCos convert to equity only when the bank applies for public‑sector support, so the government supplies the capital needed to avoid insolvency.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A CoCo converts to equity when the bondholder decides to convert after the bank's share price rises above a threshold set in the indenture.
cards.explanation: Holder-option conversion at a high share price describes a traditional convertible bond, not a CoCo.
cards.originalText: The bondholder’s decision to convert when the bank’s share price rises above a threshold set in the indenture.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A CoCo can be converted to equity or written down when the bank's Tier 1 equity capital to risk-weighted assets ratio falls below a specified threshold.
cards.explanation: A capital-ratio breach signals stress and is a standard automatic CoCo trigger, alongside supervisory judgement of nonviability and a minimum market capitalization to assets ratio.
cards.originalText: The bank’s Tier 1 equity capital to risk‑weighted assets ratio falling below a specified threshold.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A one-notch rise in a bank's credit rating is a recognized trigger for a CoCo to convert to equity or be written down.
cards.explanation: A rating upgrade signals improvement, not distress, so it is not a CoCo trigger.
cards.originalText: A rise in the bank’s credit rating by one notch.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Describe the mechanics of contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) and explain the motivations for banks to issue them.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The liquidity coverage ratio rising above 100% is a recognized trigger for a CoCo to convert to equity or be written down.
cards.explanation: A rising liquidity coverage ratio signals stronger liquidity, not distress, so it is not a CoCo trigger.
cards.originalText: The bank’s liquidity coverage ratio rising above 100%.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: The advanced measurement approach (AMA) for operational risk was introduced as part of the Basel III revisions.
cards.explanation: The AMA came from Basel II (2006). The Basel III standardized approach replaced it.
cards.originalText: The advanced measurement approach (AMA) was introduced as part of the Basel III revisions.
cards.correction: The advanced measurement approach (AMA) for operational risk was introduced as part of the Basel II framework.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: The advanced measurement approach (AMA) for operational risk was more flexible in its application than the standardized approach.
cards.explanation: The AMA was principles-based and allowed a wide range of internal models. The standardized approach is a single non-model-based method designed to improve comparability and reduce complexity.
cards.originalText: The AMA was more flexible in its application than the standardized approach.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: The Basel III standardized approach for operational risk accounts for internal loss experience that was not factored into the AMA.
cards.explanation: The AMA already used internal loss data, so internal losses are not a new feature of the standardized approach.
cards.originalText: The standardized approach accounts for internal loss experiences that were not factored into the AMA.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: The standardized approach for operational risk uses a model-based methodology, while the AMA was more flexible and principles-based.
cards.explanation: The standardized approach is non-model-based, using the business indicator and the bank's loss experience in a prescribed formula. The AMA was the model-based, flexible approach.
cards.originalText: The standardized approach uses a model‑based methodology, while the AMA was more flexible and principles‑based.
cards.correction: The standardized approach for operational risk uses a non-model-based methodology, while the AMA was more flexible and principles-based.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: The AMA permitted such a wide range of internal modeling practices that capital outcomes were difficult to compare across banks, and the standardized approach replaces it with a single non-model-based method.
cards.explanation: The AMA's flexibility produced inconsistent, hard-to-compare and complex capital results. The standardized approach was designed for comparability and simplicity.
cards.originalText: The AMA permitted such a wide range of internal modeling practices that capital outcomes were difficult to compare across banks, and the standardized approach replaces it with a single non‑model‑based method.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: The AMA ignored bank-specific loss experience, so the standardized approach was created to introduce internal loss data into the operational risk capital calculation for the first time.
cards.explanation: The AMA did incorporate internal loss data, so internal losses are not new to the standardized approach.
cards.originalText: The AMA ignored bank‑specific loss experience, so the standardized approach was created to introduce internal loss data into the capital calculation for the first time.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: The AMA was a rigid, rules-based framework, so the standardized approach was created to give banks more discretion over how they model operational risk.
cards.explanation: The facts are reversed: the AMA was the flexible, principles-based framework, and the standardized approach reduces banks' modeling discretion.
cards.originalText: The AMA was a rigid, rules‑based framework, so the standardized approach was created to give banks more discretion over how they model operational risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: The Basel III standardized approach for operational risk is an optional alternative, and banks that have received supervisory approval may continue to use the AMA for regulatory capital.
cards.explanation: The standardized approach replaces all existing approaches in the Basel II framework, including the AMA, so continued AMA use is not permitted.
cards.originalText: The standardized approach is an optional alternative, and banks that have received supervisory approval may continue to use the AMA for regulatory capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: Under the Basel III standardized approach for operational risk, a loss component below the business indicator component raises the internal loss multiplier above one.
cards.explanation: A loss component below the business indicator component gives an internal loss multiplier below one, and so lower capital.
cards.originalText: Under the standardized approach, Bank Y would hold more capital than Bank X because a low loss component raises the internal loss multiplier above one.
cards.correction: Under the Basel III standardized approach for operational risk, a loss component below the business indicator component lowers the internal loss multiplier below one.

changes.from: raises the internal loss multiplier above one
changes.to: lowers the internal loss multiplier below one

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Compare the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) to earlier methods of calculating operational risk capital, including the Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA).
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: Under the Basel III standardized approach for operational risk, differences in banks' capital depend on each bank's internal model of its loss distribution, as was the case under the AMA.
cards.explanation: The standardized approach is non-model-based. The internal loss multiplier follows a prescribed formula, so internal loss-distribution models play no role.
cards.originalText: Under the standardized approach, differences in the two banks’ capital would depend on each bank’s internal model of its loss distribution, as was the case under the AMA.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: P&L provisions or reserves against potential loss impacts are included in the gross loss computation for operational loss data.
cards.explanation: Provisions and reserves charged to the P&L for a potential operational loss are an explicit component of gross loss, recognised at the date of accounting.
cards.originalText: P&L provisions or reserves against potential loss impacts are included in the gross loss computation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: All internal operational loss events must be included in the gross loss computation regardless of the size of the loss.
cards.explanation: A minimum loss data collection threshold of EUR 20,000 applies, so events below it need not be included in the data set.
cards.originalText: All internal loss events must be included in the gross loss computation regardless of the size of the loss.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: Legal expenses are excluded from the gross loss computation because they represent the realization of legal risk.
cards.explanation: External expenses with a direct link to the operational loss event, such as legal and advisor fees, are included in gross loss.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: Receivables are counted as recoveries unless the particular receivable causes the current ratio to exceed an internal limit.
cards.explanation: Receivables do not count as recoveries: only payments actually received can reduce a loss. The current-ratio test does not exist.
cards.originalText: Receivables should be counted as recoveries unless the particular receivable causes the current ratio to exceed an internal limit.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: Legal fees with a direct link to an operational risk event are included in the gross loss calculation.
cards.explanation: External expenses directly tied to the event, such as legal and advisor fees, are part of gross loss.
cards.originalText: legal fees of €900,000 associated with an unusual risk event.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: A settlement tied to an operational risk event is included in the gross loss calculation.
cards.explanation: Settlements are direct charges to the P&L and are included in gross loss.
cards.originalText: a €2 million settlement tied to a recent operational risk event.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: A reserve booked to the income statement to cover a potential operational loss is included in the gross loss calculation.
cards.explanation: Provisions or reserves booked in the P&L against a potential operational loss are included in gross loss.
cards.originalText: a €1.4 million reserve booked to the income statement to cover a potential operational loss.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Describe general and specific criteria recommended by the Basel Committee for the identification, collection, and treatment of operational loss data.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: Costs of general maintenance contracts on property, plant and equipment are included in the gross loss calculation.
cards.explanation: Gross loss excludes the cost of general maintenance contracts on property, plant and equipment, as well as post-event improvement spending and insurance premiums.
cards.originalText: €1.75 million spent on maintenance contracts tied to the bank’s property, plant and equipment.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: RCSA action plans should be owned by the operational risk function that ran the workshop, because the business line is not independent of its own risks.
cards.explanation: The second line facilitates and tracks, while the first line, the business-line managers who sign off the results, owns the action plans.
cards.originalText: The action plans should be owned by the operational risk function that ran the workshop, because the business line is not independent of its own risks.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: RCSA action plans should be owned by the business-line managers who sign off the results and tracked by the second or third line, and mitigation need not mean adding new controls.
cards.explanation: Action plans should be owned by the first line and tracked and reported by the second or third line. Mitigation can also mean reducing volumes, limiting access rights, redesigning controls or buying insurance.
cards.originalText: The action plans should be owned by the business-line managers who sign off the results and tracked by the second or third line; mitigation need not mean new controls.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain operational risk-assessment processes and tools, including risk control self-assessments (RCSAs), likelihood assessment scales, and heatmaps.
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: In an RCSA, financial impacts should be rated in absolute currency amounts, so that the same loss receives the same rating in every department of the firm.
cards.explanation: Relative scales, such as a percentage of revenue or operating income, let one definition fit departments of different sizes. An absolute amount that is significant for one unit may be minor for another.
cards.originalText: Financial impacts should be rated in absolute currency amounts, so that the same loss receives the same rating in every department of the firm.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: A metric that measures back-office performance cannot serve as a KRI because it records events that have already happened.
cards.explanation: Control and performance metrics can also be risk indicators. Rising overdue confirmations signal a rising likelihood of future losses, which is what a preventive KRI does.
cards.originalText: The metric is a KPI only: it measures back-oﬀice performance, and it cannot serve as a KRI because it records events that have already happened.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: Any metric linked to a control must be classified as a key control indicator (KCI) rather than as a risk indicator.
cards.explanation: Control indicators and risk indicators overlap, so one metric can serve as both.
cards.originalText: The metric is a KCI only, because any metric linked to a control must be classified as a control indicator rather than as a risk indicator.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: A KRI must measure the impact of a risk, so a metric that says nothing about loss size cannot be a KRI.
cards.explanation: KRIs measure the likelihood or the impact of a risk. A metric that signals a rising likelihood of loss is a valid likelihood KRI.
cards.originalText: The metric should leave the KRI set, because KRIs must measure the impact of a risk and overdue confirmations say nothing about loss size.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe the differences among key risk indicators (KRIs), key performance indicators (KPIs), and key control indicators (KCIs).
cards.reading: ORR-4: Risk Measurement and Assessment
cards.statement: A metric such as overdue trade confirmations can act at once as a KPI, a KRI and a KCI, signalling poor back-office performance, a higher risk of disputes or rogue trading, and a failing control.
cards.explanation: A key control failure always constitutes a source of risk, so the same metric can be read from the performance, risk and control angles.
cards.originalText: The metric can act at once as a KPI, a KRI and a KCI: poor back-oﬀice performance, a higher risk of disputes or rogue trading, and a failing control.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Automating a control removes the risk of control failure, because a coded rule is executed in exactly the same way every time.
cards.explanation: The system can fail or the code can be wrong or outdated, so the risk changes form rather than disappearing.
cards.originalText: Automation removes the risk of control failure, because a coded rule is executed in exactly the same way every time.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Automating a control lowers both the likelihood and the impact of control failures, so the control no longer needs to be tested.
cards.explanation: Automation can raise the impact of a failure, and automated controls still need testing, for example by examination.
cards.originalText: Automation lowers both the likelihood and the impact of control failures, so the payment control no longer needs to be tested.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Automating a control converts technology and model risk into human error risk.
cards.explanation: The conversion runs the other way: automation turns human error risk into technology and model risk.
cards.originalText: Automation converts technology and model risk into human error risk, which is easier for line managers to supervise.
cards.correction: Automating a control converts human error risk into technology and model risk.

changes.from: technology and model risk into human error risk
changes.to: human error risk into technology and model risk

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: Automating a manual control turns frequent, small manual errors into a rarer but potentially large systemic breakdown, and adds technology and model risk.
cards.explanation: Automation shifts high-likelihood, low-impact risks of isolated manual errors into the low-likelihood, high-impact risk of a systemic control breakdown. It also adds the risk that the system fails or the code is wrong or outdated.
cards.originalText: Automation turns frequent, small manual errors into a rarer but potentially large systemic breakdown, and adds technology and model risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.statement: The Knight Capital loss was caused by a rogue trader who concealed positions in suspense accounts, made possible by weak segregation of duties between front and back office.
cards.explanation: Concealed positions and weak segregation of duties describe rogue-trading cases. Knight Capital's loss came from poorly tested new routing code.
cards.originalText: A rogue trader who concealed positions in suspense accounts, made possible by weak segregation of duties between front and back oﬀice.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
cards.loText: Describe control automation, internal control design, and control testing, including risks and challenges that arise in these processes and ways to make them more effective.
cards.reading: ORR-5: Risk Mitigation
