cards.loText: Describe the recommendations by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) that supervisors should consider in order to make effective use of internal risk measures, such as economic capital, that are not designed for regulatory purposes.
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: The BIS identifies VaR as the single preferred risk measure for all risk types in economic capital.
cards.explanation: The BIS states that there is no singularly preferred risk measure. Every measure has advantages and disadvantages that must be understood in the context of its intended use.
cards.originalText: The bank adopts VaR as the single preferred risk measure for all risk types, on the basis that BIS identifies it as the best measure for economic capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Describe the recommendations by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) that supervisors should consider in order to make effective use of internal risk measures, such as economic capital, that are not designed for regulatory purposes.
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: There is no singularly preferred risk measure for economic capital, and a bank should understand the limitations of the measures it uses and the implications of its choice.
cards.explanation: All risk measures have advantages and disadvantages, so the BIS recommendation is to understand them in the context of the intended application rather than to adopt one measure.
cards.originalText: There is no singularly preferred risk measure, and a bank should understand the limitations of the measures it uses and the implications of its choice.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Describe the recommendations by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) that supervisors should consider in order to make effective use of internal risk measures, such as economic capital, that are not designed for regulatory purposes.
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: Expected shortfall is free of limitations and should therefore replace VaR as the economic capital risk measure.
cards.explanation: No risk measure is free of limitations. Expected shortfall is hard to interpret and has no clear link to the target rating, and it still needs validation.
cards.originalText: Expected shortfall should replace VaR because it is free of limitations and so needs no further validation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Explain benefits and impacts of using an economic capital framework within the following areas: - Credit portfolio management - Risk-based pricing - Customer profitability analysis - Management incentives
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: A loan with higher stand-alone risk always contributes more risk to the portfolio, so ranking loans by stand-alone risk is sufficient to assess concentration.
cards.explanation: Under an economic capital framework, a loan's incremental (marginal) contribution to portfolio risk, not its stand-alone risk, drives the assessment of concentration.
cards.originalText: A loan with higher stand‑alone risk always contributes more risk to the portfolio, so ranking loans by standalone risk is sufficient to assess concentration.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Explain benefits and impacts of using an economic capital framework within the following areas: - Credit portfolio management - Risk-based pricing - Customer profitability analysis - Management incentives
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: In credit portfolio management under an economic capital framework, the creditworthiness of each borrower is assessed in a portfolio context rather than on a stand-alone basis.
cards.explanation: What matters is how each borrower adds to the risk of the whole portfolio, which depends on concentration and diversification as well as the borrower's own credit quality.
cards.originalText: In credit portfolio management, the creditworthiness of each borrower is assessed in a portfolio context rather than on a stand‑alone basis.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Explain benefits and impacts of using an economic capital framework within the following areas: - Credit portfolio management - Risk-based pricing - Customer profitability analysis - Management incentives
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: In risk-based pricing, deals whose expected RAROC falls below a given threshold are rejected, so the allocated economic capital sets a floor on the interest rate.
cards.explanation: Allocated economic capital drives a minimum RAROC or a minimum rate that at least does not reduce shareholder value.
cards.originalText: In risk‑based pricing, deals whose expected RAROC falls below a given threshold are rejected, so the allocated economic capital sets a floor on the interest rate.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Explain benefits and impacts of using an economic capital framework within the following areas: - Credit portfolio management - Risk-based pricing - Customer profitability analysis - Management incentives
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: Linking incentive pay to economic capital does tend to motivate participation in the economic capital allocation process and some such linkage should be attempted, but actual linkage in practice is quite low.
cards.explanation: Incentives are the most sensitive element for most managers, so linkage helps engage them in the allocation process. In practice, compensation schemes rank quite low among the actual uses of economic capital at business-unit level.
cards.originalText: Linking incentive pay to EC DOES tend to motivate participation in the EC allocation process; some such linkage should be attempted, but actual linkage (EC metrics to pay) in practice is quite low

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Explain benefits and impacts of using an economic capital framework within the following areas: - Credit portfolio management - Risk-based pricing - Customer profitability analysis - Management incentives
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: In practice, the linkage of economic capital metrics to pay is already prevalent.
cards.explanation: Compensation schemes rank quite low among the actual uses of economic capital at business-unit level, even though some linkage is encouraged.
cards.originalText: Linking incentive pay to EC DOES tend to motivate participation in the EC allocation process; some such linkage should be attempted, and actual linkage (EC metrics to pay) in practice is already prevalent
cards.correction: In practice, the linkage of economic capital metrics to pay is quite low.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Explain benefits and impacts of using an economic capital framework within the following areas: - Credit portfolio management - Risk-based pricing - Customer profitability analysis - Management incentives
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: An economic capital framework helps a bank reduce concentration risk by quantifying the incremental risk each loan adds to the total portfolio, which guides rebalancing and hedging decisions.
cards.explanation: A loan's marginal contribution to portfolio risk, rather than its stand-alone risk, shows where concentration lies and which loans to hedge or transfer.
cards.originalText: By quantifying the incremental risk each loan adds to the total portfolio, guiding rebalancing and hedging decisions

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Explain benefits and impacts of using an economic capital framework within the following areas: - Credit portfolio management - Risk-based pricing - Customer profitability analysis - Management incentives
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: Under risk-based pricing, the minimum loan rate covers the cost of funding, expected loss, the cost of the allocated economic capital and the extra return required by shareholders.
cards.explanation: This minimum rate, or equivalently a minimum RAROC, is the floor at which a loan does not reduce shareholder value.
cards.originalText: The minimum rate covers the cost of funding, expected loss, the cost of the allocated economic capital, and the extra return required by shareholders

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Explain benefits and impacts of using an economic capital framework within the following areas: - Credit portfolio management - Risk-based pricing - Customer profitability analysis - Management incentives
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: An economic capital framework supports customer profitability analysis by segmenting customers by net return per unit of risk, which identifies unprofitable customers so that capital can be reallocated to more profitable relationships.
cards.explanation: Economic capital provides the risk base that makes relationship returns comparable per unit of risk, although measuring risk and cost per customer remains difficult.
cards.originalText: By segmenting customers by net return per unit of risk, it identifies unprofitable or marginally profitable customers so capital can be reallocated to more profitable relationships

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Describe best practices and assess key concerns for the governance of an economic capital framework.
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: Good governance of an economic capital framework includes formalized change processes and active senior management engagement.
cards.explanation: The reliability of economic capital rests on strong controls over changes to risk measurement techniques, thorough documentation and senior management that is committed to and responsible for the whole process.
cards.originalText: Establishing governance controls, including formalized change processes and active senior management engagement.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Describe best practices and assess key concerns for the governance of an economic capital framework.
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: Economic capital oversight can be assigned to the finance department with minimal involvement from senior management.
cards.explanation: Senior management must be committed to and responsible for governance of the entire economic capital process and is a main driver of the framework.
cards.originalText: Assigning economic capital oversight to the finance department, with minimal involvement from senior management.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Describe best practices and assess key concerns for the governance of an economic capital framework.
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: Good governance of an economic capital model requires responsible parties to sign off on methodology changes, diagnostics and formal validation after each change, and internal escalation procedures for unexpectedly large changes in economic capital.
cards.explanation: The reliability of economic capital depends on strong controls over changes, including sign-off, post-change diagnostics and escalation procedures.
cards.originalText: Require responsible parties to sign off on methodology changes, run diagnostics and formal validation after each change, and set internal escalation procedures for unexpectedly large changes in economic capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Describe best practices and assess key concerns for the governance of an economic capital framework.
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: An economic capital model that is used only internally does not need to follow formal change-control processes.
cards.explanation: Being used internally does not remove the need for formal controls, because the reliability of economic capital depends on strong control over changes to the model.
cards.originalText: Allow the economic capital model to be changed at the discretion of the model owner, since the model is used only internally and need not follow change‑control processes.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Describe best practices and assess key concerns for the governance of an economic capital framework.
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: Economic capital should not be the only measure determining required capital, because banks typically also align capital with target external credit ratings, balancing shareholders' preference for lower capital against rating agencies' preference for higher capital.
cards.explanation: Required capital reflects the tension between shareholders, who want profitability from lower capital, and rating agencies, who encourage solvency through higher capital.
cards.originalText: Economic capital should not be the only measure determining required capital; banks typically also align capital with target external credit ratings, balancing shareholders’ preference for lower capital against rating agencies’ preference for higher capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Describe best practices and assess key concerns for the governance of an economic capital framework.
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: All banks define available capital resources identically.
cards.explanation: There is no common definition of available capital across banks. Most start from Tier 1 capital and adjust it in different ways.
cards.originalText: The proposal is appropriate provided available capital is defined as the standard Tier 1 figure, since all banks define available capital resources identically.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.loText: Describe best practices and assess key concerns for the governance of an economic capital framework.
cards.reading: ORR-19: Range of Practices and Issues in Economic Capital Frameworks
cards.statement: A high-confidence economic capital model makes integrated stress testing unnecessary.
cards.explanation: Integrated stress testing is encouraged to assess the impact of scenarios on economic capital, and a high confidence level does not replace it.
cards.originalText: The proposal is appropriate because a high‑confidence economic capital model makes integrated stress testing unnecessary.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approach for the calculation of operational risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II advanced measurement approach, a bank cannot recognize insurance or other risk mitigants in its operational risk capital calculation.
cards.explanation: The AMA is the approach that allows banks to reflect risk mitigants such as insurance, subject to conditions.
cards.originalText: Under the advanced measurement approach, a bank cannot recognize insurance or other risk mitigants in its capital calculation.
cards.correction: Under the Basel II advanced measurement approach, a bank can recognize insurance or other risk mitigants in its operational risk capital calculation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approach for the calculation of operational risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II basic indicator approach, operational risk capital is 15% of average annual gross income over the past three years, ignoring years with negative gross income.
cards.explanation: The basic indicator approach applies a single 15% factor to the three-year average of positive annual gross income.
cards.originalText: Under the basic indicator approach, capital is 15% of average annual gross income over the past three years, ignoring years with negative gross income.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approach for the calculation of operational risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II advanced measurement approach, operational risk capital is based on a one-year loss measure at the 99.9% confidence level from the bank's internal model.
cards.explanation: AMA banks estimate a loss distribution from internal models and read the 99.9th percentile over a one-year horizon.
cards.originalText: Under the advanced measurement approach, capital is based on a one‑year operational loss measure at the 99.9% confidence level from internal models.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approach for the calculation of operational risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel II was the first bank capital accord to introduce an explicit operational risk capital charge.
cards.explanation: Basel I covered credit risk only, the 1996 Amendment added market risk for the trading book, and Basel II added operational risk with the basic indicator, standardized and advanced measurement approaches.
cards.originalText: Basel II

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approach for the calculation of operational risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Basel I required banks to hold capital for operational risk.
cards.explanation: Basel I addressed credit risk only. Operational risk capital was first required under Basel II.
cards.originalText: Basel I
cards.correction: Basel II required banks to hold capital for operational risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approach for the calculation of operational risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Two popular approaches to the operational risk advanced measurement approach (AMA) are scenario analysis and the loss distribution approach (parametric and Monte Carlo).
cards.explanation: AMA banks estimate a distribution of operational losses from frequency and severity and read the 99.9th percentile. The loss distribution approach and detailed scenario analysis are the two most widely used methods, and many banks combine them.
cards.originalText: Two popular approaches to the operational risk Advanced Measurement Approach (AMA) are Scenario Analysis and the Loss Distribution Approach (LDA; i.e., parametric and Monte Carlo)

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approach for the calculation of operational risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Basel II, expected losses are included in the credit risk capital charge but excluded from the operational risk capital charge.
cards.explanation: IRB credit risk capital excludes expected loss, which is covered by loan loss reserves. The AMA operational risk charge is read from the 99.9th percentile of the loss distribution, so expected loss is not excluded there.
cards.originalText: Expected losses are included in the credit risk charge but excluded from the operational risk charge

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approach for the calculation of operational risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Basel II internal ratings-based (IRB) approach to credit risk, the default probability (PD) increases as the correlation parameter increases.
cards.explanation: PD is an input to the IRB formula and is not driven by the correlation parameter. In the Basel IRB formula the correlation parameter is itself a decreasing function of PD, and higher correlation raises the worst-case default rate, not PD.
cards.originalText: Under the Internal Ratings Based (IRB) approach to credit risk, default probability (PD) increases as the correlation parameter increases

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Compare the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approach for the calculation of operational risk capital under Basel II.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The operational risk advanced measurement approach (AMA) persisted into Basel III and IV.
cards.explanation: The AMA lost favour because few banks could adopt it successfully, and Basel III replaced it, together with the earlier standardized approaches, with a single standardized approach.
cards.originalText: The operational risk Advanced Measurement Approach (AMA) was one of Basel II’s most successful features such that it persisted into Basel III and IV

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A Solvency II internal model must pass a use test, meaning it is genuinely used in business decision making.
cards.explanation: The three internal model tests are statistical quality, calibration and use. The use test requires the model to be embedded in real management decisions.
cards.originalText: Use test.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A Solvency II internal model must pass a calibration test, meaning risks are measured in line with the regulator's SCR target criteria.
cards.explanation: Calibration ties the internal model to the common solvency target set by the regulator rather than to a standard the insurer picks for itself.
cards.originalText: Calibration test.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A Solvency II internal model must be used in actual business decision making, not just for regulatory reporting.
cards.explanation: This is the use test: the model must be embedded in real management decisions rather than being merely a compliance exercise.
cards.originalText: The model must be used in actual business decision making, not just for regulatory reporting.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Solvency II, risks in an internal model must be calibrated to a target standard chosen by the insurer rather than by the regulator.
cards.explanation: Calibration is to the regulator's SCR target criteria, which give a common standard across insurers.
cards.originalText: Risks must be calibrated to a target standard chosen by the insurer rather than the regulator.
cards.correction: Under Solvency II, risks in an internal model must be calibrated to a target standard chosen by the regulator rather than by the insurer.

changes.from: chosen by the insurer rather than by the regulator
changes.to: chosen by the regulator rather than by the insurer

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A Solvency II internal model must be based on a 99.9% confidence level over a one-year horizon.
cards.explanation: Solvency II uses a one-year VaR at the 99.5% confidence level. The 99.9% level is the Basel II credit and operational risk level.
cards.originalText: The model must be based on a 99.9% confidence level over a one‑year horizon.
cards.correction: A Solvency II internal model must be based on a 99.5% confidence level over a one-year horizon.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Similar to Basel II, Solvency II has three pillars and three tiers of capital.
cards.explanation: Solvency II's pillars cover quantitative requirements, governance and supervision, and disclosure. Its capital is divided into Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Similar to Basel II, Solvency II is an international regulatory standard.
cards.explanation: Solvency II is a European Union regime for insurers, not an international standard.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Solvency II considers three risks: credit, market and operational risk.
cards.explanation: Solvency II also charges for underwriting risk, which is the key insurer-specific risk. Its charges cover underwriting, investment (market and credit) and operational risk.
cards.originalText: Similar to Basel II, Solvency II considers three risks: credit, market and operational risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: If capital drops below the Solvency II minimum capital requirement (MCR), supervisors are likely to insist that the insurer add new business and underwrite additional policies to increase earned premiums.
cards.explanation: A breach of the MCR leads supervisors to restrict new business or to resolve the firm, for example through sale or liquidation, not to encourage more underwriting.
cards.originalText: If capital drops below the MCR level, supervisors are likely to insist that the insurance company add new businesses and underwrite additional policies to increase earned premiums.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: If capital drops below the Solvency II solvency capital requirement (SCR), the insurer should, at minimum, deliver to the supervisor a plan to restore capital to above the SCR.
cards.explanation: A breach of the SCR calls for a capital restoration plan, and the supervisor may impose additional measures.
cards.originalText: If capital drops below the SCR level, an insurance company should, at minimum, deliver to the supervisor a plan to restore capital to above the SCR level.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: If capital drops below the Solvency II minimum capital requirement (MCR), supervisors might force the insurer into liquidation and the transfer of its policies to another company.
cards.explanation: The MCR is the absolute floor, and breaching it can lead to a ban on new policies or to resolution through sale or liquidation.
cards.originalText: If capital drops below the MCR level, supervisors might force the insurance company into liquidation, transferring its policies to another company.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under the Solvency II internal models approach, the SCR is based on a one-year VaR at the 99.5% confidence level, lower than the 99.9% level used for credit and operational risk under Basel II.
cards.explanation: Solvency II uses a one-year 99.5% VaR, while Basel II uses a one-year 99.9% level for credit and operational risk.
cards.originalText: The internal models approach uses a VaR with a one‑year horizon and a 99.5% confidence level, lower than the 99.9% level used for credit and operational risk under Basel II.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Solvency II, all qualifying capital must be Tier 1 capital.
cards.explanation: Solvency II capital has three tiers, and requirements may be met by a combination of Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3 capital. Tier 1 is equity-type capital, while liabilities subordinated to policyholders fall in Tier 2 or Tier 3.
cards.originalText: All qualifying capital must be Tier 1, which can consist only of liabilities that are subordinated to policyholders and satisfy availability criteria in wind‑down scenarios.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Under Solvency II, capital requirements may be met by a combination of Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3 capital, as under Basel II.
cards.explanation: Tier 1 is equity and retained earnings, Tier 2 is subordinated liabilities available in liquidation, and Tier 3 is subordinated capital that does not meet other criteria.
cards.originalText: Capital requirements may be met by a combination of Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3 capital, similar to Basel II.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Reputational risk carries a specific capital charge in the Solvency II solvency capital requirement (SCR).
cards.explanation: The SCR has charges for underwriting risk (life, non-life and health), investment risk (market and credit) and operational risk. Reputational risk has no separate charge.
cards.originalText: Reputational risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Underwriting risk carries a specific capital charge in the Solvency II solvency capital requirement (SCR).
cards.explanation: Underwriting risk is the insurer-specific charge and is subdivided into life, non-life and health.
cards.originalText: Underwriting risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Investment risk, both market and credit, carries a specific capital charge in the Solvency II solvency capital requirement (SCR).
cards.explanation: Investment risk has its own SCR charge, subdivided into market risk and credit risk.
cards.originalText: Investment (market and credit) risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Solvency II specifies both a solvency capital requirement (SCR) and a minimum capital requirement (MCR).
cards.explanation: The MCR is the absolute floor and the SCR is set above it, so the gap between them acts as a buffer.
cards.originalText: It specifies both a solvency capital requirement (SCR) and a minimum capital requirement (MCR).

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: Solvency II requires a single minimum ratio of capital to risk-weighted assets and allows no internal models.
cards.explanation: Solvency II allows insurers to compute the SCR with an internal model as well as the standardized approach, and it is not a risk-weighted-assets ratio.
cards.originalText: It requires a single minimum ratio of capital to risk‑weighted assets, with no internal models allowed.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The Solvency II internal models approach to the SCR is similar to the Basel II internal ratings-based approach in that the firm must calculate a VaR with a one-year time horizon.
cards.explanation: Both rest on a one-year horizon, although the confidence level differs: 99.5% under Solvency II and 99.9% under Basel II.
cards.originalText: The internal models approach to calculating the solvency capital requirement is similar to internal ratings‑based approach under Basel II in that the firm must calculate a VaR with a one‑year time horizon.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The minimum capital requirement is higher than the solvency capital requirement for insurance companies.
cards.explanation: The MCR is the absolute floor and lies below the SCR, so the SCR is the higher requirement.
cards.originalText: The minimum capital requirement is likely to be higher than the solvency capital requirement for insurance companies.
cards.correction: The minimum capital requirement is lower than the solvency capital requirement for insurance companies.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
cards.reading: ORR-21: Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The repercussion for violating the solvency capital requirement is likely liquidation and the transfer of the company's insurance policies to another firm.
cards.explanation: Liquidation or transfer of policies is a consequence of breaching the MCR. Breaching the SCR calls for a capital restoration plan and possible supervisory measures.
cards.originalText: The repercussion for violating the solvency capital requirement is likely liquidation and the transfer of company insurance policies to another firm.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Provide examples of legislative and regulatory reforms that were introduced after the 2007-2009 financial crisis.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: The Volcker Rule generally prohibits proprietary trading at firms that take insured deposits.
cards.explanation: The Volcker Rule restricts proprietary trading and investment in hedge funds and private equity at deposit-taking firms, because banks funded by insured deposits should not speculate with their own capital.
cards.originalText: The Volcker Rule would generally prohibit the desk because it restricts proprietary trading at deposit‑taking firms.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.loText: Provide examples of legislative and regulatory reforms that were introduced after the 2007-2009 financial crisis.
cards.reading: ORR-22: Solvency, Liquidity and Other Regulation After the Global Financial Crisis
cards.statement: A standardized over-the-counter interest rate swap between two financial institutions may be traded on a swap execution facility and must be cleared through a central counterparty.
cards.explanation: Post-crisis reforms moved standardized OTC derivatives onto swap execution facilities, which promote price transparency, and required derivatives between financial institutions to be centrally cleared.
cards.originalText: The swap may be traded on a swap execution facility and must be cleared through a central counterparty.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: Under the Basel standardized approach, operational risk capital is the Business Indicator multiplied by marginal coefficients of 12%, 15% and 18% and scaled by the Internal Loss Multiplier, where the Business Indicator is built from income statement and balance sheet items.
cards.explanation: The Business Indicator Component applies 12% up to EUR 1 billion, 15% from EUR 1 billion to 30 billion and 18% above EUR 30 billion, and capital equals the BIC multiplied by the Internal Loss Multiplier.
cards.originalText: The ORC is a percentage (i.e., 12\|15\|18% marginal coefficient) of the Business Indicator (BI) scaled by the Internal Loss Multiplier (ILM), where the BI is the sum of various income statement and/or balance sheet items

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: Under the Basel standardized approach, operational risk capital is the minimum of 2.25% of interest-earning assets and the absolute value of net interest income.
cards.explanation: That minimum is only the cap on the net interest term inside the interest, lease and dividend component of the Business Indicator. Capital is the Business Indicator Component multiplied by the Internal Loss Multiplier.
cards.originalText: The ORC is the minimum of either (i) 2.25% of interest‑earning assets or (ii) the absolute value of the net interest income

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: Under the Basel standardized approach, operational risk capital is a 12, 15 or 18 times multiple of the average annual losses incurred over the previous ten years.
cards.explanation: Losses enter only through the loss component of the Internal Loss Multiplier, which uses 15 times average annual loss over ten years. The 12%, 15% and 18% coefficients apply to the Business Indicator.
cards.originalText: The ORC is a multiple (i.e., 12x\|15x\|18x scalar multiplier) of the average annual losses incurred over the ten previous years

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: Under the Basel III standardized approach, a bank with a Business Indicator above EUR 1 billion must incorporate its own loss experience in the operational risk capital calculation.
cards.explanation: Banks with a Business Indicator above EUR 1 billion fall in bucket 2 or higher and use their own loss data through the Internal Loss Multiplier. Banks in bucket 1 have an ILM of 1.
cards.originalText: Bank B would be expected to use loss experience in the standardized approach calculations.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: The Business Indicator includes an administrative component covering insurance premiums paid or received, changes in goodwill and the maximum of staff expenses or outsourcing fees.
cards.explanation: The Business Indicator has exactly three components: the interest, leases and dividend component, the services component and the financial component. Administrative expenses are excluded.
cards.originalText: The administrative component (AC) includes insurance premiums paid/received, recognized changes in goodwill, and the maximum of (staff expenses; or outsourcing fees)

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: The financial component of the Business Indicator includes the net profit or loss on the trading book and the banking book.
cards.explanation: The financial component is the absolute value of net trading book P&L plus the absolute value of net banking book P&L, each averaged over three years.
cards.originalText: The financial component (FC) includes net profit/loss on the trading and banking books

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: The interest, leases and dividend component of the Business Indicator adds average dividend income to the minimum of average net interest income and a percentage of interest-earning assets.
cards.explanation: Net interest income is capped at 2.25% of interest-earning assets, and dividend income is then added.
cards.originalText: The interest, leases, and dividend component (ILDC) adds average dividend income to the minimum of (average net interest income; or a percentage of interest‑earning assets)

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: A bank first moving to the Basel III standardized approach for operational risk can use the loss component if it has at least five years of good-quality, reliable loss data.
cards.explanation: Ideally the loss component uses ten years of high-quality annual loss data, but as a transition a minimum of five years is allowed. The age of the bank is not the test.
cards.originalText: Yes, as the bank will be eligible as long as the loss data covering at least the last 5 years is deemed good quality and reliable.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: The financial component of the Business Indicator takes into account a bank's trading book and banking book P&L results.
cards.explanation: The financial component is the absolute value of net trading book P&L plus the absolute value of net banking book P&L.
cards.originalText: Financial component.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: The loss component is part of the Business Indicator calculation.
cards.explanation: The loss component is not part of the Business Indicator. It feeds the Internal Loss Multiplier and reflects the bank's internal operational losses.
cards.originalText: Loss component.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: Provisions and reversals of provisions related to operational loss events are included in the Business Indicator.
cards.explanation: Provisions and their reversals are excluded from the Business Indicator unless they relate to operational loss events, in which case they are captured in other operating income or expenses.
cards.originalText: Provision reversals related to operational loss events.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.topic: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
cards.reading: ORR-24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms
cards.statement: Administrative expenses, including staff and outsourcing costs, are included in the Business Indicator.
cards.explanation: Administrative expenses, insurance premiums paid and depreciation of tangible and intangible assets are excluded from the Business Indicator.
cards.originalText: Administrative expenses.
